L’épisode relaté par le patron de Nvidia illustre tout à la fois l’inclinaison du gouvernement à promouvoir sa start-up nationale, et la manière dont Mistral a pris appui sur l’exécutif pour se hisser auprès des plus grandes entreprises d’IA générative.

Lancée en 2023 par trois cofondateurs, Arthur Mensch, Guillaume Lample et Timothée Lacroix, Mistral AI a d’emblée fait un choix : miser sur un lien étroit avec l’exécutif français, et en particulier avec Emmanuel Macron. Interrogés par POLITICO, une douzaine de responsables publics et de représentants de l’écosystème technologique décrivent ainsi la construction d’une relation privilégiée, qui a permis à Mistral de se faire une place auprès de l’Etat et à la table des leaders internationaux de l’IA.

Or, à quelques mois de l’élection présidentielle et alors que l’Europe s’interroge sur sa capacité à défier les champions technologiques chinois et américains et à gagner en indépendance technologique, Mistral AI est face à un tournant. L’entreprise, qui compte désormais plus de 1000 salariés, doit maintenant se projeter dans l’après-Macron.

Bonnes fées et millions

Dès sa naissance et sa première levée de fonds en 2023, la start-up — qui n’a pas souhaité répondre à POLITICO dans le cadre de cet article — a fait le choix de se rapprocher du secteur public. Ainsi, Bpifrance, la banque publique d’investissement française, fait partie de ses premiers investisseurs. “Nous avions conscience des enjeux de souveraineté liés à l’IA, et avions une bonne idée des rares — quelques centaines dans le monde alors — experts crédibles dans le secteur, dont les fondateurs de Mistral faisaient partie”, se souvient Arnaud Caudoux, le directeur général adjoint de Bpifrance. “C’était un montant record pour un tour d’amorçage français, mais il y avait beaucoup de bonnes fées autour du berceau”.

Les bonnes fées en question sont le gratin du capitalisme et du secteur technologique français, qui ont joué des rôles essentiels d’entremetteurs, de mécènes et de leveurs de fonds. Parmi eux, le milliardaire Xavier Niel, mais aussi Jean-Charles Samuelian-Werve et Charles Gorintin, cofondateurs de la start-up spécialisée dans l’assurance Alan. En 2022, ils sont mus par un même objectif : contribuer à faire émerger un géant européen de l’intelligence artificielle. Ils ont ainsi activé leurs réseaux pour identifier les chercheurs français les plus prometteurs du secteur de l’IA.

Les trois cofondateurs de Mistral AI, Timothée Lacroix, Arthur Mensch et Guillaume Lample, à Paris le 28 mai 2026. | Stephane de Sakutin/AFP via Getty Images

Ce sont eux qui joueront les entremetteurs pour former le trio Arthur Mensch, Timothée Lacroix et Guillaume Lample. Au moment de “toper” avec les trois jeunes cofondateurs, l’équipe d’Alan obtient un ralliement stratégique pour tisser des liens avec le secteur public : Cédric O. L’ancien secrétaire d’Etat au Numérique, soutien d’Emmanuel Macron de la première heure, jouera un rôle majeur au moment du lancement de la start-up. C’est même lui qui montera au front à Bruxelles pour tenter d’obtenir des assouplissements sur le règlement européen sur l’IA (AI Act), présenté par la Commission européenne dès avril 2021.

Car, pour Mistral AI, ce texte est dangereux : comment bâtir un géant européen si l’Europe bride l’innovation ? Dès 2023, Cédric O se retrousse les manches et s’inscrit, au nom de Mistral, au registre de transparence de l’Union européenne afin de peser sur les négociations — au point même d’être soupçonné de conflit d’intérêts par certains parlementaires.





Ce nouveau venu s’attire rapidement les remontrances de Thierry Breton, alors commissaire européen : la start-up Mistral AI “fait du lobbying, c’est normal. Mais nous ne sommes dupes de rien. Elle défend son business aujourd’hui, et non, l’intérêt général”, critique Breton lors les dernières semaines de négociations autour de l’AI Act.

“Le rôle de Cédric O a en quelque sorte été celui d’un paratonnerre”, reconnaît un responsable du secteur privé qui a suivi les débuts de Mistral. En prenant les coups, O a permis à Mensch “de grandir et de se construire en tant que PDG”, poursuit-il.

Dans les coulisses

Dès ses débuts, Mistral joue la carte française et européenne. Les trois cofondateurs ont beau avoir fait carrière dans les laboratoires d’intelligence artificielle américains (Google Deepmind pour Mensch, Facebook AI pour Guillaume Lample et Timothée Lacroix), les premières notes de concept, élaborées pour le lancement de la start-up, placent l’enjeu de la souveraineté technologique au cœur du projet.

A l’époque, Mensch est un discret ingénieur de trente ans qui doit entamer sa mue pour porter le discours de Mistral AI sur la scène internationale. En juin 2023, quelques mois après le lancement de sa start-up, l’ancien élève de Polytechnique fait sa première apparition publique aux côtés d’Emmanuel Macron sur la grande scène du salon technologique VivaTech, et commence à développer son discours sur l’autonomie technologique européenne. De quoi séduire le président français, qui en a fait l’une de ses martingales. “Comment la France et l’Europe envisagent de permettre l’émergence de champions européens et comment faire en sorte que la régulation de l’IA ne vienne pas gêner l’innovation ?” interroge alors le jeune entrepreneur, en chemise et baskets, face au président français.

Mensch sera chargé de contribuer lui-même aux réponses. Quelques mois plus tard, Matignon décide de former un comité d’experts pour établir une stratégie française pour l’IA. Outre Mensch et Cédric O, il sera composé de Gaël Varoquaux, chercheur à l’Inria et ancien directeur de thèse de Mensch, mais aussi du futur prix Nobel d’économie Philippe Aghion, et du chercheur chez Meta Yann LeCun.

En 2024, alors que le comité rend son rapport et que Mistral AI présente “Le Chat”, le concurrent du modèle d’Open AI ChatGPT, le paysage de l’IA est déjà en pleine mutation. Et l’Europe doute : le concurrent allemand Aleph Alpha, l’autre espoir européen de l’IA générative, annonce se détourner du développement de modèles propres. Avec un constat pessimiste : “le simple fait de disposer d’un LLM européen ne suffit pas comme modèle économique. Cela ne justifie pas l’investissement”, explique son patron, Jonas Andrulis. L’annonce plombe les espoirs européens de développer des modèles souverains.

Les doutes n’épargnent pas Mistral, et les observateurs sont nombreux à redouter un décrochage technologique par rapport à ses concurrents américains ou chinois — au point de craindre que la start-up soit rachetée par un géant de la tech. En 2025, des rumeurs d’échanges avec Apple, éventées par la presse, créent un vent de panique au sommet de l’Etat. L’ambassade française aux Etats-Unis et l’Elysée s’enquièrent auprès de Mistral de la réalité de ces échanges, selon deux conseillers sollicités par POLITICO. Ils sont finalement rassurés par l’entreprise : il n’y a pas eu d’échanges “au plus haut niveau”.

Partenaire stratégique

Pour l’exécutif, l’enjeu n’est plus seulement de promouvoir une jeune pousse prometteuse. L’Etat est désormais prêt à pousser les murs pour préserver une entreprise dont les technologies sont progressivement intégrées à tous les niveaux de l’Etat. Après avoir signé un partenariat stratégique avec France Travail début 2025, Mistral AI a en effet décroché un accord-cadre avec le ministère des Armées pour le développement de l’IA dans la défense.





Depuis 2025, “Le Chat” est aussi en cours de déploiement auprès de 10 000 agents publics. Pour adouber Mistral AI, le ministère de l’Action publique a dû se contorsionner. D’une part, car la direction interministérielle du numérique (Dinum) “voyait d’un très mauvais œil de recourir à une solution venue du privée”, indique un responsable ministériel qui a répondu anonymement pour évoquer des négociations internes à l’Etat. D’autre part, parce que la commande publique est soumise à des règles strictes d’ouverture à la concurrence, qui ne sont pas censées permettre de favoriser un acteur plutôt qu’un autre, même si celui-ci est français.

“Nous avons perdu quelques semaines car il fallait border juridiquement le process”, précise le responsable cité plus haut. “L’expérimentation d’outils est généralement une manière de permettre aux entreprises de mettre un pied dans la porte”, glisse un ancien conseiller gouvernemental.

À la table des grands

Si Mensch a tendance à minimiser l’importance des subventions publiques et du soutien des autorités à son entreprise, les équipes de Mistral reconnaissent volontiers que cette relation privilégiée est un atout majeur.

Avec l’aide de l’exécutif, l’entreprise française a pu décrocher plusieurs partenariats clés, dont un accord avec le géant néerlandais des semi-conducteurs ASML, en 2025. Bruno Le Maire, ministre de l’Economie durant sept ans avant de devenir conseiller stratégique d’ASML, a d’ailleurs été l’une des chevilles ouvrières de ce rapprochement. A la fin de la même année, Emmanuel Macron était à Berlin pour officialiser un accord avec un autre acteur européen du numérique : l’entreprise allemande spécialiste du logiciel SAP.

Mensch et le président français Emmanuel Macron, en arrière-plan, après la signature d’un accord avec des dirigeants de Samsung au palais de l’Élysée, le 8 septembre 2026. | Pool photo par Gonzalo Fuentes via Getty Images

Cette proximité avec l’Elysée permet aussi à Mistral de pousser les portes des plus grands sommets internationaux. Elle a même eu une place de choix au sommet français sur l’IA, organisé à Paris début 2025. Pour l’occasion, l’Elysée a réservé le Grand Palais, ce dôme de verre bâti au cœur de la capitale pour l’Exposition universelle de 1900. Un lieu exceptionnel sur lequel Mistral AI a un temps envisagé de placer un logo géant — un “M” rouge et jaune pixellisé. Une idée finalement écartée “pour des raisons de sécurité”, s’amuse un ancien responsable public au fait des préparatifs.

Peu à peu, Mensch a donc pris ses habitudes dans les protocoles élyséens. Il est désormais de tous les déplacements présidentiels à l’étranger — ou presque. En décembre 2025, l’Elysée met presque par automatisme son nom dans la liste des chefs d’entreprises de la délégation d’Emmanuel Macron pour Pékin. Erreur : Mensch ne va pas en Chine. Un tel déplacement chez l’adversaire commercial des Etats-Unis pourrait mettre Mistral AI en délicatesse vis-à-vis des Américains, où l’entreprise compte un grand nombre d’investisseurs et de partenaires.

Ces déplacements officiels sont autant d’occasions, pour Mensch, d’affuter et d’internationaliser le contre-discours qu’il oppose à la Silicon Valley sur l’IA. Depuis plusieurs mois, le patron de Mistral AI, qui s’approprie volontiers la devise de Polytechnique (“Pour la Patrie, les Sciences et la Gloire”), martèle une position alignée sur celle d’Emmanuel Macron : il faut promouvoir l’autonomie technologique en Europe, et proposer au reste du monde un modèle plus sensible aux subtilités culturelles et linguistiques.





En février 2026, sur la scène du sommet de New Delhi où se sont pressés Dario Amodei (Anthropic), Demis Hassabis (Google Deepmind) et Sam Altman (OpenAI), Mensch poursuit sa croisade, défendant l’IA comme “un outil d’autonomisation, et non de domination”. “Je souhaite aborder un sujet un peu plus fondamental, à savoir : qui contrôle le déploiement de l’IA, qui en tire profit et comment pouvons-nous nous assurer qu’elle serve l’intérêt du plus grand nombre et non celui d’une minorité ?”, interroge-t-il.

Rebelote en juin, à Evian-les-Bains : lors d’un déjeuner avec les leaders du G7, Mensch endosse à nouveau le rôle du franc-tireur face à ses concurrents américains, qui appelaient à la rédaction de standards technologiques sous l’égide des Etats-Unis.“Les acteurs américains ont tendance à porter ce discours-là : faites-nous confiance, on va établir des standards chez nous et on vous les exportera”, mettait-il en garde auprès de POLITICO à l’issue de cette rencontre réunissant Donald Trump, Ursula von der Leyen ou encore Sam Altman.

Un consensus politique ?

Si Mistral compte indéniablement sur la scène internationale, reste à savoir ce que l’entreprise peut promettre : alors qu’elle a mis un pied dans les infrastructures en construisant des datacenters, et qu’elle poursuit le déploiement de ses solutions dans les grandes entreprises, certains commencent à douter que l’entreprise puisse rester dans la course pour produire des modèles “de frontière”, c’est-à-dire les plus performants.

Pour Emmanuel Macron, le dernier G7 a en tout cas été l’une des dernières opportunités d’imprimer sa marque dans le débat mondial sur l’IA. Et de permettre à Mistral de préparer l’après. Car la relation avec le futur locataire de l’Elysée reste à construire.

Macron prend un selfie avec de jeunes entrepreneurs français de la tech, dont Mensch, à Paris le 11 février 2025. | Amaury Cornu/AFP via Getty Images

A ce stade, aucun candidat à l’élection présidentielle n’a remis en question le soutien public à la start-up. Certains se montrent toutefois plus allants, à l’instar de Gabriel Attal, qui met volontiers en scène sa proximité avec Mistral. Le candidat Renaissance a ainsi placé l’intelligence artificielle au cœur de son programme de campagne, et même intégré Le Chat dans sa boîte à outils de communication. Son concurrent Edouard Philippe (Horizons) fait de même, appuyé par ses lieutenants — la ministre de l’IA et du Numérique Anne Le Hénanff ou encore le député Laurent Marcangeli — qui assurent Mensch de leur soutien. Si Mistral ne s’affiche pas publiquement auprès du RN, le parti à la flamme voit lui aussi l’entreprise comme un atout souverain.

À gauche, personne n’a encore pris officiellement position, mais les partis ont unanimement soutenu l’entreprise — et appelé à une IA souveraine — face au risque de blocage de modèles américains illustré par Mythos, d’Anthropic, que Donald Trump a souhaité restreindre aux utilisateurs américains en juin dernier.





Mistral n’est toutefois pas pleinement souveraine : elle s’appuie, rappelons-le, sur des fonds internationaux et des partenariats d’ampleur avec les géants américains — Amazon, Nvidia ou encore Microsoft. “Il faut tuer cette idée, très café du commerce, qu’il serait faisable de détenir le capital, et donc financer seuls à l’échelle française ou européenne ces centaines de milliards qu’exigent les infrastructures IA. C’est juste impossible”, souligne le Secrétaire général pour l’investissement rattaché à Matignon, Bruno Bonnell.

Un détail qui pourrait mettre à mal l’unanimisme français en faveur de Mistral, alors que l’IA s’invite peu à peu dans les thèmes forts de la campagne.

Le front a d’ailleurs déjà commencé à se fissurer avec la proposition de loi de la sénatrice LR Laure Darcos, qui entend forcer les géants de l’IA à rémunérer le secteur culturel — un texte soutenu par la gauche et une partie de la droite, mais vivement rejeté par Mistral qui a finalement obtenu le soutien du bloc central et du gouvernement.

Macron, le PDG de DeepMind Technologies Demis Hassabis et Mensch à Londres, le 9 juillet 2025. | Pool photo by Ludovic Marin via Getty Images

Autre caillou dans la chaussure de Mistral : un rapport parlementaire de juillet dernier, piloté par les députés Philippe Latombe (Modem) et Cyrille Chatelain (Ecologistes), estime que l’entreprise est devenue trop stratégique. Les deux élus proposent donc d’instaurer une “golden share” étatique au capital de la start-up pour éviter qu’elle ne soit vendue sans droit de regard de l’État.

Couvée dès sa naissance par le chef de l’Etat, Mistral voit donc la page de la macronie sur le point de se tourner, sans savoir exactement comment s’écrira la suivante. Ni sur quels alliés politiques elle pourra compter à partir de mai prochain.

World.title: 'Sickening' racist remarks and calls for a coup: French police under investigation
World.content:
Six hours of footage and a torrent of racist, misogynistic and conspiratorial remarks. The local newspaper Midi Libre has published video from a night-time patrol by Carcassonne's municipal police, recorded on 6 November 2025.

 

Captured inadvertently by one officer's body camera, which they thought was switched off, it contains, according to the daily, comments described as "of exceptional violence".

According to Midi Libre, a preliminary investigation has been under way since January 2026, when the footage is said to have been passed to the Carcassonne public prosecutor's office.

Following the video's publication by the newspaper, the prosecutor's office confirmed to AFP that it had already opened an investigation, without specifying when.

'These wogs drive fast'

The evening is quiet: the municipal police officers are called out to just one incident. But inside their vehicle, the remarks keep coming. From inside the police car, one of the officers insults a passer-by, calling him a "wog who stinks of kebab". On two occasions, Black people are also compared to "monkeys".

Between remarks targeting foreigners and non-white French people, the patrol also discusses women: "Back in the days of the caves, those stupid bitches, if they weren't with their bloke, they'd get bumped off outside," and about politics: "We've been eaten alive, we let everyone in, we've had 40 years of crap from the left, lefty scum."

Beyond the racist remarks, the officers' exchanges also feature rhetoric commonly associated with far-right circles, according to Midi Libre, particularly from the patrol leader. He expresses concern about what he describes as a "civilisational replacement": "We became Christian under Clovis; we're going to become Muslim under Macron," he says.

Towards the end of their shift, the team even discusses a coup, with one officer expressing surprise that it has not already happened. "What we're missing is a general with some real balls. A little coup, a little dictatorship in France wouldn't do any harm," another says.

The patrol leader also admits to having found a weapon for someone close to him.

Officers suspended over remarks

In response to the controversy, Carcassonne city council initially issued a statement describing the remarks in the video as "unacceptable" and blaming the previous municipal administration's management of the police service. A few hours later, the mayor described the remarks as "sickening" and told reporters that "all those involved have been suspended".

Later in the evening, the Carcassonne public prosecutor's office issued a statement confirming that the municipal police officers involved had been suspended and their authorisations withdrawn, saying they "no longer meet the standards of integrity required for their duties".

A member of the RN's security team

The patrol leader, identified by the initials C.R. in Midi Libre's investigation, was responsible for nearly 90% of the hateful remarks made during the evening.

The 50-year-old is a former paratrooper and reportedly volunteered with the Protection and Security Department, the internal security service of France's far-right National Rally (RN). According to Midi Libre, "no declaration of additional activity was filed with Carcassonne city hall".

After the videos were circulated internally in late 2025, the officer was on sick leave between January and March 2026. On 16 March, the day after the victory of Christophe Barthès, Carcassonne's newly elected RN mayor, C.R. returned to the night shift. No disciplinary action had been taken against him at that point.

Potentially severe disciplinary sanctions

According to Benjamin Cottet-Emard, a lawyer with the Lyon Bar, insults of this kind do not constitute a criminal offence when they are not made publicly, for example in the media. Instead, they are considered a fifth-class offence, punishable by a fine of up to €1,500.

However, "non-public racist insults constitute, for a public official, a disciplinary offence separate from any criminal classification" and can result in permanent dismissal from public service, the lawyer told Euronews.

He said the remarks that emerged were "clearly unworthy of a public official and seriously undermine human dignity".

"The Council of State has already ruled that remarks made by a police officer in a WhatsApp group, including 'racist and discriminatory remarks on four occasions', as well as his failure to condemn 'racist, antisemitic and sexist messages shared by his colleagues', justified dismissal," he added.

Given the "repeated and particularly serious" nature of the conduct revealed by Midi Libre, Cottet-Emard concluded that it "should logically lead to the same sanction".

World.title: France co-hosts major space summit with Germany despite US firms' withdrawals and Merz absence
World.content:
Astronauts, heads of state, as well as major economic players in the space industry united in Paris on Wednesday for the international space summit, co-hosted by France and Germany, at Paris’ Grand Palais.

 

On Wednesday afternoon, French President Emmanuel Macron announced that more than 50 projects are expected to be signed over the course of the two-day event, stressing the need to "strengthen the European and space research", but also to deepen partnerships with other countries around the world.

Alongside Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, he also welcomed the European Space Agency’s (ESA) next private astronaut mission, PAM-6, to the International Space Station (ISS), scheduled for 2027 — which will mark the first ever journey to space by a Greek astronaut, Adrianos Golemis.

Taking to X Wednesday evening, he also hailed a major deal signed between Amazon Leo and Arianespace, stating that “Amazon Leo is renewing its trust in Arianespace with 6 additional launches, 24 in total."

Ahead of the summit, several US companies reportedly withdrew from the event, due to pressure from Washington over support for "EU policy positions."

Challenging US dominance

Despite this, the summit comes at a strategic crossroads for the European space industry, described by President Emmanuel Macron as an opportunity to "bring Europeans together around a common ambition" and develop a "shared vision of Europe's place on the map of global space powers by 2035" when he announced the event in October 2025.

According to the Elysée, the summit will focus on international space cooperation and strengthening space security. In recent years, Europe has increasingly sought to challenge US dominance of the global space market: developing its own homegrown rockets and increasing funding for space at both a state and bloc-wide level.

Europe has historically invested 0.07% of GDP into space programmes, compared with 0.24% by the US.

But 2025 marked a turning point, as the European Space Agency (ESA) approved a record-breaking €22.3 billion budget for its three-year funding cycle (2026–2028) in November, with €35 billion for space for security and defence.

Lunar mining has also emerged as a potential avenue for securing clean-energy resources and critical raw materials, as Europe works to move away from Chinese and Russian dependencies.

Divergence between France and Germany

Nearly a year after Macron announced the summit, it encountered some bumps in the road before the event had even begun. Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz confirmed on Friday that he would not attend the summit due to domestic commitments, with defence minister Boris Pistorius and space minister Dorothee Bär set to go in his place.

Behind the scenes, France and Germany have faced a number of disagreements over space and defence projects, ditching the Future Combat Air System (FCAS) project in June 2026, after years of disagreements.

Macron has consistently stressed the importance of building up Europe's strategic autonomy, backing programs like Ariane 6, rather than relying on US providers such as Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

Meanwhile, Germany has expressed a greater willingness to rely on lower-cost US alternatives, such as SpaceX. On Saturday, German startup Isar Aerospace launched the first commercial rocket to reach orbit from mainland Europe, marking a major turning point in Europe's quest to secure independent access to space. Merz described the launch as “the beginning of a new era.”

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks during the general debate as part of the budget deliberations in the Bundestag in Berlin, 9 September, 2026 AP Photo

US companies withdraw from event

A number of US companies also withdrew from the event, after a White House official reportedly warned them that their attendance "could look like tacit support for EU policy positions," Politico reported.

A spokesperson for France's Ministry of Higher Education and Research, which oversees national space policy, told the AFP news agency that SpaceX, Blue Origin, Stoke Space, and Starcloud had withdrawn from the event, stating "it’s hard not to link it to the rumours of pressure in the press.”

Speaking to Euronews, Hermann Ludwig Moeller, Director of the European Space Policy Institute described France as a "driving force" in Europe's space sector, providing "strong political support" to the industry, stressing that the "relevance of space is only increasing."

A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket with the space observatory Roman Telescope lifts off from launch the Kennedy Space Centre, 30 August, 2026 AP Photo

"It is increasingly becoming a war fighting domain, while at the same time it has become evident also to the general public that conflict has become hybrid in nature, for instance through attacks on critical infrastructures in transport, energy, digital. This is where space can provide increased resilience."

Moeller stressed the role that space technologies such as satellite navigation have in terms of both civilian and military usage.

"While they are essential to everyday life, the war in Ukraine has also highlighted their strategic importance in modern warfare", he said.

Kyiv's reliance on Musk's Starlink following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has underlined the strategic importance of space services during wartime — that the satellite network provides resilient internet connectivity even when infrastructure is damaged or destroyed.

This reality also pushed Europe to develop its own independent satellite networks, notably the secure internet constellation known as IRIS².

World.title: European Commission proposes EU preference in public procurement, excluding Chinese firms
World.content:
The European Commission unveiled on Wednesday a legislative proposal allowing EU public authorities to favour European companies in public procurement for key public services such as energy, water, railways, ports, airports and postal services.

 

The move comes as European policymakers seek to shield the bloc’s market from China amid heated trade negotiations, as the EU grapples with a trade deficit with Beijing of roughly €1 billion a day.

Public procurement markets in Europe represent €2 trillion every year — 15% of Europe’s GDP.

“Public money must serve our collective interests,” Commission Vice-President Stéphane Séjourné said on Wednesday. “A public buyer will be able to organise his European preference and to exclude operators coming from countries with which we do not agree on public markets, both on the basis of the nationality of the company or on the base of the origin of the products.”

Under the Commission’s proposal, EU public authorities will be able to exclude non-European companies from public contracts when they come from countries that do not allow Europeans access to their own public procurement markets.

“A municipality will be very clearly able to exclude a Chinese company or a European company that offers Chinese products,” Séjourné added. “It will also be able to give more points and more visibility in his offer to European offers compared to competition offers.”

Swift reaction from China

The Commission proposes that at least 30% of the evaluation of supplies for public procurement rely on quality criteria and not only on price, which will also hit low-cost Chinese products.

“The new standard is the best quality-price ratio, and not just the price,” Séjourné said. “Our choices must also be able to meet social and environmental demands, but also sovereignty.”

The legislation, which still has to be adopted by the EU co-legislators — the European Parliament and the EU Council — prompted a swift reaction from China. In a statement released after the commission’s announcement, China’s Chamber of Commerce to the EU said that such a European preference could “distort a level playing field” for Chinese companies participating in the European public procurement market.

“Public procurement should not discriminate against suppliers or goods on the basis of the supplier’s nationality or the country of origin of the goods.”

In March, another proposal creating a European preference in EU strategic sectors such as green tech, cars and energy-intensive industries also prompted Chinese ire, with Beijing threatening to retaliate.

EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič will travel to China in early October, hoping to reach a political deal with Beijing to rebalance the trade relationship with the EU.

World.title: ‘Migration is very much back on the agenda,' EU diplomat forewarns
World.content:
I am travelling to Latvia for a work trip centred on three d’s: drones, defence and debesmanna. Squeezing in time to the Rīga Conference and other sites relevant to the country’s upcoming EU council presidency is a must, too.

 

Meanwhile, my colleagues in Brussels are holding down the fort, where one topic is stealing the spotlight. “Migration is very much back on the agenda,” one senior EU diplomat said to a crowd of journalists chewing on hors d'oeuvres Monday night at a rentrée party.

What is clear is the migration horse certainly has bolted, with no signs of abating, and the Ceuta crisis – of 80,000 migrants storming the Spanish enclave in July from Morocco – is the new springboard into the debate.

Taking the scenic route: Mared Gwyn reports that Ceuta’s leader, Juan Jesús Vivas, was in Brussels on Tuesday to call on the EU’s senior leadership. He requested a permanent presence from the EU’s border agency Frontex and the EU’s asylum agency and financial contributions to the work of securing the border with Morocco.

But crucially he also asked for a firmer and more forceful EU position towards Morocco, citing leaked police reports claiming Moroccan officers helped orchestrate the crossing. His stance is significantly sharper than the Spanish government’s strategy of cooperation with Rabat, with my colleague Vincenzo Genovese diving deeper into the crisis.

Spain’s former foreign minister Arancha González Laya just told Europe Today that this incident should be characterised as a "hybrid attack" with migration as the weapon. Watch.

Meet and greet: Vincenzo also reports that European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will meet the leaders of the European Parliament’s political groups today, who are set to convey to her their priorities for the State of the Union speech next week. This is the EU chief’s annual address, laying out her priorities for the next 12 months.

Cloak and dagger: The Hungarian government on Tuesday ordered 10 Russian diplomats to leave the country for committing “unacceptable activities”, according to the country’s foreign minister Anita Orbán. “This does not mean the severance of diplomatic relations with Russia,” she said. “Hungary intends to continue the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and compliance with the rules.” Moscow has reportedly vowed a “harsh and painful” response.

But the plot thickens, with Romania suffering from its own espionage scandal. A Russian national believed to be involved in a foiled sabotage operation was arrested on Tuesday. According to reporting by Euronews Romania, the individual stands accused of taking photos and filming military installations across the country, as well as North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) bases.

Getting Fico on board: EU ambassadors will try — again — to secure Slovakia’s blessing to renew the sanctions on almost 3,000 individuals and companies accused of propping up Russia’s war on Ukraine, Jorge Liboreiro writes.

Envoys want to prolong the sanctions for 12 months, rather than the traditional six, to align with the economic sanctions, which EU leaders agreed to extend for 12 months in mid-June. The 12-month frame is meant to reinforce the regime’s predictability and shield it from unpleasant surprises. But Slovakia has slapped a veto and demands that Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, two oligarchs accused of having close ties to the Kremlin, be removed from the blacklist.

Diplomats don’t expect a resolution today. However, a bilateral meeting on Thursday between Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico and Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, whose country holds the EU Council’s rotating presidency, could pave the way for a deal. The clock is ticking, though: the individual sanctions are set to expire on 15 September.

Locking horns: Several European countries and allies — Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and the UK — yesterday called on Israel to implement the two-state solution. More importantly, however, they supported restrictions on trade with illegal Israeli ⁠settlements in the occupied West Bank.

“France will end trade with Israeli settlements located in the Occupied Palestinian Territories, alongside eleven other countries that have made similar commitments,” foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot clarified in an online statement.

“Why? Because the West Bank is on the brink of explosion: unchecked expansion of colonization in violation of international law, surge in violence perpetrated by extremist settlers against Palestinians, acts of terror denounced by the Israeli authorities themselves.”

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband went one step further by accusing “settler terrorists” of “ethnic cleansing” in the area, serving as the UK government’s strongest condemnation of the matter.

Tit for tat: Israel has responded with its own measures, with the country’s foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar — who suffers from soured relations with the EU’s own top diplomat Kaja Kallas — announcing the closure of the British Consulate in Jerusalem and banning a dozen British nationals from entering the country.

“The accusations made today by the Foreign Secretary of the Labour Government in the British Parliament were outrageous lies,” Sa’ar said, referring to the British foreign secretary’s comments.

Brussels blacklist: A journalist asked the EU executive on Tuesday whether it was considering reviving sanctions against Israel in line with the uptick in settler violence in the occupied West Bank. European Commission spokesperson Anouar El Anouni said that settlements under international law are illegal and Brussels’ position is “long standing and extremely clear”.

A total of 12 individuals and nine entities as part of the extremist settler camp have been sanctioned by the EU, with “additional proposals” discussed among those at the European Council, he said.

One final thing: My colleague Eleonora Vasques reports that the European Commission will today present its plan for affordable housing. Will it include targeted measures against the likes of short-stay accommodation platform Airbnb? All will be revealed at a press conference today.

The Russian exception: Why Moscow still has a role in Europe’s ITER fusion project despite EU sanctions

The European Union and Russia are geopolitical adversaries, with Russia under sweeping EU sanctions and its ties with the bloc severely curtailed. Yet inside one of the largest international scientific collaborations in history — and the world’s largest nuclear fusion experiment — the two remain linked by a partnership forged decades ago and built to endure for generations.

While Brussels steps up pressure on Moscow over its war in Ukraine and hybrid attacks, Russian engineers and their European counterparts continue to work together on an international project called the “International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor” (ITER), an experimental nuclear fusion machine that seeks to harness the fusion of hydrogen nuclei to generate vast amounts of energy.

Last Monday, the EU’s Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen visited ITER in Cadarache, France, calling the fusion device “key for our decarbonisation and energy independence goals.”

So, what does it all mean? Marta Pacheco and Maïa de la Baume break it down in this must-read piece.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he expects to meet Donald Trump later this month as Kyiv presses Washington for urgently needed Patriot interceptors and moves towards a new trilateral negotiating format. Read more.

Exclusive: Italy proposes no fees for digital euro payments under €10

Italy suggests exempting smaller merchant fees for payments under €10, a measure backed by the central banking community, as final talks take place in Brussels over the rollout of the digital euro. Eleonora has the details.

We're also keeping an eye on

European Commissioner for Defence Andrius Kubilius delivers a speech at the International Space Summit in Paris, France.

European Commissioner for the Budget Piotr Serafin visits a range of high-level officials in the Japanese capital including Japanese Minister of Finance, Satsuki Katayama.

That’s it for today. Mared Gwyn, Vincenzo Genovese, Jorge Liboreiro, Eleonora Vasques contributed to this newsletter.

World.title: Ceuta mass migration crisis tests European solidarity - MEPs clash in The Ring
World.content:
The same week that Ceuta’s president, Juan Jesús Vivas, travelled to Brussels in a cry for help, we are joined by Czech centre-right MEP Tomáš Svetechovský and German Socialist MEP Birgit Sippel for their points of view. One month on from the arrival of thousands of irregular migrants in the Spanish city, we hear how EU countries could have shown more solidarity and what more can be done to help Ceuta.

 

Tomáš Svetechovský criticised the Spanish government’s handling of the situation, arguing that it should have acted sooner and requested more European support.

“I think that the Spanish government did not react to the situation very well,” he said, calling for additional police and security support.

German Socialist MEP Birgit Sippel defended Spain’s response and said the priority should be European solidarity.

“Whenever things like that are happening to whatever country, the first thing that we have to do is show solidarity,” she said.

The two MEPs also disagreed over the treatment of unaccompanied minors remaining in Ceuta. Sippel stressed the need to relocate children to other EU member states under the EU migration pact, while Svetechovský rejected mandatory relocation quotas and said the Czech Republic would not be welcoming anyone from Ceuta.

“We are absolutely strict against these quotas,” he insisted.

The role of Morocco remains another point of debate. Some have accused Rabat of allowing the crossings to happen and during his trip to the EU capital, Juan Jesus Vivas said he believes the Ceuta incident should prompt Brussels to reconsider its collaboration with Rabat.

Watching The Ring in the player above and reach out to us at: thering@euronews.com

The Ring is hosted by Méabh Mc Mahon, produced by Luis Albertos Altarejos and Amaia Echevarria, and edited by Vassilis Glynos.

World.title: Spain endures 61 days of heatwave and records its hottest summer on record
World.content:
Spain has surpassed the dreaded and much-remembered summer of 2022 in terms of the number of days endured under a heatwave: 61, according to the State Meteorological Agency, 20 more than in that year. The summer of 2026 has also recorded an average temperature of 24.5°C, making it the hottest in the historical series since records began in 1961 and surpassing last year, 2025, by 0.3°C, and 2.4°C above the long-term average.

 

Aemet recalls that the ten hottest summers in the historical record have all occurred in the 21st century, and seven of the eight warmest have taken place since 2015. The agency also warns that the meteorological summer keeps getting longer.

"At the end of May, temperatures typical of July were recorded across large areas of the country. And then, in September, already in the meteorological autumn, there was another heatwave which, provisionally, ran from the 2nd to the 7th, lasting six days and affecting 16 provinces." Only in four other years has a month of September (1987, 1988, 2006 and 2016) seen such extreme heatwaves, more typical of the height of summer.

The heavy winter rains have meant that Spanish reservoirs have remained in very good condition after the summer season, with an average level of 62.58% despite tourist pressure, and above half of their capacity in basins that are usually under stress, such as the Júcar, Segura, Andalusian Mediterranean and Catalan catchments.

Even so, this has not spared the country from suffering, as in the rest of Europe, large-scale fires that have exposed the lack of forest fire prevention and of sufficient personnel with good working conditions, in regions such as Madrid, Aragón or Castilla y León.

World.title: Finland: Google announces €13 billion AI, energy investment
World.content:
Google has announced a plan to expand AI data centers and buy massive amounts of nuclear energy. Finland's security services have warned of there are risks, but the right-wing government says the deal will bring jobs.

US tech company Google on Wednesday announced that it would be investing €13 billion ($15.1 billion) in AI infrastructure in Finland as well as penning a massive deal to buy nuclear power in the Nordic country over the next two decades.

This year, Google parent company Alphabet increased global investment to around $200 billion as it rushes to catch up in the AI race. Wednesday's announced deal is Google's biggest single investment in the EU to date.

Since repurposing a former paper mill in the coastal city of Hamina in 2009 and transforming it into a data center, Google has steadily increased its presence in the country.

The northern location offers two advantages, cold Arctic temperatures mean it needs less energy to cool energy hungry servers and the fact that Finland only has 6 million residents would seem to provide relief from the growing resistance that such projects are running up against in the US and elsewhere.

Google is not alone in looking to chilly Finland with its cheap nuclear, wind and hydroelectric energy supply to expand its business — Microsoft and TikTok parent ByteDance have also set up shop — with dozens of data centers being built in the country over the past few years.

Attracting data center investment has been a priority for Finland's right-wing Prime Minister Petteri Orpo as the nation confronts record unemployment and slow economic growth.

Why communities are fighting AI data centers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Google makes big claims about boosting Finnish GDP and creating jobs

In a statement, Google said the investment, scheduled to be doled out in 2027 and 2028, will include data centers, electrical grid improvement, and clean energy and battery projects for its chatbot, search and map services.

The company claims the investment will pump some €3.6 billion into Finland's GDP and create 37,000 jobs, with 7,000 being permanent and others coming during the construction phase.

Prime Minister Petteri Orpo echoed Google's rosy outlook for his country's economy, emphasizing that it would spur further investment while downplaying fears that Google's project could drive up energy prices and gobble up resources."This investment is historical in Finland," said Orpo. "This makes us a front-runner in digitalization and AI."

Orpo said Google is, "committed to ensuring that electricity production in Finland ⁠remains sufficient and that prices remain under ​control."

The tax-avoiding US company said the deal was, "a testament to Finland's leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure."

"Now we are building more in Hamina, expanding that site on a remarkable level, and we are opening up data center operations in three new locations in the municipalities of Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala," said Antti Jarvinen, the company's director of operations for Finland.

Resources under pressure To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Beyond skyrocketing energy consumption, Finland's data center boom presents a potential security risk

Wednesday's deal also includes a purchase agreement for 50% of energy output from one of Finland's two nuclear power plants for the next 22 years according to plant operator Fortum, which will team up with the tech giant to explore new nuclear and renewable projects in the country.

Fortum shares jumped 15.5% on news of the deal, pushing them to their highest level in over four years and making the company the biggest winner on European stock exchanges for the day.

"We call this BYOP — bring your own power," ‌said Google President and ​Chief Investment Officer Ruth Porat, who noted, "This is Google's first nuclear energy deal outside of the United States."

Fortum said the deal would allow it to "continue operating the Loviisa Nuclear Power Plant until the end of its operating licenses in 2050," adding that without it, the plant, which currently supplies about 10% of Finland's electricity, would not have been able to continue operations past 2030.

Overall, Finland's data center boom is expected to create a massive spike in energy consumption, with network operator Fingrid forecasting a 40% jump over the coming years.

Beyond the environmental and energy concerns raised by such deals, Finland's Security and Intelligence Service (SUPO) has also issued explicit warnings that foreign-owned data centers pose potential security risks for the Nordic nation.

SUPO is concerned that municipalities may be weighing the economic potential of data centers more heavily than the security risk associated with them, noting that despite data center investments being fundamentally good for Finland there may be concerns if their owners are linked to authoritarian countries like Russia or China.

SUPO says authoritarian states may, for instance, try to use Finland to circumvent restrictions and sanctions on technology exports. For example, for advanced chips currently banned from export to China.

World.title: Norway's PM: Zelenskyy's plane almost hit by drone
World.content:
A drone nearly struck a plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Oslo, according to Norway's prime minister. However, a Ukrainian source said the threat may have been overstated.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said on Wednesday that a plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Oslo for the funeral of Norway's recently deceased King Harald V was almost hit by a drone.

"His flight was almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova. That is the reality he lives in," Store told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK, adding that Zelenskyy had left Norway for Canada, where he would meet with leaders in Ottawa.

Store provided no further details about the incident, which reportedly happened on Tuesday, as Zelenskyy was en route from Moldova to Norway.

Moldova's government spokesperson said later on Wednesday that the flight was delayed when the country's airspace was closed over a drone alert. The spokesperson said in a statement that Zelenskyy's plane was able to depart after a Russian drone came down on Moldovan territory.

The Ukrainian president arrived in Oslo on Tuesday evening. In the Norwegian capital, he held talks with Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide and Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg regarding military aid, including air-defense support, as well as civilian assistance.

On Wednesday, Zelenskyy then joined other foreign dignitaries at the funeral of King Harald.

At the funeral of the Norwegian King Harald V, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (center) was joined by other leaders Image: Dylan Martinez/REUTERS

Russian drone in Moldova

Meanwhile, neither Ukrainian authorities nor Zelenskyy himself have commented on the drone incident.

A claim that Zelenskyy was at risk was described as "exaggerated" by the source.

According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) — a US think tank — a Russian drone flew in Moldovan and Romanian airspace for about an hour on Tuesday.

The ISW said the defense ministries of Moldova and Romania both reported that a Shahed drone entered Moldovan airspace from Ukraine, flew over Romania, and then returned to Moldova, where it crashed.

However, it is unclear whether this was the same drone mentioned by Store and the Moldovan government spokesperson.

World.title: China: English to be removed as a graded core subject?
World.content:
A university professor is calling for English to no longer be taught as a graded core subject in Chinese schools. Opponents argue that, in a globalized world, knowing English is beneficial for the country and career.

From business and academia to social media and entertainment — English is considered the dominant global language. One in five people on Earth actively uses this lingua franca. In China, a mathematics professor specializing in vector algebra is now challenging this dominance in no uncertain terms. Tang Jiafeng believes that English should be abolished as a core subject in elementary schools, secondary schools and universities.

Tang is convinced that no other country in the world has placed as much importance on English as China has.

"Our children desperately begin learning English even before they have properly mastered their native language. Yet we are a civilization that dates back thousands of years. English is just a tool. It's enough to be able to use it. The tradition of revering and emulating Western cultures must come to an end," Tang says in social media.

China: Studying instead of Playing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

English as a required subject starting in third grade

English is considered difficult in China, since the Chinese language does not use an alphabetic script. It is a required subject starting in third grade. It is graded on par with Chinese and mathematics on the entrance exam for secondary schools, the central exam after 9th grade, and the high school graduation exam. A maximum of 150 points can be earned on the latter.

"How many resources and how much time do our children, parents and schools invest in a subject that is completely irrelevant to the majority of people in their future professional lives?" the mathematician asks, explaining his position.

He became well-known because many of his students achieved full scores on state math exams; in the class of 2011, six students from a single class did so.

Why English? 'AI translates'

Tang's opinion spread quickly online.

"Why cram for English when artificial intelligence can translate everything in seconds?" comments a user from Beijing.

Another suggestion from the southern province of Guangdong is to at least adjust the scoring — for example, to 120 points instead of 150 on the high school graduation exam.

Secondary schools in China end after 12th grade. These young people are headed to their final exam Image: HPIC/picture alliance

Many parents invest in private tutoring that focuses specifically on exam questions. In addition, all bachelor's students must pass the English exam before being admitted to master's programs. Tang suspects that this could cause many young talents in the natural sciences to fail, even though they have great potential to become top researchers.

No English proficiency, no competitiveness

There is no question that English is also important for STEM subjects. Research on future-oriented topics is typically published in English. There are fears circulating online that cutting back on English instruction could lead to a decline in China's competitiveness. A prominent advocate for English as a required subject is Hu Xijin, former editor-in-chief of the state-run "Global Times," who has previously drawn attention primarily for his nationalistic statements.

Hu emphasizes that foreign language skills are of great importance for every global citizen, "because we live primarily in the present," alluding to a debate over the ungraded history exam. "This present is shaped by globalization. China's opening up is not only state policy but also expands people's scope of action as well as the range of their diverse material and immaterial interests in life."

In Saudi Arabia, Mandarin is the second foreign language taught at schools ― after English Image: FAYEZ NURELDINE/AFP

Hu went on to say that connections to the outside world should not, therefore, be compared to intellectual ties to ancient history.

"Forcibly pitting them against each other — by asking whether foreign languages or traditional Chinese culture are more important — runs the risk of setting the wrong priorities and unnecessarily politicizing public discussions."

For him, an open engagement with the outside world is the top priority. English as a core subject also promotes equal opportunity, he noted, as it gives children in rural areas access to this important foreign language and thus to the world.

Why Mandarin Chinese courses are growing in African schools To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Little interest in language studies

Even Chinese universities specializing in foreign languages are feeling the pressure to adjust their educational goals and prepare incoming freshmen for future job markets. For example, fewer and fewer high school graduates are interested in German language studies, explains a university professor from Beijing who spoke to DW on condition of anonymity.

The new curriculum at Beijing Foreign Studies University has adopted a "foreign language plus major" model: English combined with law, information technology, or economics.

Similar cultural struggles already took place during the Self-Strengthening Movement in the late 19th century under the Qing Dynasty.

"Learn the superior skills from abroad so that you can later conquer the outside world," said Wei Yuan, a court scholar at the time.

Learning from abroad simply works better in the language used there. Even though it may be becoming apparent that, in some areas, other countries are more interested in learning from China— as is already the case today, for example in battery technology for the automotive industry, and humanoid robotics.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Ceuta: Documents show Spanish intelligence warned of crisis
World.content:
Spain declassified documents that showed warnings issued a day before more than 70,000 migrants rushed the Ceuta border fence. Meanwhile, the EU announced funds to strengthen the border and return migrants to Morocco.

Spain's national intelligence agency issued a warning about possible "mass entries" by migrants into Ceuta a day before more than 70,000 migrants stormed the border fences of the enclave in North Africa, according to documents declassified on Wednesday.

The Spanish government declassified a trove of more than 40 documents, including internal alerts, intelligence reports, charts and communications from multiple law enforcement and intelligence agencies.

One urgent memo sent by the National Intelligence Center to authorities in Ceuta on the day before the incident warned of "several calls to carry out entries into Ceuta."

"There are two different groups with a total of 180,000 followers," the declassified memo read, “just to give you an idea of its scale."

CENIF, a border division of the National Police, also published a warning about the social media groups a day before the incident.

"Internal communications have been detected in migrant groups in which they are trying to organize mass entries on the night of 29/07/2026," a document from CENIF read.

Sanchez downplays level of warning

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the documents prove his government had not been warned of the magnitude of the crisis that was about to unfold.

He said the National Intelligence Center only alerted authorities in Ceuta and not the military or Ministry of Defense.

"This is understandable because, with the information available at the time, no one could have foreseen the migration crisis that unfolded on the 30th and 31st," Sanchez said on social media. "No competent body did so. Neither in Spain nor in the EU."

Spain: Tensions in aftermath of Ceuta mass migrant crossing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

EU to fund Ceuta border enhancements

The European Union (EU) on Wednesday announced that it would grant Spain some €115 million ($130 million) in emergency financial aid to help bolster the bloc's external borders and return thousands of individuals who overwhelmed authorities in the country's North African exclave Ceuta in late July.

Spain initially requested the funding on August 24.

Brussels said the funds would help finance "measures to enhance border surveillance, border protection and security-related infrastructure" such as thermal cameras, floating buoy systems and underwater drones: "It will also serve to set up facilities for the screening of migrants, as well as to support returns of those who remain illegally in Ceuta."

"The situation in Ceuta has put pressure on our external borders," said European Commission Vice President Henna Virkkunen. "Our message remains clear: We are committed to combating illegal migration and ensuring the swift return of those who remain illegally in Ceuta."

What happened in Ceuta?

On July 30 and 31, images of migrants storming the borders of the exclave sent shockwaves across the EU and beyond as more than 72,000 individuals crossed into Spanish territory from Morocco.

Scores of migrants died in their attempt to reach EU territory, most by drowning.

Although most of those who breached Ceuta's borders have been returned, thousands remain, many of them unaccompanied minors living in dire conditions.

Unaccompanied minors at risk of sexual assault in Ceuta To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The incident caused a major rift among EU member states, most publicly between Spain's left-wing government and Italy's far-right leadership.

Although Sanchez has said that there is "no solid proof" that Morocco was to blame for the incident, Madrid's top criminal court on Monday opened an investigation into whether African authorities had facilitated the illegal rush.

World.title: Germany's connection to the September 11, 2001 attacks
World.content:
The 9/11 attacks were partly planned in Hamburg, via the so-called Hamburg cell, whose members played key roles in the plot. A look back at a day that shook up Germany’s approach to national security.

"This day has changed the world," German President Johannes Rau said. He had watched in shock as the burning Twin Towers of the World Trade Center collapsed in New York.

Nearly 3,000 people were killed on September 11, 2001, when Islamist terrorists hijacked four passenger planes and turned them into deadly weapons.

Eleven Germans among the victims

Germany’s head of state struggled to find the right words: "We do not know what political or social consequences what happened today will have — what we have watched unfold on our television screens in shock, barely able to comprehend or even reflect on it."

It soon emerged that the victims include people from 92 countries, among them 11 Germans.

The following day, a rapidly spreading rumor was confirmed: Three of the four suspected hijackers had recently lived in Hamburg. The Islamist terrorists were thought to have been led by Egyptian-born Mohammed Atta, who had come to the northern German city in the early 1990s to study.

Mohammed Atta becomes radicalized at a mosque

At some point, the young man became radicalized, particularly at Hamburg's Al-Quds Mosque, which was later closed by German security authorities. He spent the final three years of his life in an apartment shared with two other suspected attackers in the Harburg district.

On September 11, 2001, Islamist terrorists crashed hijacked passenger planes into the towers of the World Trade Center in New York Image: Spencer Platt/Getty Images/AFP

The so-called Hamburg terrorist cell was believed to have included six men, among them Moroccan national Mounir al-Motassadeq. He was charged as an accomplice in the world's first trial related to the September 11, 2001, attacks. In 2003, the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court sentenced him to the maximum 15-year prison term for aiding and abetting thousands of murders and for membership in a terrorist organization.

A man from Bremen at Guantanamo

After serving his sentence, al-Motassadeq was deported to his native Morocco. Another suspected attacker from the circle around pilot Mohammed Atta was Ramzi Binalshibh, who was born in Yemen and had been held without trial at the US detention facility at Guantanamo Bay since 2006.

The United States detained hundreds of suspects at the prison, which human rights groups and international bodies have described as contrary to international law. Among them was Murat Kurnaz, who was born in Bremen. He was released in August 2006 after nearly five years without evidence establishing his involvement in the terrorist attacks.

Kurnaz later recounted his experience in a book that was adapted into a film in 2013.

Guantanamo still open 20 years on To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Frank-Walter Steinmeier before investigative committee

Meanwhile, investigative committees in the German Bundestag sought to determine why Kurnaz and other suspects had wrongly come under the scrutiny of American and German intelligence agencies. Among those called to testify was then-Foreign Minister and current German PresidentFrank-Walter Steinmeier.

At the center of the inquiry was the question of why German security authorities rejected the possible return in 2002 of the German-born detainee, who held a Turkish passport.

"No one doubts, and neither do I, that Mr. Kurnaz suffered terribly in Guantanamo," Steinmeier said. "That is why we also sought to ensure that he was treated in accordance with the rule of law. But at the same time, please understand that we were also obliged to ensure security in our own country."

Gerhard Schröder voiced 'unconditional solidarity'

The Kurnaz case illustrated the pressure on German policymakers in the aftermath of the terrorist attacks in the US. Chancellor Gerhard Schröder addressed parliament the following day.

"Yesterday, September 11, 2001, will go down in history as a dark day for all of us," the Social Democrat said.

He said he had expressed to the American president the deeply felt condolences of the entire German people.

"I also assured him of Germany's unconditional — I emphasize: unconditional — solidarity," Schröder said.

Germany, he added, would offer the US any assistance they requested, "of course, also by identifying and pursuing those responsible for and behind these despicable attacks."

Bundestag passes anti-terror laws

Schröder's remarks set the tone and opened the door for a series of tougher laws. Just weeks after the attacks, the governing coalition of Social Democrats and Greens unveiled its first so-called security package, involving more funding, more personnel as well as greater powers for police and intelligence agencies.

Religious organizations that had previously been granted special protection could now be banned like other associations if their activities were directed against the Basic Law, Germany's constitutional order based on freedom and democracy, or if they pursued other criminal aims. Less than four months after the terrorist attacks in the US, Germany's Anti-Terrorism Act took effect.

Intelligence agencies were given access to personal data held by banks, airlines and telecommunications companies. Immigration laws were tightened.

Through data-mining searches, in which large amounts of data were cross-checked without any specific suspicion, authorities sought to identify so-called sleeper agents — people like Mohammed Atta from the Hamburg terrorist cell, who had not been identified by security agencies in time.

The Federal Constitutional Court brought an end to the legally questionable practice. Such searches were permissible only when there was a specific threat, the court said in a 2006 ruling. Seven years later, Germany's highest court also ruled that parts of the country's anti-terrorism database were unconstitutional.

Germany signs up for the war in Afghanistan

The Islamist terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, also had far-reaching and lasting military consequences. The US launched attacks on the Taliban in Afghanistan as early as October 2001. The Taliban had refused to hand over Osama bin Laden, the head of the al-Qaeda terrorist network and suspected mastermind of the attacks.

Germany joined the US-led war in December 2001. The conflict lasted 20 years and ended in August 2021 with the Taliban's return to power. Around 3,600 soldiers from the international forces were killed, including 59 members of Germany's Bundeswehr. Three German police officers also died.

The words spoken by German President Johannes Rau on Sept. 11, 2001, in the aftermath of the Islamist terrorist attacks in the US, still resonate today: "This day has changed the world."

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Serbia, the conflicted EU candidate
World.content:
On paper, Belgrade has pursued EU membership for years. But accession has long been stalled. The hero's farewell given to war criminal Mladic exposed just how far Serbia has alienated itself from Europe.

The state-supported funeral of Ratko Mladic in Belgrade this week has raised a pressing question in Brussels: Can a country seek EU membership while giving a hero's farewell to a convicted war criminal? For many, the event has shown that Serbia's accession process has not merely stalled. It has largely lost its political drive.

"For too long, the EU has kept treating Serbia as a normal candidate country," Engjellushe Morina of the European Council on Foreign Relations told DW, despite Belgrade's continued backsliding on democracy and the rule of law.

Naim Leo Besiri of Serbia's Institute for European Affairs adds: "The ruling majority in Serbia has not performed anything that was promised on the reform agenda during the last five years."

Serbian armed forces stood guard at Mladic's funeral Image: Oliver Bunic/AFP

A candidate moving away from Europe

Both experts point out that Belgrade has refused to join EU sanctions against Russia. Democratic standards have deteriorated under nationalist President Aleksandar Vucic, while relations with Kosovo remain tense.

Despite having been sentenced to life imprisonment by a UN court for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, Ratko Mladic was buried in Belgrade on Monday with military honors and the participation of government representatives. President Vucic stayed away, but facilitated and defended the public mourning.

Serbia: Thousands attend 'Butcher of Bosnia' funeral To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Brussels reacted unusually strongly. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the images shocking. European Council President Antonio Costa condemned the glorification of war criminals. Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos canceled a visit to Serbia.

Has the EU been too lenient?

But both Morina and Besiri say that this is not enough. They believe Vucic has been given too much room to maneuver for too long. In their perception, he has been treated as an indispensable partner who could secure stability in the Western Balkans and keep Serbia anchored to the West, despite disregarding basic European values.

Besiri says Serbian civil society had warned Brussels for years about attacks on media freedom, the rule of law and democratic institutions. But, he adds, the EU largely turned a blind eye.

In June 2026, senior European Union and Western Balkan leaders gathered for the EU-Western Balkans Summit Image: Michailidis/Betaphoto/SIPA/picture alliance

Economic relations demonstrate the strong ties between the EU and Serbia. The bloc is Serbia's largest trading partner, investor and financial donor. Politically, however, Serbia has developed a close partnership with Moscow.

A common argument for continuing relations with Serbia is therefore based on the concern that greater pressure could push the country further towards Russia or China.

Strong economic ties, close relations with Moscow

Morina accepts that isolating Serbia would be dangerous, but sees other options between accommodation and abandoning relations altogether. The EU should remain engaged with Serbian society while forcing Vucic to make clear political choices, she argues.

Besiri says Russia and China could never replace the European market. In his view, Vucic uses both countries as a threat to discourage Brussels from taking firmer action.

Both researchers see strategies behind the current approach: Vucic benefits from cooperation without implementing the necessary reforms. Brussels, meanwhile, can continue to claim that Serbia remains tied to Europe.

In 2007 already, Aleksandar Vucic decided to put on placards made like street-name signs reading 'Ratko Mladic boulevard' on a major Belgrade street Image: Oliver Bunic/dpa/picture alliance

The limits of financial pressure

The EU has not remained entirely inactive. It has started applying financial pressure. Further payments under the Growth Plan for the Western Balkans have been withheld because of concerns about judicial independence.

Besiri doubts that this will change Vucic's calculations. Broad funding cuts could hurt the population more than the political elite, he argues. Instead, he advocates targeted measures against those responsible for the country's democratic decline and the misuse of its institutions.

Thousands attended Mladic's funeral in Belgrade Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

Could the election bring change?

The early parliamentary election on October 25 could put Vucic's model to the test. After 12 years as president, he now wants to remain Serbia's dominant political figure by becoming the next prime minister.

Besiri says that the political opposition in Serbia remains fragile and that "it is extremely difficult to win democratically in undemocratic elections."

Neither expert expects one election to repair Serbia's institutions or fundamentally change its relationship with the EU.

Aleksandar Vucic did not attend the funeral himself Image: Marko Dimic/ZUMA/IMAGO

Reconciliation remains a distant prospect

Reconciliation in the region appears even more distant. According to Besiri, Serbia would first have to acknowledge its role in the wars of the 1990s and accept established facts about the crimes committed. Instead, narratives portraying Serbs exclusively as victims remain deeply embedded in Serbian politics, education and the media.

"What has been happening recently is basically the reverse of everything that has been built for so many years," Morina underlines.

Mladic's funeral did not cause this development, she adds. It simply revealed once again how far Serbia currently remains from both regional reconciliation and EU membership.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

World.title: Switzerland: Two killed in power plant explosion
World.content:
A fire and subsequent explosion have killed two workers at a Swiss hydroelectric power plant. Authorities say the facility suffered major damage in the incident.

Two workers were killed in an explosion at a hydroelectric power plant in the village of Piotta in southern Switzerland on Wednesday, according to local authorities.

Police say a fire was reported at the Ritom Hydroelectric Station in the canton of Ticino around 9:30 a.m. (0730 GMT). The blaze trapped two workers inside.

Shortly thereafter, an explosion rocked the plant, severely damaging the building and gravely injuring the men, both of whom died from their injuries shortly thereafter.

Authorities say one of the men was a a 55-year-old Swiss citizen, the other has yet to be identified.

State prosecutors have launched an investigation into the cause of the deadly incident.

The facility, which is owned by Swiss rail carrier SBB, is currently undergoing renovations as part of a plan to reconfigure the 100-year-old site.
