Around 30 robots protested outside Poland’s digital affairs ministry on Monday, calling for tougher regulation of artificial intelligence and robotisation. The human organisers say there needs to be greater public debate over the impact of new technologies on the labour market. Digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski met with the demonstrators, telling them that his department is working on regulations. However, one of the organisers said that plans currently being discussed by parliament contain insufficient protection for workers. Around 30 robots joined a protest in front of Poland’s digital affairs ministry, calling for stronger AI regulations. The demonstration was organised by campaigners to spark debate on how AI and robots could replace workers. pic.twitter.com/QEbvchb2RS — Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) September 7, 2026 Standing in several rows, the robots waved Polish flags and chanted slogans such as “We want regulations, we want rules, we want law” and “Don’t wait, regulate, protect jobs”. The organisers, a group called Democratism, said the event was intended to highlight the need for debate and legislation before automation has a more profound impact on employment. “Some people will benefit from new opportunities, while others may need to retrain or adapt to completely different roles,” they wrote. Society needs to discuss “who is responsible for preparing people for these changes, how workers should be protected during the transition and how reskilling should work”. Democratism appears to have been launched shortly before the protest, with the announcement about the demonstration among the first material published on its social media accounts. The initiative was launched by Delta Robots, a company that rents robots for events. However, a website they have set up to gather support for greater debate over the impact of AI and robotisation has so far only obtained signatures from 61 people. Grzegorz Kuliś of Delta Robots admitted to news website Gazeta.pl that their “campaign also has public relations value” for the company. However, he added that, “even though we’re deploying robots, we’re also humans, and we have a whole host of concerns that, if we don’t regulate this, we’ll soon find ourselves in an unprecedented situation that no human being will be able to cope with”. “We are constantly debating the impact of migrants on our society, whilst the vast majority of ‘migrants’ will arrive either via undersea cables across the Atlantic in the form of AI agents, or as humanoid robots in shipping containers from China,” he warned. Gawkowski, who went out to address the organisers, said the ministry’s objectives were aligned with the protesters’ concerns. “People come first, and that is what matters most to us,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Eska. The minister also announced plans to establish a committee on AI development and safety as well as to introduce so-called sandboxes, where companies will be able to test AI solutions before deploying them more widely, reports local news website O!Polska. Kuliś, however, told Gazeta.pl that a draft law on AI systems currently being considered by the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament, contains too little practical protection for workers affected by automation. A Polish radio station that launched a channel run almost entirely by AI – including its presenters – has decided to end the project after less than a week The head of the station admitted they were "surprised by the level of emotion" the idea had caused https://t.co/9iMlRVamSF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 28, 2024 The rapid development of AI and robotics has sparked debate around the world on how such technologies will impact humans, including to what extent and in what ways they will replace human labour. However, a number of recent reports have found that the impact of AI on jobs has so far been smaller than many previously predicted. Analysis by the Institute of Economic Policy Research at Stanford University, published in July, found that “AI’s effects on overall employment are likely small”. A further concern has been the prospect of AI “going rogue” by starting to act without or beyond human control. Those fears were strengthened after it emerged in July this year that some of OpenAI’s AI agents had autonomously hacked Hugging Face, another AI company. The incident prompted more than 100 companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Hugging Face, to sign an open letter calling on companies and governments to step up cybersecurity efforts amid emerging threats. A recent rise in unemployment in Poland has raised concern. The candidate of the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja), one of Poland’s main political groups, has been disqualified from Kraków’s mayoral election after over 2,000 of the signatures from local residents collected in support of his candidacy were found to be invalid. One of Confederation’s leaders, Sławomir Mentzen, admitted that the situation was an “embarrassment” and “catastrophe”. He responded by dismissing the candidate, Bartosz Bocheńczak, as head of his party’s local structures in Kraków and launching an investigation into how the blunder occurred. Podobnie jak i wielu naszych działaczy, wolontariuszy, sympatyków i wyborców, czuję się bardzo zawiedziony brakiem rejestracji kandydatury Bartosza Bocheńczaka w Krakowie. Przyczyną braku rejestracji było to, że spośród około 5000 zebranych podpisów, ponad 2000 były błędnych.… — Sławomir Mentzen (@SlawomirMentzen) September 7, 2026 Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, is holding a mayoral election this month after the previous incumbent, Aleksander Miszalski, was removed mid-term in a rare recall referendum earlier this year. Over a dozen potential candidates announced plans to stand. But, in order to be registered, they had to collect at least 3,000 signatures from residents of the city supporting their candidacy, then submit them to the municipal electoral commission by 3 September. Twelve candidates made such submissions, after which the commission began assessing all signatures to ensure that each candidate had at least 3,000 that were valid. On Monday, reports began to emerge that, although Bocheńczak had submitted just over 4,600 signatures, the commission had found that fewer than 3,000 of them were valid. That evening, the candidate himself confirmed the news. Mentzen, who is leader of the far-right libertarian New Hope (Nowa Nadzieja) party that makes up one half of Confederation, revealed that over 2,000 signatories had listed their address as their place of residence rather than where they are officially registered as living. In Poland, it is common for people to live somewhere different from where they are officially registered. That is particularly the case for young people, who are often registered at their parents’ address while residing elsewhere. Confederation is particularly popular among young people, and Kraków has a large student population. Moja kandydatura na Prezydenta Krakowa nie została zarejestrowana. Zabrakło ważnych podpisów. Nie będę snuł teorii spiskowych, szukał winnych ani przerzucał odpowiedzialności na kogokolwiek. Uważałem, że złożenie niemal 5000 podpisów zapewni nam wystarczający margines… — Bartosz Bocheńczak (@BBochenczak) September 7, 2026 Mentzen said that the regulations regarding collecting signatures for candidates are “absurd”, yet admitted that Bocheńczak’s campaign should have done a better job of complying with the rules. There must now be “consequences from this embarrassment”, said Mentzen, who announced that Bocheńczak had been dismissed as New Hope’s local leader in Kraków and that a party commission would “determine responsibility for this disaster”. Confederation also faced scrutiny last year when the National Electoral Commission (PKW) rejected its financial report for the 2024 European elections after it found irregularities. The party also failed to submit the required documents on time. As a result, it lost access to state subsidies. The Supreme Court has rejected an appeal by the far-right Confederation against the electoral commission's decision to reject its financial report for last year's European elections due to irregularities. The group will now lose access to state subsidies https://t.co/hNGu2Zvzii — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 14, 2025 Bocheńczak is not the only candidate who has struggled with collecting signatures. Last week, just days before the deadline, it emerged that over 3,000 signatures collected in support of the favourite in the elections, Łukasz Gibała, an independent, were invalid because the word “Kraków” was missing from the form. Gibała – a perennial candidate in mayoral elections who finished runner-up to Miszalski in 2024 – quickly scrambled to collect more signatures, and his team managed to gather an additional 9,000 in three days. On Monday this week, it also emerged that three other independent candidates, Marian Banaś, Stanisław Kułach and Marta Ratuszyńska, had failed to gather enough signatures. All three have taken up their right to appeal against the commission’s decision to reject their candidacies. Dziś złożymy dodatkowe podpisy do komisji wyborczej – ponad 9 tysięcy (oprócz wcześniejszych 5,5 tys.). Skala Waszego zaangażowania i pomocy była bezprecedensowa – w 3 dni zebraliśmy więcej podpisów niż którykolwiek z naszych rywali przez 3 tygodnie 💪 Bardzo Wam dziękuję i… — Łukasz Gibała (@LukaszGibala) September 3, 2026 Six candidates have so far been accepted, including Gibała; Monika Piątkowska, who is supported by the centrist Civil Coalition (KO) and Polish People’s Party (PSL); Michał Drewnicki of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS); Aleksandra Owca of the left-wing Together (Razem); and Michał Klimek of the radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). Two candidates, Daria Gosek-Popiołek of The Left (Lewica) and Sławomir Pietrzyk of Social Democracy of Poland (Socjaldemokracja Polska), are still awaiting confirmation from the electoral commission that they submitted enough valid signatures. A decision is due to be announced today. The first round of the election will take place on Sunday 27 September. If any candidate receives over 50% of the vote, they will become mayor. If not, a run-off between the top two candidates will take place on 11 October. There has been little polling on support for candidates, but one survey by the Opinia24 agency for Polityka Insight two weeks ago showed Gibała with 25.2%, ahead of Piątkowska (15.3%) and Gosek-Popiołek (8.7%). Bocheńczak was in sixth with just 3.2%. Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland urges EU to deny asylum to migrants who violently cross its borders

Poland wants the European Union to deny the right to asylum for migrants who cross EU borders in organised, aggressive groups, just as Poland has itself done on its border with Belarus. “This is about depriving people who illegally cross the border in organised groups, using violence or destroying border security measures, of the right to international protection,” Maciej Duszczyk, the deputy interior minister who oversees migration policy, told broadcaster RMF. Polska zabiega o to, by Unia Europejska przyjęła jej interpretację przepisów dotyczących ochrony międzynarodowej. „Chodzi o pozbawienie prawa do ochrony międzynarodowej osób, które nielegalnie przekraczają granicę w zorganizowanych grupach, z użyciem przemocy albo niszcząc… — Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) September 6, 2026 The station reports that, at a meeting of the European Council next month, Poland will propose expanding the interpretation of article 33 of the United Nations’ Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees. That section outlines the principle of “refoulement”, under which states are barred from expelling or returning refugees to places where their life or freedom would be threatened. The article includes a clause saying that the principle does not apply if “there are reasonable grounds for regarding [a refugee] as a danger to the security of the country” in which they have arrived, or if they have a criminal conviction that makes them “a danger to the community of that country”. Poland wants that clause to be applied in situations where someone applies for asylum after being part of an organised and aggressive border crossing. Since last year, Poland has itself banned asylum claims from people who illegally cross the border from Belarus. Since 2021, the Belarusian authorities have encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to try to irregularly – and often aggressively – enter the EU. Poland’s asylum ban, which has exceptions for certain vulnerable categories of people, was introduced as a temporary measure in March 2025 but has been repeatedly renewed since then. Warsaw now wants a similar interpretation of international refugee law to be applied across the EU Its proposals come in the wake of July’s incident in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, where tens of thousands of migrants irregularly entered from Morocco. Soon afterwards, Poland urged the EU to adopt tougher measures, including making migrants who enter the bloc illegally ineligible for obtaining residence rights. Prime Minister Donald Tusk was also one of 22 EU leaders who signed a letter expressing “serious concern” at the situation in Ceuta and warning that the EU “cannot allow uncontrolled mass border crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration, or other hybrid threats to create the impression that illegal entry…is possible”. After last week's migration crisis in Ceuta, Poland has called for tougher EU measures, including an automatic ban on residence for anyone who enters illegally. It pointed to its own experience of dealing with "weaponised" migration from Belarus https://t.co/2VHn5ZUJx7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 5, 2026 Poland has long argued that the situation on the Belarus border is an example of how migration has been “weaponised” by Russia and its allies to sow social discord in EU countries. In response, Poland has invested billions in strengthening physical and electronic barriers along the border, has deployed thousands of additional officers there (and granted them expanded rights to use firearms), and has banned asylum claims. In 2021, Poland recorded almost 40,000 attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, and the figure remained as high as 30,000 in 2025. However, in the first half of this year, only 235 attempted crossings were recorded, which the Polish government has hailed as evidence of the success of its tough measures. However, Poland’s human rights commission recently raised concern at how long the technically “temporary” asylum ban has been in place. Some Polish courts have also ruled that Polish border guards acted unlawfully when forcing migrants back into Belarus. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Has Karol Nawrocki’s first year as Poland’s president been a success?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak Poland’s right-wing president has been largely successful at transforming his office into an assertive centre of resistance to the liberal centrist-led government, frustrating its agenda through extensive use of constitutional powers. He has emerged as the leading unifying figure on the fragmented Polish right but faces new challenges moving towards the next election. Scuppering the government’s reform agenda Last month, Polish President Karol Nawrocki marked the first anniversary of his inauguration following a surprise victory in the May-June 2025 presidential election over Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski, the candidate of the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO), Poland’s main governing party since autumn 2023, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. A relatively unknown conservative historian and head of the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical research institute, Nawrocki ran formally as an independent but was backed by the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping. The election result represented a significant upset, ushering in a period of tense “cohabitation” between the Tusk government and a hostile president. The Polish presidency is not a day-to-day governing role, and in many respects largely ceremonial, but retains important constitutional powers. Karol Nawrocki has now issued more vetoes than any other president in Polish history Three vetoes on Thursday took his total to 37 in just ten months since taking office, surpassing the 35 issued by Aleksander Kwaśniewski during his ten years as president https://t.co/xf27K8Fyn6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2026 These include a legislative veto, which the government lacks the required three-fifths parliamentary majority to overturn, and the ability to suspend a piece of legislation coming into law by referring it to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK). Given that a majority of tribunal members were appointed under previous PiS-dominated parliaments, this also functioned as a de facto veto. As a result, Nawrocki was able to severely complicate the Tusk government’s plans to push through its legislative and elite replacement programme, notably efforts to roll back PiS’s judicial reforms. This, combined with the political authority that stemmed from Nawrocki’s strong electoral mandate, meant that the government faced continued resistance for the remainder of its term of office until the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027. An assertive presidency From the outset, Nawrocki has been a much more assertive president than his predecessor Andrzej Duda, leveraging his mandate to carve out a role as an active centre of resistance to the government. Although both presidents were PiS-aligned, during cohabitation with the Tusk administration, Duda used his powers more selectively and occasionally sought common ground. Nawrocki, by contrast, interpreted his strong electoral mandate as authorising a more confrontational approach. He has surrounded himself with a strong political support base who have helped him to develop and carry forward a blaze of independent initiatives in both the domestic and foreign policy spheres. As well proposing a series of his own draft laws, Nawrocki has used the legislative veto far more frequently than Duda (who issued only 19 across two full five-year terms) or any previous post-1989 president in a comparable period. By mid-2026, he had already surpassed previous records, blocking over 40 government-sponsored laws on issues such as judicial reform, socioeconomic policy and defence financing. In foreign policy, where the president’s formal competencies are more limited, Nawrocki pursued independent initiatives that often diverged from, or complicated, the government’s line. He has, for example, prioritised close personal and strategic ties with the USA, positioning Washington as Warsaw’s primary security guarantor. He cultivated a high-profile relationship with the Trump administration that yielded commitments to ongoing US troop deployments in Poland, sometimes bypassing or challenging the Tusk government. On Ukraine, while supporting continued military and diplomatic aid, Nawrocki has adopted a more transactional and assertive approach, opposing rapid Ukrainian EU and NATO accession until bilateral issues are addressed, and taking symbolic steps such as removing a Polish state honour from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over unresolved historical grievances. Polish President Nawrocki has announced that he will strip @ZelenskyyUa of Poland’s highest honour in response to him naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles during WWII Ukraine's foreign minister condemned Nawrocki's "reckless" decision https://t.co/CEqj4aaHYg — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 These have drawn criticisms that he is playing into Russian hands by weakening regional unity, but were clearly in line with changing Polish public attitudes towards its eastern neighbour. Uniting the fragmented right? Nawrocki has also emerged as the most important unifying figure on the increasingly fragmented Polish right. PiS, long the hegemonic force on the conservative side, has seen radical-right challengers, the free-market Confederation (Konfederacja) and ultra-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), gaining ground. In July, PiS also suffered its biggest ever internal split, with a significant group of parliamentarians aligned with former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki breaking away. All of this weakened PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński’s once unquestioned authority as the central broker on the Polish right; he is now one leader among several. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland's largest opposition party, PiS, has called on President @NawrockiKn to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections https://t.co/Q3BFSOSfTG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 Alone among leading right-wing politicians, Nawrocki possesses genuine crossover appeal across the fractured conservative landscape. His 2025 presidential victory showed that he could consolidate a broad right-wing coalition and attract support well beyond traditional PiS loyalists, capturing the vast majority of voters from both Confederations. Although he was the PiS candidate, Nawrocki operates as an independent authority outside of direct party control and has cultivated an image as an authoritative independent figure, which gives him greater moral and symbolic stature than any partisan leader. Nawrocki’s assertive use of his constitutional powers has further reinforced his position as a natural focal point around which the broader right can unite. Many conservatives now look to him as a potential patron or broker ahead of the 2027 election. Nawrocki can use the presidency to set a broad conservative agenda and mediate negotiations among the various right-wing groupings to secure pre- and post-election agreements. However, he has no unifying mandate and his ability to bring together the right depends ultimately on whether the various actors are willing to be led. Moreover, not only is the president expected to remain formally non-partisan and not engage too openly in day-to-day politics, Nawrocki lacks the party organisational levers needed to enforce messy backroom deals. Focus of government attacks The Tusk government knows that Nawrocki’s is now the most potent counterweight to its authority and potential unifier of the fragmented right, which is precisely why he has become the main focus of its attacks on the opposition. An essential element of this has been trying to portray Nawrocki’s more active presidency as destructive and undermining the unity of the Polish state. This forms a principal component of its broader “security” narrative, a calculated strategy to reframe political debate around the ongoing Russian threat. At a time of heightened geopolitical risk with hybrid threats against Poland, the government has portrayed presidential obstruction as undermining the country’s military readiness and ability to co-ordinate with its allies. Karol Nawrocki has sought to redefine Poland's presidency and become the figurehead of the right-wing opposition. So far, it is working, but questions remain over what his end goal is and whether these tactics will get him there, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/TNDRGGv2QT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 22, 2025 The Tusk administration cites Nawrocki’s veto of legislation enabling Poland to access its €43.7 billion allocation from the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defence procurement initiative as an apparently perfect example of this, although the president argues that the loans saddle future generations with a huge, long-term debt and undermine Polish sovereignty. In fact, Nawrocki is fairly relaxed about the government’s attempts to portray his more active presidency as obstructive. Rather, he feels he needs to be assertive because that is precisely what those who voted for him expect: action and change, not passivity or compromise. Nawrocki’s 2025 presidential victory was based on a sharp critique of the Tusk administration and framed, and widely interpreted, as a vote of no confidence in the government’s performance. The president believes that this gives him a strong mandate to confront the ruling coalition across a wide range of issues and that the greater political risk lies in undermining the political momentum that his win created and appearing weak or inactive, rather than in the government’s counternarrative that he is a “blocking” president. A clash between the right-wing president and more liberal government over Poland's receipt of EU defence loans has sharpened polarisation and turbocharged the ruling coalition’s “Polexit” and security narratives, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/Iu7rcJfj5e — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 2, 2026 More broadly, Nawrocki is not too concerned about what the Warsaw opinion-forming elites say about him. His approach stands in stark contrast to earlier presidents, even right-wing ones such as Duda, who, conservative critics argue, paid excessive attention to elite and liberal media criticism and received no meaningful political reward or pay-off for doing so. Instead of seeking to present himself as a “president of all Poles” in the traditional, consensus-seeking sense, Nawrocki has deliberately prioritised appealing directly to his core electoral base: Polish voters living beyond the large urban agglomerations in smaller towns, rural areas, and the provinces. By maintaining an assertive, unapologetic style that resonates with this electorate’s sense of cultural and political marginalisation, Nawrocki has sought to consolidate that support rather than diluting it in pursuit of metropolitan elite approval. Poland’s most popular politician There have obviously been plenty of missteps along the way. One clear risk has been the sheer volume and sometimes seemingly indiscriminate nature of the legislative vetoes. While this has successfully blocked key elements of the government’s agenda and reinforced Nawrocki’s image as an assertive counterweight, it has also handed the Tusk administration a ready-made narrative that the president is simply an obstructive “veto machine”. A number of Nawrocki’s more high-profile vetoes, such as the cryptocurrency regulation law, have proved highly contentious. PM @donaldtusk called a classified meeting of parliament in a bid to persuade opposition MPs to overturn the president's veto of crypto-asset regulation, which Tusk said threatens national security. However, in a subsequent vote, the veto was upheld https://t.co/Vj0Zh9wxpH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 5, 2025 Moreover, some of the other constitutional instruments that he has sought to utilise have not been particularly successful or even proved counterproductive. These include attempts to introduce his own legislation or referendum initiatives that have been stymied in parliament, as well as his original idea of holding the government to account via the so-called “Cabinet Council”, a formal meeting of the Council of Ministers chaired by the president. Nonetheless, in general, Nawrocki’s strategy appears to have delivered political dividends for him. He can, for example, point to a number of foreign policy successes, particularly in cultivating close personal and strategic ties with the USA under the Trump administration and positioning himself as a significant actor on security issues. President @NawrockiKn has recorded the highest ever level of trust (54.8%, up 8.4pp since May) of any politician in the history of regular polling by @IBRiS_PL for @onetpl Foreign minister @sikorskiradek (42.6%) was second and PM @donaldtusk (38.1%) third https://t.co/POuUFR3Khk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 26, 2026 At the same time, Nawrocki has asserted a greater degree of independence from PiS than Duda was ever able to achieve. This has been helped by the simple fact that PiS is now in opposition rather than in government, which reduces the formal and informal constraints that tied his predecessor more closely to the party. As a result, Nawrocki has emerged as Poland’s most popular politician, with consistently high approval ratings that set him apart from both the government and right-wing opposition party leaders. Challenges ahead There are clear challenges ahead for Nawrocki in the run-up to next year’s election and beyond. The first is how to respond to the argument that electing a right-wing government would concentrate excessive power in one side of the political spectrum. This is an awkward point for Nawrocki because he himself used a version of this argument during the 2025 presidential campaign, presenting his candidacy as a necessary check on the Tusk government. Opponents of the right will inevitably turn this logic against the broader conservative camp in the run-up to the 2027 election, claiming that the combination of a sympathetic president and a right-wing parliamentary majority risks the very imbalance Nawrocki once warned against. A second, related strategic challenge arises if a right-wing government does take office, and Nawrocki finds himself cohabiting with an ideologically and programmatically aligned administration rather than a hostile one. In that situation, he would still need to carve out a distinct and independent role for himself. The risk is falling into the trap that afflicted Duda during the years of PiS government: being widely perceived as little more than the government’s “notary” or a passive rubber stamp for its agenda. Maintaining personal authority, visibility, and a sense of autonomy, while avoiding conflict with an ideologically allied government, would demand a different style of presidency from the approach that has defined his first year. The very assertiveness and independence that have served him well in cohabitation with the Tusk government will prove harder to sustain if the political balance shifts after 2027. World.title: Polish PM condemns opposition “idiots or traitors” celebrating AfD victory in Germany
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Note: This article has been updated to include later comments from a senior aide to President Karol Nawrocki. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has condemned as “idiots or traitors” those among the right-wing opposition who have celebrated Sunday’s state election victory by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). However, the response from the Polish right to the election result has so far been relatively muted. The rise of the AfD has been watched with concern by many in Poland due to the party’s attempts to downplay the significance of Germany’s Nazi history and its sympathy towards Russia. W Polsce tylko idioci albo zdrajcy mogą się cieszyć z tryumfu AfD w Niemczech. Trochę się ich nazbierało w Konfederacjach i PiS. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 6, 2026 The AfD came first by a large margin in Sunday’s election in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, with preliminary results giving it around 44% of the vote. The centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of federal Chancellor Friedrich Merz is trailing in second on around 17%. The victory continues a recent rise for the AfD, which also came first in the Thuringian state election in 2024, with 33% of the vote, and second in the federal elections of 2025, with 21%, making it the main national opposition party. The AfD’s latest result was welcomed by some figures from Poland’s right-wing and far-right opposition. “Germany is waking up,” tweeted Jacek Wilk, a former member of Poland’s parliament who is part of the radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party. Wg tej prognozy AfD brakuje już tylko 3 miejsc do samodzielnej większości Landtagu Saksonii-Anhalt. Niemcy się budzą. https://t.co/oHUIkYV1aQ — Jacek Wilk (@JacekWilkPL) September 6, 2026 Zdzisław Krasnodębski, a former deputy president of the European Parliament for the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party, described the Saxony-Anhalt elections as “a great celebration of democracy”, pointing to the almost 80% turnout. Krasnodębski called on the minister-president of the German state, Sven Schulze of the CDU, to “end the anti-democratic ‘firewall’ [Brandmauer]” policy under which mainstream German parties refuse to form administrations with the AfD. However, other PiS figures expressed concern over the AfD’s victory, including former education minister and current MEP Anna Zalewska, who said that “the AfD is a powerful threat to European values and Polish-German cooperation”. Sven Schulze ist ein besonnener, konservativer Politiker (den ich persönlich aus dem Europäischen Parlament kenne). Er sollte einer Koalition mit der angeblich demokratischen, postkommunistischen „Linken“ nicht zustimmen. Er sollte vielmehr mit Merz’ Politik der… https://t.co/10rtEnO4yN — ZdzisławKrasnodębski (@ZdzKrasnodebski) September 6, 2026 On Sunday evening, Tusk also commented on social media. “In Poland, only idiots or traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD in Germany. Quite a few of them have gathered in Confederation and PiS,” he wrote. Confederation is another far-right opposition group. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński, who is from Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, called those celebrating the AfD’s victory in Poland “a modern-day Targowica” – referring to a group of 18th-century Polish nobles who allied with Russia against the Polish national cause and are a symbol of treachery. Another government minister, Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, leader of KO’s coalition partner Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), pointed to the fact that one of the two parties that make up Confederation is allied with the AfD in the European Parliament. “Neo-fascists aligned with Russia won the elections in Saxony [sic],” she wrote, misnaming the German state. “For Polish patriots, it was a defeat for the values ​​of our world. For Mentzen and half of Confederation, it was a victory for an ally.” Sławomir Mentzel is the leader of the New Hope (Nowa Nadzieja) party that makes up one of the two main factions in Confederation and which sits in the Europe of Sovereign Nations group alongside the AfD. Mentzen has, at the time of writing, not commented on the election result in Saxony-Anhalt. The AfD’s growth has been watched with concern by many in Poland, a country that suffered enormously under Nazi-German occupation in World War Two. Some senior AfD figures have sought to downplay the significance of the Nazi era. In 2025, when the German parliament approved plans for a memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of World War Two, the AfD was the only party not to vote in favour. Last year, Tusk also criticised remarks by billionaire Elon Musk at an AfD election rally, in which he urged Germans to “move beyond” their guilt over Nazi crimes. The Polish prime minister called them “ominous”, especially as they were delivered hours before the anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz. Germany’s parliament has passed a motion calling on the government to establish a permanent memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of the German-Nazi occupation. The measure was supported by all parties apart from the far-right AfD https://t.co/8dk0ZSpmjJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 3, 2025 The AfD’s sympathy towards and links with Russia have caused further concern in Poland. Last year, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said he “does not see any current threat to Germany from Russia” and that, in fact, “Poland could also be a threat to us”. This year, another senior AfD figure, Kay Gottschalk, called for Poland to pay his country €1.3 billion as reparations for its “complicity” in the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines that used to bring Russian gas to Germany through the Baltic Sea but were damaged by explosions in 2022. On Sunday evening, responding to Tusk’s latest social media post, AfD MEP Tomasz Froelich, who holds both German and Polish citizenship, wrote: “Herr Tusk, eat a Snickers!” – a reference to an advertising campaign for the chocolate bar suggesting that people should eat one when they need to calm down. Late on Monday morning, a senior aide to right-wing Polish President Karol Nawrocki – who is aligned with the opposition and an opponent of Tusk’s government – told broadcaster Kanał Zero that “the AfD is pursuing a programme that is contrary to Poland’s interests”. “The AfD’s pro-Russian agenda, such as the proposal to lift sanctions against Russia, is dangerous and unacceptable from Poland’s perspective,” said Paweł Szeferneker, who is head of the president’s cabinet. However, he also argued that the AfD’s rise has been the result of a backlash against policies previously implemented by former German Chancellor Angela Merkel as well as by Tusk himself when he served as president of the European Council. 🗣️ @jprusinowski: "AfD i lokalne wybory w Saksonii – 45% prawie. World.title: Prague Botanical Garden to Host Grape Harvest Festival
World.content:
The Prague Botanical Garden will host its traditional grape harvest festival at St. Clare’s Vineyard on September 12 and 13, bringing two days of wine, fresh burčák, live music and activities for visitors.

The festival, known as Vinobraní na Vinici sv. Kláry, will feature wines from producers across the Czech Republic, Moravia and other countries.

Visitors will also have the chance to taste white and red burčák made from grapes harvested this year at St. Clare’s Vineyard.



The first grapes for the festival have already been picked by hand. Workers harvested 2,700 kilograms of table grapes and the Modrý Portugal variety. The grapes are now being used to produce this year’s burčák, a young wine that is still undergoing fermentation and is traditionally associated with the Czech grape harvest season.

Alongside wines from the St. Clare’s winery, the festival will present a selection of wines from other producers from the Czech Republic, Moravia and abroad.

Two days of live music

Music will be a major part of the weekend program. Saturday’s main stage lineup includes Jordan Haj and Emma Smetana, YES BROTHERS and 20 MINUTES.

On Sunday, visitors can see the Děda Mládek Illegal Band, BRASS AVENUE, MOVEBREAKERS and OFF BEAT ORCHESTRA. A second music stage will also operate near the St. Clare’s wine shop.

The festival program includes more than music and wine. Visitors can join guided tours of the vineyard, take part in workshops and creative activities, or attend the Vínohrátky educational program. The guided tours are included in the admission price.

The event will run from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both September 12 and 13. Activities will take place at St. Clare’s Vineyard and in the Ornamental Garden of the Prague Botanical Garden.

Tickets bought at the venue cost CZK 280 for adults and CZK 180 for children and young people aged 3 to 17.

Online tickets purchased by September 11 are CZK 250 for adults and CZK 150 for children and young people. Children under three can enter free of charge.

World.title: September 28 Holiday in Czechia: What Will Be Open and Closed
World.content:
Czech Statehood Day falls on Monday, September 28, giving people across Czechia a three-day weekend. But anyone planning to shop should be aware that many large stores will be required to close.

The public holiday commemorates Saint Wenceslas, the patron saint of the Czech lands and one of the most important figures in Czech history. September 28 has been observed as Czech Statehood Day since 2000 and is a statutory day off.



For shoppers, however, the key issue is the country’s restrictions on retail opening hours.

Which shops will be closed on September 28

Under Czech law, shops with a sales area of more than 200 square metres must close on September 28.

This means most large supermarkets, hypermarkets and shopping centres will not be able to operate as normal.

The restriction does not apply to all businesses. Smaller shops with a sales area of up to 200 square metres can remain open, although individual owners decide whether to operate during the holiday.

Some types of businesses are also exempt from the restrictions. These include pharmacies, petrol stations and shops located at airports and major railway stations.

Restaurants, cafés and most other services are not covered by the retail law and can therefore open according to their normal schedules or the decision of their operators.

People planning to use smaller independent shops should still check opening hours in advance. Many owners choose to close during public holidays, particularly when the holiday creates a long weekend.

Why is September 28 a public holiday

Czech Statehood Day is linked to Saint Wenceslas, the medieval ruler who became the patron saint of the Czech lands.

Wenceslas was the son of Duke Vratislav I and Drahomíra. His grandmother, Ludmila, who was later canonised, played a major role in his upbringing and is traditionally credited with influencing his Christian education.

Wenceslas is believed to have been killed in Stará Boleslav on September 28, either in 929 or 935, depending on the historical source.

His death turned him into a martyr and helped establish his lasting importance in Czech religious and national traditions.

World.title: Prague Unemployment Reaches 4% with 40,509 Job Seekers
World.content:
Unemployment in Prague rises to 4% at the end of August, with 40,509 people registered as job seekers at the Labour Office.

The figure was 2.1% higher than in July and 15.7% higher than a year earlier.

Despite the increase, Prague continued to record the lowest unemployment rate among Czechia’s regions. The national unemployment rate stood at 5% at the end of August.



More people registered as job seekers

A total of 5,368 people registered with the Prague Labour Office in August. That was 133 fewer than in July but 1,033 more than in August 2025.

At the end of August, Prague had 37,811 people considered reachable for employment. This category covers people aged 15 to 64 who are not temporarily unable to work and are not taking part in retraining.

The number of reachable job seekers increased by 822 compared with July and by 5,475 compared with the same month last year.

Women accounted for 55.2% of all registered job seekers, with 22,378 women listed in the Labour Office records.

More than 22,000 vacancies remain available

Employers in Prague had 22,519 registered vacancies at the end of August. That was 708 fewer positions than in July and 565 fewer than a year earlier.

There were an average of 1.8 registered job seekers for every vacancy.

Of the total number of registered vacancies, 1,676 were not marked as positions available to foreign workers. Employers could recruit workers from abroad for a further 20,843 positions.

Construction, accommodation and food services, and wholesale and retail were among the sectors with the largest number of vacancies.

World.title: AIGEL to Celebrate 10th Anniversary with Prague Concert
World.content:
On October 21, electronic duo AIGEL will perform at Futurum Music Bar in Prague as part of a special concert marking the band’s 10th anniversary.

AIGEL was formed by Tatar poet and singer Aigel Gaisina and St. Petersburg producer Ilya Baramiya. Over the past decade, the duo has developed a distinctive sound combining electronic music, trip-hop and psychedelic influences.

Get your ticket here

Their music crosses linguistic and cultural boundaries, with songs performed in Russian, Tatar, English and German.

AIGEL gained international attention with the viral tracks “Tatarin” and “Pyyala.” The latter topped streaming charts in 25 countries and reached No. 1 on the global Shazam chart.

Over 10 years, the duo has released five albums and dozens of singles. They have also received a Cannes Lion for the music video “You’re Born” and toured extensively across Europe and beyond.

Now based in Europe, AIGEL is preparing a special anniversary show in Prague, combining the duo’s electronic sound with Gaisina’s distinctive and expressive vocals.

The concert will take place on October 21 at Futurum Music Bar.

World.title: Prague to Add 51 New Trams Next Year as Network Expands
World.content:
Prague is set to receive 51 new trams next year as the city expands its tram network and begins replacing some of its oldest vehicles.

The Prague Public Transport Company (DPP) has ordered another 25 Škoda 52T trams under an existing framework agreement with Škoda Transportation.

Each tram costs CZK 82.5 million, including CZK 40 million in European subsidies. Prague has now committed to buying 71 of the new vehicles in three separate orders.



The first 20 Škoda 52T trams entered regular service in Prague last year. Another batch is being delivered this year, while the latest orders will continue into 2027.

The newest order for 25 additional trams is due to be completed by December 3 next year.

The new vehicles are needed not only because Prague is building new tram lines but also because the existing fleet needs to be renewed. Some of the oldest trams still in operation are the T3M models, while a large part of the fleet consists of reconstructed T3R.P and T3R.PV vehicles and their derivatives.

Replacing older models with a smaller number of standardised tram types should also reduce maintenance and servicing costs, according to the deputy mayor. The new trams are expected to remain in service for around 20 to 30 years, compared with approximately 15 years for buses.

The Škoda 52T is 32 metres long and 2.5 metres wide and can carry up to 243 passengers. Of these, 173 can travel standing. The tram therefore offers almost 16 percent more capacity than Prague’s Škoda 15T trams.

The maximum operating speed is 70 kilometres per hour.

The 52T was designed specifically for Prague’s tram network, including sections with narrow and sharply curved tracks. This allows the vehicles to operate on existing routes without requiring major changes to the infrastructure.

World.title: Prague Castle to Celebrate Václav Havel With Four-Month Festival
World.content:
Prague Castle will host a four-month festival celebrating the legacy of Václav Havel, with theatre, film, music, design and public debates taking place from October through January.

The Havel ALIVE festival will mark what would have been Havel’s 90th birthday and explore the continued relevance of his ideas. Most events will be free.

One of the main highlights will be the Czech premiere of The Warning, an unfinished Havel play that remained hidden for almost 40 years. The manuscript was discovered by David Dušek among the papers of writer Zdeněk Urbánek.



The production has been prepared by Jiří Havelka, artistic director of Dejvické Theatre, and will feature actors Martin Myšička and Ivan Trojan. The theatre will also present We’ll Start It Tomorrow, or Who’s the Gentleman Here at Prague Castle’s Riding Hall.

The festival will also focus on Havel’s influence on Czech design. In cooperation with Designblok, Prague Castle will present Design for Václav Havel, featuring objects connected with his presidency, including Bořek Šípek’s Olga chair, original glass pieces and Castle Guard uniforms designed by Theodor Pištěk.

For the first time, the exhibition will also show the entire presidential office, including Havel’s library. It will open during Designblok on October 7 and remain at the Riding Hall from October 21 to January 17.

Music and dance will feature prominently as well. On November 18, students and teachers from the Academy of Performing Arts in Prague will present a gala evening directed by Magdalena Švecová. Other performances will draw on Havel’s writings, his Anticodes poetry collection, his relationship with the underground music scene and the events of November 1989.

The programme will also include screenings of Citizen Havel and Leaving, a musical evening led by Pavel Klusák, and discussions about art, architecture, freedom and democracy.

Selected festival events

October 4 — Guided tours of Lány Chateau and Prague Castle focused on Havel’s presidency. Free.

October 7 — Opening of Design for Václav Havel at the Prague Castle Riding Hall.

October 8 — Pavel Klusák’s All the President’s Rockers: Václav Havel & Music. Free.

October 14 — Citizen Havel screening followed by a discussion. Free.

October 22 — Thinking Havel Live: Democracy and the Future of Europe. Free.

November 4 — Dejvické Theatre presents We’ll Start It Tomorrow, or Who’s the Gentleman Here. Tickets CZK 390–490.

November 5–6 — Czech premieres of Havel’s The Warning. Tickets CZK 390–490.

November 12 — Thinking Havel: Between the Individual and the System. Free.

November 18 — Havel: Inspiration for a New Generation, a gala evening at the Prague Castle Riding Hall from 7 p.m. Tickets CZK 250.

November 26 — Lecture on Havel’s designer and architect Bořek Šípek at the Supreme Burgrave’s Office from 5 p.m. Free.

December 3 — Thinking Havel: Politics and Spiritual Values, a debate with Alice Koubová, Milena Bartlová and Petr Kratochvíl at the Riding Hall from 6 p.m. Free.

December 8 — Literature at the Castle: Writing Havel, a lecture at the Supreme Burgrave’s Office from 5 p.m. Free.

December 15 — Screening of Leaving, followed by a discussion with Dagmar Havlová and other guests at the Supreme Burgrave’s Office from 6 p.m. Free.

January 14 — Ceremonial presentation of the Jindřich Chalupecký Award 2027 at Prague Castle.

World.title: Prague Airport to Expand Border Control at Terminal 1
World.content:
Prague Airport is expanding and modernising the border control area for arriving passengers at Terminal 1 to increase capacity and reduce waiting times.

The project will add five new passport control desks and four EasyGoGate (EGG) self-service gates for eligible European passport holders.

The work is scheduled to begin in September 2026 and is expected to be completed by the end of April 2027.



The expansion comes as Prague Airport faces increased pressure at border control, particularly during peak hours. The introduction of the European Entry/Exit System (EES) in October 2025 has added to the workload at the airport.

The project will also enlarge the waiting area before passport control and upgrade the ventilation system throughout the border control area.

The total investment is estimated at CZK 290 million, including construction, design and engineering work, technical supervision and safety coordination. The new passport control equipment will be supplied and installed by the Police of the Czech Republic.

Police representatives said the changes are also intended to strengthen security at the Schengen Area’s external border while ensuring the new facilities meet current security and legal requirements.

Some queues and restrictions are expected

The renovation will take place in stages to limit disruption to airport operations. However, passengers may encounter temporary restrictions at passport control and longer queues during some phases of the work.

At one stage, three passport control desks will be temporarily closed. This phase will be scheduled during a period of lower passenger traffic.

EU citizens will continue to be able to use the passport control desks and EGG self-service gates designated for European passport holders. They are not required to register through the EES.

During the other stages of construction, restrictions will mainly affect the area immediately before passport control. Passenger routes will be adjusted around the construction zones, while the overall flow through border control will remain unchanged.

World.title: Prague Bids to Host 2029 European Figure Skating Championships
World.content:
Prague is preparing a bid to host the 2029 European Figure Skating Championships, with the O2 Arena expected to serve as the main venue if the Czech capital wins the right to stage the competition.

Prague City Council approved the candidacy on Monday following an approach from the Czech Figure Skating Union.

The proposal comes several months after Prague hosted the 2026 World Figure Skating Championships in March.



City councilor for education and sports Antonín Klecanda (STAN) said the success of that event helped encourage the city to pursue another major international competition.

“The response was very positive, and other countries asked whether another event of this kind could be held in Prague,” Klecanda said on Monday. “We reached an agreement, and today we approved our candidacy to host the European Figure Skating Championship in 2029.”

The 2026 World Championships attracted a record number of spectators for a figure skating world championship, according to Klecanda. He also said international visitors had responded positively to Prague’s role as host city.

The city has not yet determined when the 2029 championship would take place. The date will be discussed at a later stage, while Prague currently expects the competitions to be staged at the O2 Arena.

The financial impact of hosting the championships has not yet been calculated. The city would have to cover not only the direct costs of organizing the competition but also additional expenses linked to public services, including increased public transport capacity, emergency services and police deployment.

Klecanda said these costs could reach tens of millions of Czech crowns. He argued, however, that part of the expenditure could be offset by additional tax revenue generated by the event, while the championship would also strengthen Prague’s international profile.

The final decision on the host city for the 2029 European Figure Skating Championships has yet to be made.

World.title: Buying rural property as a foreigner: The legal map all foreign buyers in Hungary should know
World.content:
For foreign buyers in Hungary, the question appears simple: can I buy this property? In the rural property market, however, the answer is rarely straightforward. It depends on precisely what the buyer intends to acquire, the buyer’s nationality and the legal structure through which the purchase is proposed. My earlier articles examined the structure of the premium Lake Balaton market and the pitfalls of zártkert property. This article completes the picture: it provides the legal map showing which rural properties a foreign buyer may acquire in Hungary, and under what conditions.

Author: Emese Széll, Private Real Estate Advisor to Premium Clients in Hungary

The first question: what is the property in legal terms?

Hungarian law does not treat all rural properties alike. The following three groups provide a useful practical starting point, but they are not separate statutory categories. In every case, the land-use category or non-agricultural (“kivett”) designation recorded on the land-registry title sheet, the property’s location status, the legal status of any building and the applicable local planning rules together determine which acquisition rules apply.

The first group comprises residential or holiday property that does not qualify as agricultural or forestry land. If the title sheet records, for example, “kivett lakóház, udvar” (non-agricultural residential house and yard), “lakás” (apartment) or another non-agricultural designation, the acquisition restrictions in the Land Transaction Act generally do not apply. Nationals of EU and EEA Member States, and persons accorded equivalent treatment under an international treaty, may generally acquire such property without authorisation. Other foreign natural persons who are subject to the authorisation requirement generally need the approval of the Government Office of the Capital City Budapest or the competent county government office. This is usually the simplest category.

The second group is zártkert property. Under the current land-registration rules, zártkert is a special type of outlying-area land unit, but the word “zártkert” does not in itself determine whether the Land Transaction Act applies. If the property is registered under an agricultural or forestry land-use category, the Act applies. If, under a municipal decree, it has been registered as land exempt from cultivation through the procedure in Section 72/E of the Land Registry Act, its treatment under the land transaction rules may be different. Its permitted use under the local building regulations (HÉSZ) and the legal status of any building must also be examined separately. This is an area in which the wording of a property  can be particularly misleading.

The third group is agricultural and forestry land as defined by the Land Transaction Act. This may include not only arable land, meadow, pasture and forest, but also vineyards, gardens and orchards, irrespective of whether the land lies inside or outside the built-up area. A Hungarian natural person, or a national of a Member State, who is not registered as a farmer may generally acquire no more than one hectare of land, subject to the statutory exceptions. A foreign natural person who is not a Member State national is generally prohibited from acquiring ownership of such land.

This might also interest you: The zártkert trap: when a rural Hungarian property is not what it seems

Foreign buyers in Hungary: EU/EEA nationals versus those requiring authorisation

Nationals of EU and EEA Member States, and persons accorded equivalent treatment under an international treaty, may generally acquire property that does not qualify as agricultural or forestry land without authorisation. Where land within the meaning of the Land Transaction Act is concerned, however, the Act’s restrictions also apply to them: a Member State national who is not registered as a farmer may generally acquire up to one hectare, subject to the statutory exceptions.

Foreign buyers who are not Member State nationals and are subject to the authorisation requirement, including UK nationals following Brexit and, as a general rule, US, Canadian, Australian and Chinese nationals, may acquire property that does not qualify as agricultural or forestry land with the approval of the competent government office. Government Decree 251/2014 (X. 2.) sets a 45-day administrative time limit for the procedure. A foreign natural person who is not a Member State national is, however, generally prohibited from acquiring ownership of land falling within the Land Transaction Act.

A corporate structure: a solution, but not in every case

In some cases, a foreign buyer can structure the purchase of rural property through a Hungarian limited liability company (korlátolt felelősségű társaság, or Kft.). A Kft. incorporated in Hungary is a domestic legal entity. When it acquires property that does not qualify as agricultural or forestry land, the authorisation rules applicable to foreign natural persons do not govern the acquisition. This is not, however, a universal loophole. A corporate structure has tax, accounting, financing, use and exit implications, and must therefore be tailored to the purpose of the transaction.

The Kft. structure also has clear limits. Under the Land Transaction Act, the acquisition of land ownership by legal entities is generally prohibited, subject only to narrow, expressly listed exceptions. A standard Kft. established to purchase real estate therefore cannot be used as a vehicle for acquiring agricultural land.

The concept of a “newcomer” (betelepülő) under Act XLVIII of 2025 is defined by reference to a natural person, so a Kft. acting as buyer is not a newcomer. Even so, the land transaction rules, pre-emption rights and local requirements applicable to the particular property must be checked in every case. A Kft. also entails continuing administration, including bookkeeping, annual accounts, tax obligations and, where the statutory conditions are met, an audit.

What foreign buyers in Hungary cannot bypass

Certain principles cannot be bypassed. If the property qualifies as land under the Land Transaction Act, the first question is whether the buyer is eligible to acquire ownership at all and, if so, what acreage limits, pre-emption rights and authority procedures apply. Farmer status is not the same as holding any one qualification, such as the Hungarian Aranykalászos gazda agricultural qualification; it is a registered legal status under the Act and its implementing rules.

A foreign natural person who is not a Member State national is generally prohibited from acquiring agricultural or forestry land. For other real property, a foreign buyer who is subject to the authorisation requirement needs government-office approval. Local identity protection rules apply only where the municipality has introduced the relevant protective measure by decree and the buyer does not fall within a statutory exemption. For zártkert property, it is also necessary to determine whether the property qualifies as land, whether the Section 72/E procedure for registration as land exempt from cultivation is available, and whether the legal status of any building is in order.

A practical guide: what should a foreign buyer do?

Classify the property. Obtain a full legal classification based on the title sheet, cadastral map data and other land-registry records, not on the . Assess the buyer. Compare the buyer’s nationality, farmer status and intended purchasing structure, whether individual or corporate, with the property’s legal classification. Check local rules. Review the local building regulations (HÉSZ), the zoning plan and municipal decrees, including any local identity protection decree. Verify the building and plan the structure. Confirm the building’s legal status under construction law, then plan any foreign acquisition authorisation, land transaction procedure or corporate structure that may be required.

The order matters, because a single point of legal classification can change the entire transaction.

The map that helps buyers navigate

Hungary’s rural property market is widely open to foreign buyers, but the legal classification of the property and the status of the buyer are decisive. Residential and holiday properties that do not qualify as agricultural or forestry land can generally be acquired, with authorisation required for certain foreign buyers, while zártkert properties require especially careful classification. Land governed by the Land Transaction Act is not closed to all foreign nationals: Member State nationals may acquire it subject to the conditions of the Act, whereas acquisition by foreign natural persons who are not Member State nationals is generally prohibited. Buyers who clarify this distinction at the outset are far less likely to build the transaction on the wrong legal structure.

Legislation cited

This article provides general market and legal information only and does not constitute individual legal advice. Before any transaction, a lawyer should review the particular legal position of both the property and the buyer. The English titles of Hungarian legislation are descriptive translations; the Hungarian-language legal text is authoritative. Legislation checked as at 3 September 2026.

World.title: Autumn is here: Summer’s final heatwave fades as Hungary braces for chilly nights
World.content:
Hungary is finally set to feel the arrival of autumn, with a significant cooling trend expected over the coming days. After temperatures soared to 30–34°C earlier this week — around 7–9°C above the seasonal average — a cold front is now sweeping across the country, bringing cooler temperatures, cloudier skies and showers.

According to HungaroMet, temperatures rose further on Wednesday ahead of the approaching cold front, reaching 30–35°C in places. The front then began moving into the country from the northwest, bringing stronger winds and stormy weather, particularly to western Hungary.

The Őrség region was already experiencing overcast skies and strong winds on Wednesday afternoon as the change in weather began to make itself felt.

Temperatures could drop below 10°C at night

The coming days will be considerably cooler. On Thursday, daytime temperatures are expected to fall to between 21 and 29°C, while scattered rain, showers and thunderstorms could occur in the evening. Night-time temperatures will also become noticeably lower, ranging from 13 to 19°C on Thursday.

The biggest change is expected over the weekend, when temperatures could fall to around 10°C or even below in some areas overnight, particularly in the northern counties. Despite the chilly nights, daytime temperatures are still expected to remain above 20°C in most places.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

A Mediterranean cyclone could briefly bring the heat back

The weather could remain unsettled, however, as a Mediterranean cyclone is expected to approach from the southwest. Its exact path remains uncertain because the system has not yet fully developed.

The cyclone could temporarily bring warmer air back into Hungary, particularly to the south-eastern parts of the country. As a result, temperatures in these areas could climb back towards 30°C on Friday, with some locations potentially exceeding that mark.

The brief warm spell would, however, come after the arrival of the cold front and is not expected to signal a return to the prolonged summer heat experienced earlier this week. For now, the message from forecasters is that Hungary’s exceptionally warm summer weather is giving way to much cooler autumn-like conditions, particularly after dark.

World.title: Hungary loses another EU Court case over frozen Russian assets and Ukraine aid
World.content:
The EU General Court has dismissed Hungary’s legal challenge against a decision to use extraordinary revenues from frozen Russian state assets to support Ukraine’s armed forces. However, the court did not rule that Hungary’s legal arguments were unfounded: it said it had no jurisdiction to review the political and strategic decision at issue.

Court rejects Hungary’s challenge

Hungary has lost another legal battle against the European Union after the EU General Court dismissed a case brought by the Hungarian government against a decision concerning military support for Ukraine, HVG reported.

The case, originally launched under Viktor Orbán’s government, centred on a decision by the committee of the European Peace Facility (EPF) to allocate extraordinary revenues generated by frozen Russian state assets to support the Ukrainian armed forces.

Importantly, the court did not dismiss Hungary’s case because it found the country’s legal arguments to be without merit. Instead, it concluded that the EU courts generally do not have jurisdiction to review the legality of political or strategic decisions adopted within the EU’s Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP) in circumstances such as this one.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

What is the European Peace Facility?

The European Peace Facility was established by the EU Council in 2021 to finance the bloc’s foreign and security policy actions. In May 2024, the Council adopted two decisions concerning extraordinary revenues generated by immobilised Russian state assets.

The first established rules for using the revenues to support Ukraine, while the second concerned the actual allocation of the funds. Hungary supported the first decision but constructively abstained from the second.

Under the EU’s system of constructive abstention, a member state can refrain from supporting a decision without blocking its adoption, while making clear that it does not consider itself bound to implement it.

On 21 June 2024, the EPF committee subsequently decided, through a written procedure, to allocate the first tranche of extraordinary revenues from the frozen Russian assets to support the Ukrainian armed forces.

The committee took the view that Hungary, having constructively abstained from the earlier decision, could not participate in the vote on the allocation. Budapest challenged this position before the EU General Court.

If you missed it: Hungary blocks Ukraine’s EU accession again: Budapest demands action on Hungarian minority rights

Hungary argued that EU rules had been breached

The Hungarian government argued that the EPF committee had acted unlawfully, including by allegedly violating the applicable voting rules. Hungary also claimed that fundamental EU principles had been breached, including the rule of law, equality between member states and the democratic functioning of the European Union.

The court, however, did not examine these arguments on their merits. The judges acknowledged that the European Peace Facility has legal personality, meaning that a challenge to a decision adopted by its committee could, in principle, fall within the General Court’s jurisdiction. The court nevertheless reached a different conclusion when considering the substance of the dispute.

Have you heard? A surprise exception for Hungary: US gives Hungarians visa priority

Why the court said it could not rule on the decision

The General Court pointed out that EU courts generally have limited jurisdiction over the CFSP. Although the EU treaties provide for certain exceptions, the court concluded that Hungary’s case did not fall within any of them. According to the ruling, the EPF committee’s decision was directly linked to political and strategic decisions taken as part of the EU’s foreign and security policy.

The contested decision determined that revenues generated by frozen Russian assets would be used to finance military equipment for Ukraine’s armed forces. It also identified the specific assistance measure for which the money would be used.

Because of this direct connection to CFSP political and strategic decisions, the General Court concluded that it was not empowered to assess whether the decision complied with EU law.

Hungary can appeal

The ruling does not necessarily mark the end of the legal dispute. Hungary can appeal the General Court’s decision to the Court of Justice of the European Union within two months and ten days of the judgment being notified.

However, any appeal would be limited to points of law, rather than allowing the entire case to be reheard on its facts. The case comes amid continued disputes between Budapest and Brussels over Hungary’s position on support for Ukraine, the use of frozen Russian assets and the EU’s response to Russia’s war against Ukraine.

World.title: Man stabbed several times by 18-year-old on busy Budapest tram
World.content:
A 33-year-old man was seriously injured after being stabbed several times in the thigh during a confrontation on a Budapest tram on Wednesday morning. Police arrested the suspected attacker within minutes.

Passenger stabbed during confrontation

The incident happened at around 9:50 AM on Wednesday on tram 4, near the Wesselényi Street/Erzsébet Boulevard stop, according to the Budapest Police Headquarters. Police said an 18-year-old man stabbed a 33-year-old passenger several times in the inner thigh before getting off the tram.

According to HVG that shared information from the National Ambulance Service, the injured man suffered a serious thigh injury and was taken to hospital. The driver and several passengers reportedly rushed to help the injured man and attempted to provide assistance until paramedics arrived.

The suspected attacker did not remain at the scene for long. Officers from the Rapid Response Police arrested him within minutes in Budapest’s District 8 and took him to the District 7 police station, where he is being questioned.

Tram services briefly disrupted

The incident also temporarily disrupted public transport along one of Budapest’s busiest tram routes. Due to police action, replacement buses operated between Blaha Lujza Square and Oktogon, replacing trams 4 and 6 for a short period.

According to BKK Info, the disruption began shortly before 10 AM, while normal tram services were restored at around 10:50 AM. Trams 4 and 6 have since resumed running along their full routes. Police have not disclosed further details about the circumstances that led to the confrontation or the suspected motive.
