World.title: Exclusive interview – Chinese Ambassador: Hungary-China ties on a ‘steady track’ as Budapest emerges as a potential robotics hub
World.content:
China’s ambassador to Budapest, Gong Tao, says Beijing remains confident in the long-term development of Hungary-China relations under Prime Minister Péter Magyar, while signalling opportunities for deeper cooperation in robotics, artificial intelligence and other high-tech industries. In an exclusive interview with Daily News Hungary, the ambassador also discussed the Budapest-Belgrade railway, BYD’s controversial appointment of Péter Szijjártó, the Semcorp case, cheap Chinese online shopping and efforts to attract more Chinese tourists to Hungary.

Daily News Hungary (DNH): Péter Magyar and his government have now passed the symbolic 100-day mark in office. What have been your first impressions of the new Hungarian government, and how would you assess the development of Hungary–China relations since the change of government?

His Excellency Gong Tao: Under the leadership of Prime Minister Magyar, the new government has been advancing the reform and restructuring of government institutions, worked to secure EU funds, led the Hungarian people in tackling the challenges posed by extreme heat and drought, and achieved notable progress in both domestic and foreign affairs. I would like to extend my congratulations on these achievements.

Regarding China-Hungary relations, I still clearly recall Prime Minister Magyar’s remarks at his first international press conference, when he expressed appreciation to the Chinese side for respecting the choice of the Hungarian people and highlighted that developing relations with China serves not only Hungary’s interests but also the common interests of both countries. From his remarks, I perceived the positive attitude of the Hungarian government toward developing relations with China, which left a strong “first impression” on me.

Since the new government took office, the leaders of our two countries have maintained good interaction through exchanges of letters and messages, with a common understanding of moving China-Hungary relations forward. I have met with several ministers of the Hungarian government and maintained close communication with them on important issues concerning bilateral relations and cooperation. China-Hungary relations are kept on a track of steady development.

Developing China-Hungary relations serves the common interests of both sides and meets the expectations of our peoples. As Chinese Ambassador to Hungary, I am full of confidence in the long-term development of China-Hungary relations and am ready to work with the Hungarian government and friends from all sectors to deepen friendly exchanges and cooperation between China and Hungary across various fields, so as to achieve mutual benefit and win-win outcomes and bring greater benefits to the peoples of both countries.

Read our previous interview with His Excellency Gong Tao: Exclusive interview: China’s ambassador to Hungary talks government ties, the Budapest–Belgrade railway and more

Daily News Hungary (DNH): The Budapest–Belgrade railway is one of the flagship projects of Hungarian–Chinese economic cooperation. Passenger services are expected to begin once the remaining testing and safety procedures have been completed. What can you tell us about the current status of the project, and when do you realistically expect passengers to be able to travel directly between Budapest and Belgrade?

H. E. Gong Tao: The Budapest-Belgrade Railway is an important government-to-government cooperation project between China and Hungary. Thanks to the joint efforts of both sides, all infrastructure construction on the Hungarian section has been completed. Freight services were officially launched on February 27, with operations kept safe and stable. The railway is expected to significantly strengthen Hungary’s geographical advantage as a transportation hub in Europe and contribute to regional economic development.

Chinese participating businesses, consistently guided by the principles of green development, environmental protection, and regulatory compliance, strictly adhering to EU and Hungarian laws and regulations as well as railway technical standards. Meeting challenges with painstaking efforts, they have applied China’s advanced railway construction management experience, technologies, and equipment to the project, while also training a large number of specialized local professionals in Hungary.

Regarding the launch of passenger services, Chinese enterprises involved in the project have been working with MÁV since last October to conduct ETCS testing. The Hungarian government attaches great importance to this matter and expressed hope for passenger services to open at an early date. Now, both sides are working faster toward this goal.

The Chinese Embassy will continue to play its coordinating role and work closely with the Hungarian government and MÁV to support the Chinese participating enterprises in completing the remaining testing work on the Hungarian section to a high standard and launching passenger services as soon as possible, so that the Hungarian people can experience the convenience brought by the railway’s upgrade and modernization.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Daily News Hungary (DNH): BYD recently appointed former Hungarian foreign minister Péter Szijjártó to a senior international role dealing with external relations and new business development. The appointment has generated considerable political and public debate in Hungary. How is this appointment viewed from the Chinese side?

H. E. Gong Tao: This is Mr. Szijjártó’s personal career choice as well as a market-based hiring decision by the enterprise, on which we have no comment. The Chinese side takes note of the investigations conducted by the Hungarian government in accordance with the law. The Chinese government has always required Chinese enterprises, including BYD, to strictly abide by Hungarian and EU laws and regulations and to actively fulfill their corporate social responsibilities.

In recent years, BYD has deepened its presence in the Hungarian market and continuously advanced the localization of employment and supply chains. BYD has invested in and built a bus plant, a battery plant, and an electric vehicle production base in Hungary, while also establishing its European headquarters and R&D center in the country. These projects are expected to create more employment and development opportunities for Hungary and contribute to the country’s sci-tech innovation and green transition. The company is also active in local community affairs, cooperating with Hungarian universities and vocational education institutions, and strengthening its integration into local society.

Economic and trade cooperation between China and Hungary is and must be mutually beneficial and win-win. China stands ready to work with Hungary to further deepen practical cooperation for the benefit of the two peoples.

Daily News Hungary (DNH): A few days ago, the Chinese Embassy shared Semcorp Hungary’s open letter and stressed that China consistently requires Chinese companies operating abroad to comply with local laws, fulfil their social responsibilities and take strict measures to protect the environment. Why did the Embassy consider it important to emphasise this message publicly at this particular moment?

H. E. Gong Tao: In June this year, Semcorp’s Debrecen facility was ordered by the Hungarian authorities to suspend production on suspicion of environmental pollution. Following the incident, the company actively cooperated with the competent authorities in carrying out rectification and inspections. Meanwhile, it invited retesting by qualified and professional laboratories and sought professional opinions from environmental experts. The retesting and assessment results were disclosed by the company. The conclusion was that no evidence was found to indicate that the factory had caused the environmental pollution stated in the shutdown order. The relevant reports were also submitted by Semcorp to the Hungarian authorities.

The Embassy’s forwarding of the company’s open letter was intended both to ease concerns among the Hungarian public about possible pollution and to urge and remind all Chinese businesses operating in Hungary to strictly abide by local laws, actively fulfill their social responsibilities, and adopt rigorous measures to protect the environment, so as to better integrate corporate development with local social and environmental interests.

We fully understand and respect the Hungarian government’s policy of strict supervision of the battery and other key sectors, which reflects its commitment to environmental protection and the sustainable development of businesses in the long term. At the same time, we hope that, while conducting supervision in accordance with the law, the Hungarian side will provide a fair, just, transparent, predictable and non-discriminatory business environment for all Chinese and foreign investors alike.

Daily News Hungary (DNH): China’s rapid development in humanoid robotics has attracted enormous international attention. Just recently, a Chinese-backed humanoid robot production facility was established in Šabac, Serbia, with plans for significantly larger production in the future. Could Hungary also become a manufacturing or development centre for Chinese robotics?

H. E. Gong Tao: Recently, the humanoid robot factory jointly built by China and Serbia officially commenced production. This is Europe’s first mass-production base for humanoid robots and represents a new direction for deepening practical cooperation between China and friendly countries.

This also represents an area where China-Hungary cooperation holds great promise.

First, there is a high degree of alignment in our priority areas for development. Both China and Hungary are committed to achieving high-quality development, with a focus on high value-added industries, commitment to sci-tech innovation and the cultivation of high-quality talent, and close attention to cutting-edge technologies such as AI and intelligent robotics.

Second, there is a solid foundation for industrial cooperation between us. Robotics and automobile manufacturing share many technological commonalities and are mutually reinforcing at the industrial level. Practical cooperation between China and Hungary in new energy and automobile manufacturing has already yielded fruitful results, laying a solid foundation for both sides to further explore cooperation in the field of robotics.

Third, there is enormous potential for future cooperation. China and Hungary are already exploring cooperation in such fields as AI and embodied robotics. For instance, Unitree’s products are quite popular in Hungary; Chinese and Hungarian businesses and institutions have initiated cooperation in autonomous driving; and universities and research institutes from both countries are also exploring future opportunities for cooperation.

Daily News Hungary (DNH): Many Hungarians are interested in the “Temu topic.” Since July, the European Union has imposed a €3 customs duty on low-value parcels entering the EU, a measure that particularly affects platforms such as Temu, Shein and AliExpress. Many European consumers appreciated these platforms precisely because they offered extremely low prices. Do you see the new rules as legitimate consumer and market protection, or as a form of protectionism directed primarily at Chinese businesses? Is there a way back to the era of extremely cheap Chinese online shopping for European consumers?

H. E. Gong Tao: Cross-border e-commerce is a new form of trade that has emerged alongside the growing trend of global consumption and benefits hundreds of millions of consumers. Policy adjustments in relevant areas should aim to facilitate trade. China respects the EU’s customs regulatory sovereignty and understands its concerns over false declarations and tax compliance. However, the fact that the new small-parcel rule passes costs on to EU consumers and deals a blow to normal cross-border e-commerce trade is also a matter of concern. At the same time, we oppose de facto country-specific discrimination.

The Chinese government always stands for an open and inclusive multilateral trading environment and opposes all forms of unilateralism and trade protectionism. We hope that the EU can uphold the principles of a market economy and non-discrimination, and create a fair, transparent, and predictable business environment for businesses from all countries, including Chinese ones, rather than making consumers bear the costs of trade barriers and protectionism.

Daily News Hungary (DNH): Hungary has become an increasingly visible European destination for Chinese travellers. What do you think Hungary could do better to attract more Chinese tourists and encourage them to stay longer and explore destinations beyond Budapest?

H. E. Gong Tao: I am pleased to see that, with exchanges and cooperation deepening between China and Hungary across various fields, Hungary is becoming an increasingly popular European destination for Chinese tourists. This is attributable to the high level of political mutual trust between the two countries and also the shared aspiration of our two peoples for mutual understanding and friendship.

Hungary boasts a rich historical and cultural heritage as well as beautiful natural scenery. Beyond Budapest, Lake Balaton, the Tokaj wine region, and other destinations also boast their own unique charms. I believe that by further optimizing flight and domestic transport connections, improving services such as Chinese-language guided tours, mobile payment, catering and accommodation, launching more themed programs that integrate hot springs, gourmet food, wine, and folk experiences, and strengthening targeted promotion in China, Hungary can attract more Chinese tourists to explore the country in greater depth and encourage them to extend their stays.

China stands ready to deepen tourism cooperation with Hungary and promote people-to-people exchanges and mutual understanding, to inject new vitality into China-Hungary friendship.

Daily News Hungary (DNH): The Chinese Embassy and the China Cultural Centre in Budapest have invested considerable effort in bringing Hungarian and Chinese culture closer together. Based on your experience, how receptive are Hungarians to Chinese culture, and which programmes or initiatives have proved particularly successful in strengthening mutual understanding between the two countries?

H. E. Gong Tao: In recent years, the growing participation of Hungarian people in various cultural activities has reflected an increasing interest in and appreciation of Chinese culture. Traditional Chinese festivals, calligraphy, music, martial arts, and cuisine are all widely popular. To better engage with the Hungarian public and connect with them on a more personal level, the Embassy recently launched its official TikTok account. The account has attracted widespread attention from Hungarian friends, garnering more than 600,000 views and nearly 10,000 followers in just one month. Many of them have also left comments asking a wide range of interesting questions about China.

It is heartening to see that Hungarian friends are not only interested in China’s traditional culture but are also increasingly eager to learn about contemporary China’s development and social life. Events such as Spring Festival temple fairs, Chinese film screenings, art exhibitions, and youth exchange programs have received enthusiastic responses, bringing the peoples of the two countries closer together in a direct, warm, and interactive way. Recently, young people from Hungarian universities, think tanks, and media organizations have visited China’s Hunan, Hubei and Fujian provinces, witnessing firsthand the country’s development and transformation, experiencing its rich and diverse culture, and coming away with good memories.

Looking ahead, China stands ready to further facilitate exchanges and cooperation with Hungary among cultural institutions, schools, local communities, and young people, so that mutual learning among civilizations can better promote people-to-people bonds and consolidate the social and public foundation for China-Hungary friendship.

Daily News Hungary (DNH): Finally, if you looked five or ten years ahead, what would you like Hungary–China relations to look like? What would you consider the greatest opportunity – and the greatest risk – for the relationship between the two countries?

H. E. Gong Tao: The traditional friendship between China and Hungary has a long and rich history. The close friendship and cooperation between the two countries represent an important historic achievement, built through more than seven decades of dedicated efforts by the two governments and peoples. With enormous potential for cooperation and a promising future, China-Hungary relations are well positioned to reach new heights.

Over the next five years, China will steadily advance the implementation of the various tasks set out in its 15th Five-Year Plan. Over the coming decade, it will continue to work toward the goal of basically achieving socialist modernization. Hungary, for its part, is committed to building, by 2030, a “human and well-functioning Hungary.”

Looking ahead, the greatest opportunity for our two countries lies in our shared pursuit of modernization and the improvement of people’s well-being. This common aspiration has enabled China and Hungary to remain committed to moving in the same direction and making progress together amid 77 years of changes and challenges in the international landscape. It will also provide strong impetus for the two countries to further align our development strategies and explore cooperation in emerging and innovative fields, including the digital economy, new energy, artificial intelligence, and intelligent manufacturing.

There is no fundamental conflict of interests between China and Hungary. The greatest challenges facing our bilateral relationship arise instead from an increasingly turbulent and complex international environment. Today, the world is undergoing profound changes unseen in a century, while instability and uncertainty are on the rise. These developments will inevitably pose new challenges to China-Hungary relations.

Looking to the future, it is important for our two countries to continue upholding the principles of mutual respect, equality, and win-win cooperation; strengthen dialogue and communication; jointly explore opportunities for cooperation; work together to address risks and challenges; and shoulder our shared international responsibilities. By doing so, we can add new dimensions to China-Hungary relations and ensure that our enduring friendship continues to flourish in the new era.

World.title: Hungary blocks Ukraine’s EU accession again: Budapest demands action on Hungarian minority rights
World.content:
Hungary has once again blocked progress on Ukraine’s EU accession talks, preventing the approval of screening results needed to open two key negotiating clusters. Budapest says Kyiv must first take further steps to guarantee the rights of Ukraine’s Hungarian minority.

Hungary blocks two more accession clusters

Hungary has again prevented the European Union from moving forward with the next stage of Ukraine’s accession negotiations.

The EU’s Working Party on Enlargement (COELA) failed on 8 September to approve the screening results for Ukraine’s negotiating clusters 2 and 3, with Hungary maintaining its opposition to opening the two areas, according to EU sources cited by Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda.

European diplomats reportedly made another attempt to persuade Budapest to change its position, but Hungary did not back down.

“Member states have not changed their positions. Hungary does not agree to move forward with the opening of clusters 2 and 3 for Ukraine,” a source told the Ukrainian outlet.

EU accession negotiations are divided into clusters, grouping together related areas of EU law and policy.

Cluster 2 covers the internal market, including areas such as the free movement of goods, services, capital and people. Cluster 3 focuses on competitiveness and inclusive growth, covering areas such as digital transformation, taxation, economic and monetary policy, and social policy.

Budapest links progress to minority rights

The latest blockade follows a similar decision last week, when Hungary again refused to approve the screening results required to open the two clusters. The Hungarian government has said it will not support further progress in Ukraine’s accession process until Kyiv takes the necessary steps to fulfil its bilateral commitments concerning national minority rights.

The issue is particularly sensitive for Budapest because of the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia, in western Ukraine. Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said on Monday that progress had nevertheless been made in negotiations over the rights of Transcarpathian Hungarians.

According to the minister, minority-rights consultations resumed on 20 May, and Ukraine has undertaken to incorporate the rights agreed during bilateral talks into legislation. She pointed to a decision by the Ukrainian government to preserve the network of small educational institutions and continue providing them with state funding from 1 September as the first tangible result.

Orbán also said the EU had, at Hungary’s initiative, recorded that Ukraine’s minority action plan should be brought into line with the outcome of the Hungarian-Ukrainian negotiations. “Now it is time for implementation; both sides are working on this,” she wrote.

If you missed it: FM Anita Orbán reports progress on minority rights for Hungarians in Ukraine

Hungary’s position has changed under Péter Magyar

The latest developments mark a somewhat different approach from that of former prime minister Viktor Orbán. Orbán strongly opposed Ukraine’s EU membership and repeatedly cited concerns over the rights of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine. His government blocked progress on the opening of the first negotiating cluster for years.

Under Prime Minister Péter Magyar, however, Budapest has sought a different approach, reaching what Magyar described as a “historic agreement” with Ukraine in June. The agreement is intended to formally guarantee the Transcarpathian Hungarian community’s educational, cultural, linguistic and political rights.

However, Hungary has continued to use its position in the EU accession process to push for the implementation of those commitments. In July, Budapest agreed to allow the EU to send an official letter to Ukraine and Moldova concerning the launch of the procedure for opening cluster 6, but it maintained its blocking position on the remaining four clusters.

Moldova caught up in the dispute

The issue is also affecting Moldova’s accession process. Hungary had indicated that it was prepared to approve the screening results for Moldova’s cluster 3, but other EU member states have so far opposed treating Moldova and Ukraine separately in the accession process. As a result, progress on Moldova’s cluster has also become entangled with the dispute.

World.title: Austria reportedly takes Hungary to Brussels over Paks weir, but Vienna denies filing a complaint
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar has accused Austria of complaining to Brussels over the emergency construction of a weir on the Danube near the Paks Nuclear Power Plant. Vienna, however, says it has not filed a formal complaint, while confirming that it has raised concerns about the project with Hungarian authorities and EU institutions.

Austria challenges Hungary over Paks project

A new dispute is emerging between Hungary and Austria over the controversial weir built on the Danube to help keep the Paks Nuclear Power Plant operating during periods of extremely low water levels.

Péter Magyar claimed on Wednesday that Austria had “filed a complaint against Hungary in Brussels” over the construction.

“The only reason why the Paks Nuclear Power Plant is currently able to operate without interruption is thanks to the weir that has been built,” the Hungarian prime minister said in a Facebook post. He then took a swipe at Austria, adding: “It would be nice if the Austrians were this active regarding the asbestos issue as well.”

Austria, however, disputes the description of its actions.

According to Hungarian news outlet Világgazdaság, Austria’s Ministry of Innovation, Mobility and Infrastructure told the APA news agency that it had not filed a complaint. The ministry did confirm that both the European Commission and the Budapest-based, non-EU Danube Commission are in direct contact with the relevant Hungarian authorities regarding the issue.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar during a recent visit to Dunaszentbenedek near the ongoing Danube works at Paks. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

Why was the Paks weir built?

The dispute comes after an exceptionally difficult summer for Hungary’s only nuclear power plant. Record-low water levels in the Danube severely affected Paks, which relies on river water for cooling. At the height of the crisis, the plant was forced to reduce its output dramatically, and a near-total shutdown became a real possibility.

Hungary ultimately avoided a complete shutdown by keeping one turbine operating during the most critical period. The government then approved an emergency solution: the construction of a bottom weir on the Danube near Paks.

The structure was intended to raise water levels around the plant’s water intake and ensure that sufficient cooling water could continue to reach the facility even when the river level was exceptionally low. The measure was implemented at remarkable speed and helped Hungary navigate the immediate threat to the plant’s operation.

Paks has since returned to full capacity, making the emergency infrastructure particularly significant for Hungary’s energy security.

Austria says EU countries have raised concerns

Although Vienna says it did not formally lodge a complaint, Austria has clearly been involved in discussions about the project. The Austrian ministry said representatives of countries participating in the EU Strategy for the Danube Region had developed a joint position on the issue.

That position has already been sent to Hungarian Transport Minister Dávid Vitézy and Prime Minister Péter Magyar, according to the Austrian ministry.

The EU Strategy for the Danube Region was adopted in 2011 during Hungary’s presidency of the Council of the European Union. It brings together countries across the Danube region to address issues including transport, environmental protection, water management and economic development.

Importantly, however, the strategy is not legally binding. That means the existence of a joint position does not in itself amount to an EU legal procedure against Hungary.

Could Brussels launch proceedings against Hungary?

The European Commission is responsible for enforcing EU law. If Hungary were found to have breached binding EU legislation, the Commission could potentially launch an infringement procedure. Such a process generally begins with dialogue and formal requests for information before potentially escalating to legal action.

At present, however, the information available does not indicate that Austria has formally triggered such a procedure against Hungary. Instead, the Austrian government says it has communicated its concerns through the relevant European and regional channels. That distinction is important as the political row develops.

Magyar’s statement suggested that Austria had taken Hungary to Brussels over the project, while Vienna’s account describes discussions and a joint regional position rather than a formal complaint.

World.title: Hungary releases classified government decisions from the past 16 years
World.content:
The Hungarian government has begun publishing previously classified government decisions dating back 16 years, with the first batch revealing billions of forints in state-funded research, polling and media analysis linked to the pro-government Századvég group. Around 100 classified decisions are expected to be made public.

First batch reveals billions in public spending

The Hungarian government has published the first batch of previously classified government decisions issued over the past 16 years, opening up a new window into how public money was spent under Viktor Orbán’s governments.

The so-called “3000-series” government decisions were classified and were originally intended for sensitive matters involving, for example, national security or defence. However, the current government says its review has found that the classification system was also used to conceal decisions whose confidentiality can no longer be justified.

The first documents concern state-funded research and studies commissioned from the Századvég group. According to the government, the first batch contains 14 decisions worth a combined roughly HUF 65 billion. The documents include decisions covering public opinion polling, media research and analysis, financial consultancy and strategic advice.

Billions spent on polling and media research

Among the documents now available are decisions dating from several different years. One 2014 decision authorised more than HUF 500 million for financial consultancy. A 2018 decision allocated HUF 1.8 billion for work involving European public opinion, media monitoring and research into pensioners. In 2019, the government approved HUF 12.2 billion for public opinion polling and consultancy.

Two particularly large contracts date from 2022: one involved media analysis in Hungary and Europe worth HUF 7.1 billion, while another allocated HUF 9.6 billion for public opinion research in Hungary, the European Union and the Balkans. The latter decision was originally classified until 3 August 2032.

The released document even shows the formal structure of the classified decision, including the signature and official stamp of the prime minister’s office at the time.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

What is Századvég?

Századvég has long been closely associated with Hungary’s political right. The organisation’s roots go back to the generation that founded Fidesz, with Viktor Orbán and current Fidesz politician László Kövér among those who were involved with the group’s journal in its early years.

After 2010, when Orbán’s Fidesz returned to government, Századvég’s role and state funding expanded significantly. The organisation has provided public opinion polling, political and policy analysis, media research and strategic consultancy for the Hungarian state.

The new government’s website claims that Századvég became one of the main analytical and consultancy centres supporting the Orbán government’s policies, while receiving billions of forints in government contracts over the years. The government also says the newly released documents demonstrate how classified decisions were used to conceal some of these expenditures from public scrutiny.

If you missed it: Magyar government targets thousands of billions in Orbán-era private equity deals

More secret decisions to be published

The publication is not limited to the first batch. The government says the process will continue, with around 100 previously classified government decisions ultimately expected to be made public. That could provide further insight into decisions made during the 16 years of Orbán-led governments, particularly where significant amounts of public money were involved.

The publication comes after the new government had already raised questions about the scale of state spending on Századvég. According to Telex, the Orbán government paid the organisation more than HUF 7.6 billion between January and March 2026 alone for various studies and measurements. The organisation had already begun a strategic “shift in focus” and layoffs in early May, shortly before the new government took office.

Government says it will pursue the matter

Ruff Bálint, the minister heading the Prime Minister’s Office, previously told Telex that the government was preparing to publish around 100 classified “3000-series” decisions. He said these included decisions concerning hidden commissions for Századvég studies and estimated that HUF 20–30 billion had been spent on the organisation in recent years.

Ruff also said the government planned to file a criminal complaint over the matter. The new administration has already taken similar legal steps in another case involving public funding: the Prime Minister’s Office recently filed a complaint concerning almost HUF 28 billion in state support received by the Kommentár Foundation.

World.title: Letter from Brussels: Glorification of Mladic a Test for EU’s Position on ‘Dear Aleksandar’
World.content:
Aleksandar Vucic might have unintentionally found his campaign message, and it’s far from subtle: the European Union doesn’t want us. The Serbian president has been road-testing the claim for weeks now, but the death and funeral of Ratko Mladic have given it a stage no strategist could have built better.

Mladic died on August 27, aged 84, in The Hague, his final years spent serving a life sentence for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes committed during the 1992-95 Bosnian war, atrocities the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia called “amongst the most heinous known to humankind”.

His body was flown home on a Serbian government plane. It lay in state at the Church of St Luke in Belgrade. On September 7, he was buried with military honours, his coffin wrapped in the Serbian flag, his officer’s cap and sabre resting on top, the Patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox Church presiding.

Vucic did not attend. His counterpart from Uzbekistan was visiting. It was a tidy piece of choreography: the coffin arrived in Belgrade on September 3, but the family “decided” the funeral would take place exactly on the day when Vucic couldn’t be there. But the president was represented anyway – by his son, and by cabinet ministers from Serbia’s ruling party.

World.title: Serbia’s Vucic Calls Early Parliamentary Elections for October 25
World.content:
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic on Tuesday set a date for early parliamentary elections on October 25, signing a decree dissolving parliament and the decision calling the elections – in which he is expected to run for prime minister, facing down a strong challenge from opponents.

“We need election results that will clearly demonstrate and determine the will of the citizens as to where, in what direction, and along which path Serbia is heading,” he said, adding that Serbia has been enduring “turbulence for more than a year and a half”.

Student-led protests have gripped the country since November 2024, sparked by the collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad that left 16 people dead, sparking nationwide outrage over alleged official corruption and negligence. The protests have posed the strongest challenge to Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party since it came to power in 2012.

Vucic claimed the “turbulence” in society was not merely the result of “conflicts between political parties or political actors here in Serbia” but also involved “significant interference by foreign powers”. He and his Progressive Party have often claimed that foreign states, including European countries, have been involved in supporting or inciting the student-led protests.

In his comments on Tuesday, however, he also insisted that Serbia, an EU candidate state, had chosen “a good European path, while [also] preserving traditional friendships, national pride, and dignity” – referencing Belgrade’s continued friendly relationship with Russia.

As one of the reasons for calling early elections, Vucic cited the organisation of the high-profile international EXPO 2027 exhibition, which will be held in Belgrade starting in May next year.

“If it were not for these tensions, if it were not for these political disagreements and conflicts, we certainly would not need [elections]. But any delay would jeopardise both EXPO and the survival of democracy as the best form of political system in our country,” he said.

On Monday, Prime Minister Djuro Macut proposed the dissolution of parliament, which was adopted by the government and sent to the President as part of the official procedure.

Many experts see the upcoming elections as the most challenging for Vucic and his party since 2012. The main opponent this time is Student List, made by the students who have been protesting. Its official candidates have been chosen by student groups whose names haven’t been published yet.

“The elections have been called after 492 days. It’s time for victory,” student organising group Students Blockade wrote on X on Tuesday. It was alluding to May 2025, when it first publicly demanded early elections.

Last Saturday, the Main Board of the Progressive Party named Vucic as their candidate for prime minister and as first on the electoral list “Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia” at the upcoming elections.

At the December 2023 elections, the Progressive Party won 46.75 per cent of the votes, while the largest opposition coalition, Serbia against Violence, won 23.66 per cent. The Progressive Party’s junior partner, the Socialist Party of Serbia, SPS, won 6.55 per cent.

World.title: Montenegro Opposition Moves to Oust Speaker for Mladic Condolences
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Montenegro’s main opposition party has moved to oust Speaker of Parliament Andrija Mandic over his public condolences following the death of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, media reported on Wednesday.

The initiative led by the Democratic Party of Socialists, DPS, was signed by 35 of the chamber’s 81 lawmakers, while 29 opposition MPs submitted a request for an extraordinary session on September 24 to debate Mandic’s dismissal.

The proposal says the speaker’s position carries “special political and institutional responsibility” and an obligation to safeguard the reputation and integrity of parliament, which represents all citizens.

Mandic publicly expressed condolences following the death on August 27 of Mladic, who was convicted by the UN war crimes tribunal in The Hague of genocide, crimes against humanity and other war crimes. He died serving his sentence.

The DPS said expressing sorrow for a convicted war criminal, particularly someone convicted of the 1995 genocide in Srebrenica, is incompatible with the responsibilities of the speaker and Montenegro’s obligation to respect international court rulings and good neighbourly relations.

The proposal denies that Mandic expressed his condolences in a personal or party capacity, saying his institutional responsibility remains because he simultaneously holds the position of speaker.

The document cites critical reactions to the funeral from the European Commission and neighbouring Croatia, which condemned the glorification of war criminals and Mandic’s expression of condolences as incompatible with European Union values.

“When the actions of the speaker of parliament of a candidate country produce such reactions from EU institutions and a neighbouring member state, they can no longer be presented as a matter of his personal or party convictions,” the proposal says.

The DPS also argues that the episode is not isolated but forms part of a broader pattern in Mandic’s exercise of the speaker’s office.

The proposal also raises concerns about his alleged use of the speaker’s office to promote political and ideological positions.

The proposal recalls that Montenegro is entering a decisive phase of its EU integration process and that membership requires more than meeting technical conditions, including a clear commitment to European values, confronting the past, respecting international court judgments and maintaining good-neighbourly relations.

“We believe that the speaker’s latest action has crossed the line beyond which the question of his responsibility can no longer be relativised by the need to preserve the parliamentary majority or political stability,” the proposal says.

The ruling coalition’s three main groups, Prime Minister Milojko Spajic’s Europe Now Movement, the Democrats and the New Serb Democracy, which together hold 41 seats in the 81-member parliament, said they will not support the opposition initiative.

But parties representing Montenegro’s Bosniak and ethnic Albanian communities, which are also part of the governing coalition, have announced they will back the motion.

An absolute majority of all 81 lawmakers is not required to dismiss Mandic. The motion can pass with a majority of lawmakers present at the session, provided that at least half of all MPs are present.

Montenegro’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs this week also expressed concern about the glorification of Mladic during the recent commemorations of his death.

“It is our obligation to preserve the dignity and memory of the victims, to preserve the truth about crimes and individual responsibility for them, and to resolutely oppose any attempt to deny genocide, war crimes and other serious violations of international humanitarian law,” the Montenegrin ministry said in a statement on Tuesday.

World.title: Serbia, Bosnian Serbs Slate Sarajevo’s Expulsion of Diplomats over Mladic
World.content:
The Serbian embassy in Sarajevo. Photo: Serbian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Serbia’s Foreign Ministry on Tuesday condemned the expulsion of two of its diplomats from Bosnia and Herzegovina as “yet another unconstructive move” that serves neither good-neighbourly relations, regional stability, nor the easing of political tensions.

It said Bosnia’s Foreign Minister, Elmedin Konakovic, “continues to resort to escalation and uses extremely difficult and painful issues from our shared past as an instrument of day-to-day politics and an election campaign”, adding that “such issues require responsibility and serious dialogue, rather than political instrumentalisation and unilateral moves that further deepen divisions.”

The ministry said Serbia will “examine all legal and political aspects of the announced decisions, including the issue of jurisdiction and the procedures for adopting them,” as well as their consequences for diplomatic relations.

On Tuesday, Konakovic announced the expulsion of two members of the Serbian embassy in Sarajevo after Serbia hosted the funeral with military honours of the convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic in Belgrade.

Konakovic said Serbian military attache Milan Dulanovic and Danko Maksimovic, an adviser to Serbia’s BIA intelligence service, were personae non grata and had 48 hours to leave Bosnia.

Officials in Bosnia’s mainly Serb Republika Srpska entity, also condemned the move and challenged its legality.

Republika Srpska Justice Minister Goran Selak insisted such foreign policy decisions fall under the authority of Bosnia’s tripartite state presidency, while the Foreign Ministry merely carries out adopted policy – which he said Konakovic “would have to know” before making moves that are “unconstitutional and illegal.”

He said the expulsion order “can hardly even be called a decision,” since such a decision must have grounding in the constitution and law. “This looks more like a pre-election pamphlet than a serious act of an institution,” Selak said, referring to upcoming national elections next month.

Selak said Konakovic has the right to his opinions, “including personal antipathy toward Serbia”, but not to present them as the country’s position or speak for Republika Srpska, adding that “Serbia is Republika Srpska’s most important partner”.

The Serb member of Bosnia’s three-member state presidency, Zeljka Cvijanovic, said Konakovic “cannot determine what Bosnia and Herzegovina is, or dictate to Serbia”. She claimed one of the two embassy staff had already left Bosnia after his mandate expired.

Konakovic based the decision on a 2004 rulebook of the state presidency, Under it, only the presidency can expel heads of diplomatic missions but the foreign minister can expel other embassy staff for cases including interference in internal affairs, espionage, or insulting statements.

World.title: Ex-Yugoslavia’s Queer Literary Heroes Tell Tales to Inspire
World.content:
After the Belgrade Pride march last weekend, Pride season in the former Yugoslavia – stretching from June to September – has drawn to a close. Whistles, rainbow flags and glitter (the queer community has a microplastics problem that we really need to discuss) are being stored away for the next time.

The intensified vitriol directed at those who believe their non-normative genders and sexualities are worth celebrating begins to wane. Familiar polemics within the LGBTQ+ community, however, continue: we keep asking ourselves, and those marching alongside us, whether Pride parades – organised by professional NGOs in coordination with the state and the police – are still worth showing up for.

As the season ends, and that question remains open, let’s keep Pride going through a Yugo Queer reading list.

World.title: ‘Disposable’ IP Firms in Serbia, Montenegro Obscure Origins of Russian Cyber Meddling
World.content:
Between late 2022 and February 2024, Azarov’s eServer said it was managing two IP ranges that subsequently came under the control of Stark Industries Solutions.

Following the EU sanctions, Stark Industries Solutions rebranded as PQ Hosting and transferred its IP resources under the umbrella of Dutch WorkTitans.

In May this year, Dutch police arrested the owners of WorkTitans and MIRhosting on suspicion of aiding Stark Industries Solution in circumventing sanctions.

Archived routing data show that at the end of 2024, Azarov was an upstream provider for PQ Hosting, i.e. the rebranded Stark Industries Solutions.

BIRN identified at least eight IP ranges that WorkTitans listed as being located in or used from Serbia and Belgrade, with Serbian Open Exchange, an internet traffic exchange point, serving as the internet gateway for all the ranges. These include two previously advertised by eServer.

Azarov said his company “had no direct business relations with Stark Industries”.

“Subnets roam between some providers and if we get request from any of our clients to announce network we just do so – that’s our part of hosting business,” he said in a response to BIRN, written in English.

“And you say it later came under control of Stark – then maybe they acquired it somehow.”

BIRN also identified three other IP ranges that have, over the past several years, moved between eServer, Stark Industries Solutions and Aeza Group.

An analysis of the RIPE NCC database shows that numerous IP ranges previously controlled by Azarov have since passed to two providers previously linked to the Russian bulletproof ecosystem and infrastructure used in cyberattacks: Cypriot-registered IT-Hostline and Russia-based Fortis.

IT-Hostline was previously a partner of Stark Industries Solutions and now provides infrastructure to Aeza Group, according to France-based cybersecurity firm Intrinsec, while Fortis’s infrastructure was used by FIN7 hacking group, responsible for mass financial theft and corporate extortion, Insikt Group reported last year.

Former eServer ranges are also now advertised by Global Connectivity Solutions and Global Internet Solutions, both linked to Aeza Group, Insikt Group said, and identified a number of ransomware groups that it said had used their infrastructure.

According to RIPE NCC data, among the current users of IP ranges previously held by eServer are: Russian provider Rost, whose infrastructure was also reportedly used in the Doppelganger campaign; Russian Timeweb, where researchers this year found more than 300 active C2 servers – systems used to send instructions to malware-infected devices and steal data; and US-based Baxet Group, whose infrastructure has been linked to cyberattacks by Russia’s military intelligence service, GRU, as reported by Arctic Wolf Networks, an American cybersecurity company, in November 2025.

Today, Azarov advertises an IP range belonging to Neterra Ltd, a Bulgarian provider previously used by the hacking-for-hire and corporate espionage group DeathStalker and whose infrastructure was also partly used to distribute Pegasus spyware, according to Amnesty International.

Azarov, however, insisted his eServer “has a strict anti cybercrime policy on all of our locations”.

“By targeting on B2B and B2C markets we always monitor our networks and try to keep environment safe and trustworthy,” he wrote to BIRN.

“You can see that our networks are not in SBL and other lists and if some IPs get into it we act immediately. So as I told you we did not work directly with Stark Industries but even if their networks were announced by some of our clients, they were applied the same strict rules and filters so I don’t think there was any malicious activity.”

Typically in cybercrime, when one network is shut down or sanctioned, attackers simply transfer IP addresses and other internet resources to linked providers and continue their operations. This is how sanctioned companies Aeza and Stark Industries have continued to operate.

“Today, it is no longer a single server, but an entire dynamic infrastructure that is constantly changing,” Radunovic told BIRN. “That makes it difficult to track because it operates across multiple jurisdictions and legal procedures, so investigators, alongside technical traces, also follow money flows, cryptocurrencies and other connections.”

World.title: Rimac Has Taken Complete Control of Bugatti
World.content:
September the 10th, 2026 – Croatia’s world famous Rimac has now officially taken complete control over the legendary Bugatti.

An investment consortium led by HOF Capital has completed the takeover of Porsche’s stakes in the Rimac Group and the company Bugatti Rimac. Index reports that the transaction, initially announced back in April this year, has been officially finalised. Through it, the consortium has taken over Porsche’s 21% ownership in the Rimac Group and 45% stake in the company Bugatti Rimac.

The Rimac Group remains the majority owner of the company Bugatti Rimac with a 55 percent stake. The joint company Bugatti Rimac was founded back in 2021, and in the new consortium the largest investor is BlueFive Capital along with other institutional investors from both the USA and Europe. “This is an important step for Bugatti Rimac and the entire Rimac Group. I’m pleased that HOF Capital and their consortium are becoming our partners in the next phase of the Group’s development and I look forward to working together on realising the full potential of our companies. We have achieved strong progress in all parts of the Group and I believe that this partnership will give us additional momentum for continued growth,” said Mate Rimac, founder and president of the Rimac Group and chief executive officer of the company Bugatti Rimac.

management changes

With the new ownership structure now formally and fully established, Bugatti Rimac is also restructuring its management team. This further strengthens the strategic and operational vision that Mate Rimac set for Bugatti when he was appointed chief executive officer in 2021.

Christophe Piochon is leaving the positions of president of the Bugatti Automobiles brand and chief operating officer of the company Bugatti Rimac. His role as president of Bugatti Automobiles is personally taken over by Mate Rimac. Marko Brkljačić, previously chief operating officer at Rimac Technology, becomes the new chief operating officer of the company Bugatti Rimac. Further changes are also planned, so Hendrik Malinowski, previously director of management at Bugatti Automobiles, will be appointed commercial director of the brand.

Rimac thanked Piochon for his contribution to the brand. “With over two decades spent at Bugatti, Christophe has strongly influenced what that brand represents today. From the Veyron to the Tourbillon, he participated in building and preserving the quality and supreme craftsmanship by which all hypercars that leave Molsheim are recognised. On behalf of the entire Bugatti Rimac team, I want to thank Christophe and wish him every success, and at the same time I take the opportunity to welcome Marko,” Rimac stated.

World.title: Will Lika Now Remain Polluted Forever?
World.content:
September the 10th, 2026 – Lika has been at the heart of a terrible hazardous waste scandal, and the findings are leading people to ask whether Lika will remain polluted forever.

The case of the illegal disposal of thousands of tonnes of waste in Lika has in recent weeks raised serious questions about possible environmental pollution, its scale and consequences for people, which is why a large protest was also held on Saturday in Zagreb. Vedran Salvia reports for Index that hazardous waste was being brought to Lika for years from neighbouring Italy and Slovenia under the guise of raw material for the alleged production of construction blocks.

It was then somewhat buried in an uncontrolled manner, and somewhat simply left out in the open. Croatian police, in an international operation with the support of Europol, have since arrested 13 people. Among them are entrepreneur Josip Šincek and his wife Monika, owners of the company Tipos Resur.

After the public was first confronted with findings about so-called “forever chemicals”, and then also microplastics in groundwater, the question opened of how much we actually know about the scale of the pollution and its possible consequences. Professor Branimir K. Hackenberger from the Department of Biology at Josip Juraj Strossmayer University in Osijek spoke out about the details of this awful case.

Hackenberger went through three publicly published expert reports from this specific case from Lika. These are the finding of the Faculty of Geotechnical Engineering from March 2026, its supplement from July, and the report of the Josip Juraj Strossmayer Water Institute on microplastics from August, which USKOK published yesterday. He emphasised that he is not a participant in the proceedings nor did he work on those expert reports, but comments on them as an ecotoxicologist.

what exactly are “forever chemicals”?

He explained that PFAS is a collective name for a family of over ten thousand synthetic compounds in which hydrogen on the carbon chain has been replaced by fluorine. This is important because the “hydrogen-fluorine bond is the strongest single bond in organic chemistry”. One of the consequences of this is persistence, says Hackenberger, “since in the environment there is neither a biological nor a chemical pathway that would break that bond under normal conditions”. Their characteristic is also that they are retained in the organism. For PFOS that time amounts to three to five years, our interlocutor explains.

The PFOS that Hackenberger mentions is one of the best-known and most long-lasting PFAS compounds, which due to its persistence and ability to be retained in the organism is considered particularly problematic. Another of the more problematic PFAS compounds is PFOA. For that “forever chemical” Hackenberger says that the International Agency for Research on Cancer in 2023 classified it among carcinogenic substances for humans, while PFOS was classified among possible carcinogens. As regards health effects, Hackenberger explained the following:

“The European Food Safety Authority has set a tolerable weekly intake of 4.4 ng per kilogram of body weight, and that for the sum of only four compounds: PFOA, PFNA, PFHxS and PFOS. The critical effect on which that value was derived is not cancer but a reduced antibody response to vaccination in children, thus an immune effect at very low doses. In addition, elevated cholesterol, changes in liver enzymes, thyroid disorders and lower birth weight have been documented,” he notes.

what was actually find in lika?

Hackenberger underlines that neither PFOA nor PFAS has been confirmed to have been discovered in Lika. According to the sampling by the Faculty of Geotechnical Engineering which was on 11 May 2026, and in which 20 compounds were analysed, other “forever chemicals” were found. “PFBS, PFBA, PFPeA and PFHxA are compounds with four to six carbon atoms and industry introduced them precisely as a replacement for PFOA and PFOS. Toxicologically they are milder per unit of mass and accumulate more weakly in the organism, but environmentally they are worse: they are more soluble, bind more weakly to soil, travel faster and, what is decisive for remediation, are significantly harder to remove from water,” he explained.

“Upstream there is nothing, and downstream it is 200.5 ng/L. The ratio is greater than 130 to 1 and cannot be explained by a natural background, because there is no natural background for PFAS; these compounds do not exist in nature,” he says. “To put 200.5 ng/L into perspective: that is twice above the parametric value for drinking water, but it is water from a borehole next to the landfill that no one drinks. No one has been exposed on the basis of that measurement and the expert expressly says so. The value of the finding is therefore not in the exposure but in that it is an early warning: it shows how the path from waste to groundwater is open,” are his words.

antimony was discovered in lika cabbages

He touched on antimony, a metal which in larger quantities can be very harmful to human health, and long-term exposure is associated with damage to the liver, heart and lungs. “The biggest chemical problem that was measured at that location is not PFAS but metals in the soil. Antimony reaches 317 mg/kg, while naturally it is below 1; copper reaches 9,946 with a maximum permitted concentration of 100; lead 1,051 with the same limit of 100. In the eluate of one sample ‘next to the silo wall’ antimony amounts to 499 mg/kg of dry matter with a limit of 0.7 for non-hazardous waste.

Antimony was also found in various plants, a piece of data that the media did not report: 0.28 to 0.34 mg/kg in woody species and around 0.3 mg/kg in cabbage at 20 to 30 metres from the pile. That means that the path from waste to edible tissue is closed, which for residents is a more direct message than any figure about PFAS,” he says.

there has been no pfas analysed carried out in the soil

He explained that by removing the waste the source is removed, but not what has already come out of it. “Exactly how much remains, honestly speaking, we do not know, and the measurement that would say that has not been done. PFAS was analysed in three water samples, while in the soil it was not analysed even once. The stock in the unsaturated zone cannot be estimated differently than by guessing without that, and I will not guess. What can be said as a framework is the following. Short chains, which predominate here, are washed out relatively quickly, realistically in a range from a few years to two decades. Longer chains and precursors, of which there are none in the water now, but which are probably in the waste, remain significantly longer. Remediation is therefore not planned in deadlines of a few years,” he also said.

teflon is also an issue

Hackenberger was then asked about a compound called PTFE, which is better known as Teflon. He says that Teflon, in the report of the Water Institute, appears only in one of six samples, and that in only two particles. They were found in a sample taken from a borehole that is located upstream of the landfill and serves as a reference point, while in the other five samples PTFE was not found. Because of that, he said, that finding is not proof that Teflon from the waste reached the groundwater.

“returning the underground area in the affected areas in lika isn’t realistic”

He warned that the location is not classic open karst, as one might conclude from some claims, but that according to geophysical measurements and drilling there is a poorly permeable base there. As the best solution he sees the removal of the source of pollution itself, that is complete remediation and disposal of the waste, whereby its further release would be stopped. As a temporary measure it is possible to cover the waste impermeably and prevent the penetration of precipitation. He concludes that returning the underground to a completely original state is not realistic, but it is possible to remove the source, prevent further pollution and monitor the state in the long term.

how dangerous are these microplastics?

He notes that nowhere in the world is there a health-based limit value for microplastics in drinking water.

“Back in 2019 and in later reviews, the World Health Organisation concluded that the evidence is not sufficient for deriving a guideline value, and Directive (EU) places microplastics on the watch list and prescribes the measurement methodology, but does not prescribe a limit,” he added. “The greatest value microplastics has here is as a marker, and not as a poison. Polystyrene in the groundwater downstream of the landfill and its complete absence upstream are a feature of a local anthropogenic source. That is how the report itself interprets it and that is logically correct,” he stated.

When it comes to public water supply, Hackenberger says that according to the data available so far there is no reason for the conclusion that it is endangered. “The Mrđenovac and Divoselo intakes are located upstream of the landfill and are hydrogeologically not connected with it, and public water supply is regularly controlled. When it comes to private wells downstream, no one has an answer to that question because no one has measured,” he says.

there can be plenty lying undetected

He was asked about what such analyses can still leave undetected, that is whether we can even ever truly know the full extent of the pollution if we analyse only the substances that we decided in advance to look for. “We cannot know it all, and that’s not a shortcoming of these specific expert reports but a limitation of the method itself. For example, the total PFAS parameter of 500 ng/L was not measured. It is measured as total organic fluorine, by AOF and EOF methods, and would be the only one to show how much fluorine there is in the water at all.

In studies where both are measured, the targeted twenty compounds usually explain between 1 and 30 % of the present organic fluorine. Translated to this case, the real load could be several times greater than the measured 200.5 ng/L, but that is an estimate from the literature, and not a measurement at this location, and that is precisely why it is worth doing that analysis. My own calculation, thus an estimate: on the basis of a base of 1,063 substances that appear in this kind of waste and the list of analyses that were actually carried out at this location, the expected number of substances that would pass unnoticed amounts to around 79%,” he noted. He warned of the fact that individual substances are assessed separately, while their mixture can have a different effect.

World.title: Croatian Motorways: Crolibertas is Being Implemented Within Deadlines
World.content:
September the 10th, 2026 – Croatian Motorways (HAC) has stated that the upcoming Crolibertas system that will replace the current toll system is being implemented within all legal deadlines.

The deadline for launching the new Crolibertas system is set by the Law on Toll Collection, states the simple message from Croatian Motorways, with Boris Huzjan at the helm. Poslovni reports that the company makes no attempt to deny that this is a long and complex process which, among other things, also includes appeal deadlines in tenders.

In recent days, several pieces of information have been published in the media according to which the project of introducing a new toll collection system in Croatia will be delayed. Back at the end of July, the State Commission for the Control of Public Procurement Procedures (DKOM) annulled the decision of Croatian Motorways (HAC) on the selection of the contractor for the sales web portal, mobile application and integration data hubs, which form the most important user part of the system.

Croatian Motorways was as such approached with a query about what exactly is happening with the deadlines and whether they are in any way at risk. “Regarding all of the media reports, we want to emphasise that the deadline for putting the new Crolibertas toll collection system into operation is determined by the Law on Toll Collection and that all activities are being carried out according to that deadline,” Croatian Motorways revealed, as touched on above.

“The establishment of a single electronic toll collection system Crolibertas along all motorways in Croatia, including concession motorways, is an implementation-complex project because it is multidisciplinary and requires the integration of several different and independent segments (e.g. technological, legal and operational). All implementation activities must be consistently and systematically connected and coordinated, all so that when the system is put into operation it is accessible to users and simple to use,” they concluded.

It should be noted that the cost of the entire Crolibertas project is estimated to stand at 160 million euros.

World.title: With Rijeka Gateway Doing Well, Railway Improvement is Necessary
World.content:
September the 10th, 2026 – Rijeka Gateway is doing excellently, but proper Croatian railway improvement is now necessary to continue the momentum.

At the Rijeka Gateway container terminal, more than 370,000 container units (TEU) were handled in the first year of commercial operations. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that one hundred ships called at the terminal, and it is expected that in 2027 the full capacity of the first phase of investment in the terminal will be achieved, with around 650,000 container units (TEU) handled.

“In Rijeka and the wider region, a technologically advanced terminal like this did not exist. Our jobs and processes are special and very complex, so building a team that can compete at that level with the best terminals is a source of pride not only for all of us at Rijeka Gateway, but also for Rijeka and the whole of Croatia.

new logistics corridors

Important new logistics corridors have connected Rijeka with the region, which is a major value brought by our terminal. The third thing is that we have continued to carefully monitor our impact on the environment and the community with the aim of being a good neighbour to the citizens of Rijeka. We have successfully certified our environmental management system according to the ISO 14001:2015 standard, confirming our commitment to environmental protection, and we continuously communicate with the local community on all topics related to the quality of life of citizens,” said Peter Corfitsen, President of the Management Board of Rijeka Gateway. Since its opening, the terminal has received more than a thousand trains and over 80,000 trucks. The current modal split for cargo leaving the terminal is 42 percent by rail and 58 percent by road. The entry and exit process for truck transport has been fully digitalised, which speeds up truck processing and reduces waiting times, thereby reducing the burden on traffic and pollution. The average truck processing time is around 15 minutes, and the shortest time achieved for a truck is ten minutes, on a day when more than 500 trucks were processed.

investment in the local community

“By handling 370,000 TEU of cargo, we have significantly increased the overall capacity of the Port of Rijeka and are rapidly approaching the figures we planned, that is, reaching a throughput of 650,000 TEU and, in the second phase, one million TEU. During the first year of operations, Rijeka Gateway maintained a high level of operational reliability, with 98 percent availability of port equipment and 99 percent availability of key systems on the operational quay and storage areas, which is at the level of the best terminals.

For the full potential of the terminal, the planned increase in railway traffic capacity will be key, and we welcome the activities of the Croatian Government in this regard. We’ll continue to invest in the local community, especially through cooperation with the Faculty of Maritime Studies and the University of Rijeka, through various scholarship and education programmes, as well as through donation programmes aimed at Rijeka kindergartens and primary schools,” said Tomislav Rosandić, Member of the Management Board of Rijeka Gateway.

World.title: Croatia: Glorifying Ratko Mladić is Contrary to EU Values – Suspend Serbia Talks
World.content:
September the 9th, 2026 – Through various political figures, Croatia has sent out the clear message that glorifying Ratko Mladić is contrary to EU values and that all talks with Serbia must be suspended.

Croatian politician Tonino Picula has warned that glorifying Ratko Mladić or relativising his crimes is “contrary to the values on which the European Union is founded.” “The burial of Ratko Mladić cannot be viewed solely as a private event because the participation of representatives of state institutions, members of the army and members of the authorities sends a clear political message.

Index reports that the disgraced war criminal Ratko Mladić was finally convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, crimes against humanity and war crimes. “Any glorification of him or relativisation of his crimes is directly contrary to the values on which the European Union is founded,” Picula stated.

serbia must confront its past

“Serbia’s desired EU path is not only a matter of opening negotiating chapters and fulfilling technical criteria, but above all a question of political choice and acceptance of European values. Serbia cannot at the same time claim that membership in the European Union is its strategic goal while tolerating or institutionally accompanying the glorification of people convicted of the most serious war crimes.

The European Union must not relativise such an event. The authorities in Belgrade must be required to make a clear break with the policy of historical revisionism and an unambiguous attitude towards the judgments of international courts. The European perspective also implies the ability of society and the state to confront the past, rather than glorify its darkest protagonists. Serbia chooses its own path, but the credibility of its European path will also depend on whether it is prepared to accept the truth about the crimes committed and stop glorifying their perpetrators,” Picula added.

a convicted war criminal for the world is apparently a man deserving of the highest honours in serbia

The former commander of the Bosnian Serb army, Ratko Mladić, who was finally sentenced to life imprisonment for the genocide in Srebrenica in July 1995, for the persecution and forced displacement of Bosniaks and Croats throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, sniper activity, shelling and terrorising of civilians during the siege of Sarajevo, and for taking members of UN peacekeeping forces hostage in retaliation for NATO bombings in 1995, died on 27 August in the prison hospital of the Hague Tribunal.

He was buried yesterday in the family tomb at Topčider Cemetery with church rites and military honours. Among the thousands of people in the procession and funeral cortège were individual ministers of the Serbian government and officials of Republika Srpska, while the service in the church was led by Patriarch Porfirije with bishops of the Serbian Orthodox Church.
