World.title: Grima grateful for helping hand in chase for first group race win
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Grima grateful for helping hand in chase for first group race win Craig Kerry September 10, 2026 — 11:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Champion apprentice Siena Grima is grateful to have jockey Adam Hyeronimus in her corner as she prepares for an exciting chance to score a first stakes-level win with I’m Ya Huckleberry on Saturday at Rosehill. Grima enjoyed a rapid rise to the Sydney apprentices’ title last season after moving from Tamworth in December to join Chris Waller, but she has been handed her greatest opportunity yet by one the premier trainer’s greatest rivals, Gai Waterhouse and Adrian Bott, in the group 3 Ming Dynasty Quality (1400m). Adam Hyeronimus and I’m Ya Huckleberry, left, finishing second to Incognito in the Breeders’ Plate last year. Getty Images I’m Ya Huckleberry ($4.60) was battling for favouritism in the three-year-old feature after returning from an injury lay-off with an easy victory in a Wyong maiden on August 30 with Hyeronimus aboard. It was the $400,000 Home Affairs colt’s first race since finishing runner-up 11 months earlier in the group 3 Breeders’ Plate on debut. With I’m Ya Huckleberry carrying 53.5 kilograms, connections had to find a new jockey for Saturday and Grima was thankful for the chance.



“I’ve had only one ride for Gai and it won, so that was nice and hopefully we go two for two,” Grima said of her Canterbury victory with Think I Will in June. Siena Grima after winning on Attractiveness last month at Rosehill. Getty Images “Adam said to me that he couldn’t get his weight, and I know the owners and they’re lovely people, so I think that connection really helped. I feel very privileged to be able to get on a horse like him in such a nice race. “I’ve had a ride in a group race for Gary Portelli and she ran midfield, and then I’ve had a couple of listed rides, but they’ve finished towards the tail, so this would be my first one that’s a really good chance. “I definitely think the lightweight really brings him into it. He’s obviously very sharp out of the gates, really nice trials, and then a beautiful first-up run where he looked like he was really finishing off quite nicely, so I definitely think he’s ready to go.”



Bott hopes I’m Ya Huckleberry can race forward from gate seven of 12 and push his claims for a start in the group 1 Golden Rose (1400m) in two weeks, and Grima was confident she could help him get the job done. “I know he has a few issues with the barriers, so I’d rather him be out there,” she said of the draw. “And the 1400-metre run, it’ll be a nice jump come across to where he’s happy and just take his time to blossom. “Unfortunately, I won’t get a chance to sit on him before, but I’ll just have a talk to Adam. He knows him like the back of his hand, and he’s been really great to me. “When I do ride on pace, which isn’t very often, if he has any advice, he’s more than happy to call me out of the room. When I had that winner for Gai, he called me out and told me I did a really great job.”



Grima also has a group race ride on God’s Window ($19) for her boss in the Theo Marks Stakes (1300m). Siena Grima winning on God’s Window at Randwick in May. Getty Images “It’s obviously a lot short of his best, but first up, he always runs a really good race,” she said. “Last prep, first up over 1400, he ran fourth, and then come out and run some really nice races, so I wouldn’t write him off.” Bott, who also has Savagram ($7.50) in the Ming Dynasty, believes I’m Ya Huckleberry will appreciate the rise to 1400m and a lighter weight than he would have carried in the group 2 Run To The Rose (1200m).



“He’s got the potential there, but he is still lightly raced and he’s still a bit of a big kid,” Bott said. “He’s got that natural speed and being able to sustain that over 1400, 1600 metres, as opposed to 1200, is going to be what hopefully separates him when we can get to a good level.” He said Savagram, fourth behind stablemate Plagiarism in the Up And Coming Stakes (1300m) at his second start, was on a likely path to the Spring Champion Stakes (2000m). “He still just did a few things wrong,” he said of last start. “He had the right run in the race to try and capitalise on it, but just inexperience showed.”



The stable has Plagiarism and Revengeance as $19 hopes in the Run To The Rose. Bott felt Plagiarism was primed for the 1200m. “We felt that he was pretty conditioned for a tougher race like that, having two runs over the 1300 metres,” he said. “It’s the main lead up to the Golden Rose. He certainly put himself in contention there off his last start, so I wanted to give him that chance. Like I’m Ya Huckleberry, Golden Gift winner Revengeance is second up off a long injury break. He was seventh behind Guest House’s track-record 1100m win in the San Domenico. “We were willing to be very forgiving,” he said of the return.



“He had a long layoff and found himself just having to do a little bit more work than anticipated. “Up to 1200 will help, he’ll be fitter for it. I still don’t think it’s necessarily the right race just yet, but it’s the right stepping stones. If we need to readjust after this, we can, but at this stage he is on the path for a Golden Rose.”

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Herald journalist Peter FitzSimons gives evidence as indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Alan Jones’ criminal trial in the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney. I will be reporting on the latest developments with my colleagues Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander.

Jones, 85, is facing 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent involving six male complainants over a 17-year period from 2003 to 2020. The former 2GB heavyweight denies the alleged physical acts occurred.

Peter FitzSimons outside the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney on Thursday. Sitthixay Ditthavong

Today, author and journalist Peter FitzSimons, a columnist at The Sydney Morning Herald, is giving evidence about his conversation with complainant “C”, a former staffer to Jones who has accused the broadcaster of unwanted touching and kissing.

The court has heard that FitzSimons had a conversation with “C” in 2019, after being put in contact with the complainant by Jones’ 2GB colleague Ray Hadley.

FitzSimons was not told the identity of “C”, the court has heard. FitzSimons did not report on the complainant’s allegations.

Years later, in 2023, the Herald’s chief investigative reporter, Kate McClymont, spoke to “C” and reported on his allegations, among others, in an anonymised form. McClymont is expected to give evidence in the trial at a later date.

NSW Police set up Strike Force Bonnefin in response to McClymont’s reporting. Jones was arrested in November 2024.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: ‘Dad, you’re singing it wrong’: Meet the real-life father-son dynamic behind an Oasis tribute band
World.content:
NationalGood Weekend ‘Dad, you’re singing it wrong’: Meet the real-life father-son dynamic behind an Oasis tribute band Dani Valent September 10, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Darren Spiby, 57, and his son, Tom, 24, play Liam and Noel Gallagher in Noasis, the Oasis tribute band, bringing their own family dynamics to a famously fractious sibling relationship. “I was nervous about getting it right because Dad’s such a professional,” says Tom Philby of joining his father Darren’s band. “He’s very specific.” Brent Lewin Darren: I’ve been playing since I was young and performing was normal in our family. Tom got his first electric guitar at seven and, within a year, he learnt to do Nirvana. He’d be wearing a wig, his brother would come in with a wig as well, they’d get it down pat. He went to drama school and was in all kinds of shows. Our first times on stage together were back when we were still living in Derbyshire in the UK [the family came to Australia in 2013]. I’d chaperone him to a ballet or opera show, then get thrown into the cast, too, because they knew I could perform – “Wear this, stand here, do this” – and then you’d go out in front of a thousand people and wing it. It was loads of fun. We knew Tom had talent, an understanding of music – and words. When he was tiny, we had placemats on the kitchen table with unusual herbs pictured on them. By the age of two, he could recite them: “Vervain!” he’d call out. It was nuts. He was very, very switched on. His brain is a little bit like mine. It’s difficult for us to just listen to music, we dissect it: “Oh, that bass is too loud.” We’ll hear the same nuances. I started Noasis in 1996. Five years after we arrived in Adelaide, I got Noasis going over here. After a while, I kicked out one guitarist and asked Tom to come in so we could keep rehearsing. The other guys said, “Oh, he’s good. Can he sing?” He could. It’s been five years and now his younger brother, Dan, is in, too, playing bass. It’s a show, a job, so we put on the costumes and get into our roles. We don’t walk around the streets like Liam and Noel Gallagher. But the perfection we seek is real and Tom is opinionated. He might stop the band during rehearsal: “You should be singing like this, Dad.” It gets heated, we’re family. “No, Tom, that’s not quite right.” It kicks off, then the whole band ducks for cover. It can be intense in that cauldron, but it’s because we both want to do a great job.



To play with your kids, it’s just amazing. On stage, Noel – or Tom – might do a lead break. I’ll step away, go to the corner of the stage, like Liam would do, and just play tambourine, let Noel have his moment. Often I’ll dive behind the speakers and record on my phone from the side. I’ve got dozens of little clips of him singing and playing. Pride is always there. That’s the bit I have to wrestle and keep down so I don’t get too emotional when I’m doing this. When I share the father-son connection, I’ve had people full-on bawling. I think they wish they’d done more with their parents or their kids. That’s the big one. Related Article Good Weekend ‘He snores pretty loud but, other than that, it’s all right’: Charlie’s life on the road with his grandpa Tom’s into his acting and he’s just made a short film. I think there’ll be a natural path where he’ll choose which way he needs to go. But there’ll always be music. We were saying yesterday how great it would be to be able to stand in the crowd, go down the front, and watch our show. If only we could do it with holograms or something, that’d be very cool. Tom: I remember Dad rehearsing for his own gigs and helping me with musical theatre; he’d be on the piano, guiding me through Memory from Cats, coaching me on notes and delivery. He’d chaperone me to auditions and then end up jumping in. I remember one where I was a little teacup and he came out in this menu costume, a head on top of a massive human poster. He wasn’t embarrassed, so there was no reason for me to be. He coached me in basketball, too. We were always talking about shooting form to get the perfect backspin. It was tough love. I respond to no-bullshit feedback because I can action it straight away. He’d instil that in me and we’d go and shoot 800 shots before school.



I was 20 when I first filled in with Noasis. We did three songs, then Dad was like, “Why don’t you sing Don’t Look Back in Anger?” They had a meeting and thought, “Yeah, we could get away with this and it brings down the age demographic of the band.” It was new and exciting, but I was nervous about getting it right because Dad’s such a professional. He’s very specific in how it needs to sound, which is great because it makes the product so good. We’ve watched so many Oasis concerts. I can hear stuff, Dad can hear stuff, then we talk about it. There’s a song, Turn Up the Sun. He thought he was hearing something, but it was just that when a bunch of you play a certain chord, harmonics ring out. He was asking, “Do you hear that note?” And I’m like, “Yes, but that’s because it’s a harmonic.” And he’s like, “No, no, it’s definitely there.” Everyone else in the room is going on their phones, avoiding eye contact because they don’t want to take sides. Those conversations usually end with him saying, “Thirty years … 30 years.” That’s him saying he’s been listening to it for 30 years and that supersedes my opinions. He’s very specific. He gave me a note the other day about the pronunciation of the word “knows” when I’m singing. I was singing it more “nose”. He wanted me to do the English accent, drop the jaw on that word. I could hear it. He was totally right. Last year, we saw Oasis together in Melbourne. That was colossal, but just as important was a Sam Fender gig a week or so later. Dad introduced me to his music. He played this song, Spit of You, which is about him and his dad. The lyrics go, “I can talk to anyone but I can’t talk to you.” It was so special having Dad next to me. There’s that whole thing about men not talking, articulating feelings. Why is that? Who puts that on us? With my dad, I’m pretty open and I don’t feel the age difference. It’s only recently I’ve started to appreciate the whole thing. A lot of people don’t see their parents because of work or because of their family dynamic. I’m lucky we have these gigs, and we’re so in sync.

World.title: Alcoa was warned about its mining by the WA government – then handed an exemption
World.content:
NationalWAAlcoa investigation Alcoa was warned about its mining by the WA government – then handed an exemption Holly Thompson September 10, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Water Corporation urged Western Australia’s peak environmental body to recommend reimposing strict guidelines on Alcoa’s mining operations near Perth’s drinking water supply, according to newly released documents. And further documents, obtained via Freedom of Information requests from online publication Boiling Cold, have revealed the state government warned Alcoa in 2023 there was a real risk of future operations being shut down if the company failed to address environmental concerns. Alcoa’s mining operations are largely situated within the northern jarrah forest in Western Australia. Getty/Nine News In March 2023, then-premier Mark McGowan wrote to Alcoa stating he was concerned the mining company was yet to address key issues raised by the state government through the Mine Management Program assessment process. That was just after this masthead revealed the government held genuine concerns over Perth’s drinking water.



“Of particular concern is the need for Alcoa to clearly demonstrate its commitment to (and effectiveness of) drinking water protection in Serpentine Dam, and the related matter of improving forest rehabilitation in areas cleared for mining,” McGowan wrote. “The Western Australian Government is concerned that if Alcoa does not appropriately address these issues, this could result in significant job losses due to the halting of future operations.” He suggested working to “explore all options to mine outside of high-risk ‘constrained’ areas within drinking water catchments”. McGowan also requested a commitment to “rapid and high-quality rehabilitation of the Northern Jarrah Forest”, the implementation of drainage controls in “current open areas that present a significant risk to drinking water quality” and “tangible guarantees that ensure Alcoa will take responsibility for remedying any negative impacts”. “As a priority, and ahead of further mine expansion, this should include reducing open mine areas within drinking water catchments and constrained areas,” the letter went on to state.



Then, in December 2023, Alcoa wrote to newly minted Premier Roger Cook, saying it was “not economically viable for Alcoa to completely retreat from operating in higher risk areas”. Related Article Environmental protection Alcoa to keep mining as WA government overhauls regulations Cook then approved Alcoa’s 2023-2027 mining plan and signed an exemption order, which allowed the company increased access to higher-risk areas. In response to Alcoa’s Mine and Management Plan back in 2023, the Water Corporation wrote that past advice aimed at protecting water quality had not been supported in the exemption order. The utility said a “relaxation in the existing conditions on Alcoa from past management plan approvals was required, allowing Alcoa to mine over a larger area and without almost any constraints outside 1 kilometre of the high-water mark of the dams”.



The newly released documents reveal that, in August 2025, Water Corporation urged WA’s Environmental Protection Authority to back reimposing stricter protections on Alcoa that were in place from 2021-2023. “Water Corporation recommends the implementation of conditions on mining that align with the historical approaches taken to ensure the protection of the catchment function,” the utility’s submission to Alcoa’s proposals read. “Moreover, the uncertainty and potential latency with the impacts, potentially occurring in a few decades, requires an approach which aligns with the precautionary approach. “The proponent’s current mitigation needs to be updated to reflect key catchment management principles.”



In June, the WA government announced it would update Alcoa’s exemption order to reflect a new mining plan from the company and to provide “certainty and consistency to both the regulator and Alcoa”. Related Article Mining Alcoa faces more federal scrutiny over Willowdale mine clearing Environment Minister Matthew Swinbourn said the new plan and exemption order would be “aligned to deliver strong environmental protection while providing certainty for ongoing mining activity”. That order is still being finalised. An Alcoa spokesperson said as part of the ongoing approvals process, the company had committed to “further mitigate risks to water supply, including ceasing mining activities in the 2 kilometre reservoir protection zones, with the exception of required works related to rehabilitation and critical infrastructure”.



The spokesperson said the company was committed to responsible mining operations, and that there had been “no reduction in controls related to water protection applied to our operations”. “The current Section 6 exemption order and 2024-2028 Mining and Management Program conditions should be read together,” they said. “The conditions significantly increase the applicable controls to further mitigate risks to water, including formalising RPZ avoidance, significantly enhancing engineering controls, groundwater avoidance measures, accelerated rehabilitation, and strict monitoring and reporting requirements. “Alcoa has not had a negative impact on WA’s drinking water supply since operations commenced in 1963.” The state government has been contacted for comment.

World.title: The coach’s bake that proved finals are not just another game
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion The coach’s bake that proved finals are not just another game Wayne Campbell Age columnist and former Richmond captain September 10, 2026 — 11:00am

September 10, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Twenty-five years ago this week, in the lead-up the 2001 qualifying final between my Tigers and the all-conquering Essendon team, the message was consistent and simple. “It’s just another game.” The Essendon team of 2001. Sebastian Costanzo We hadn’t played in finals for six years and our coach Danny Frawley had only played two elimination finals, so he handed over to his trusted assistant Darren Crocker, who had played many finals and multiple grand finals, to sell the message. We met in the old social club to change things up from the usual Graeme Richmond Room in the football department.



We went with the “embrace the week” model, and Crock told us that, while the game would be a bit quicker and there would be a big crowd, there were still four posts at each end of the ground and a footy to win in the middle of the ground. A solid plan. Related Article Scoop in September

AFL 2026 Scoop in September: What Saints ruckman’s trade request has to do with Butters and English It was Mike Tyson who said everyone has a plan until they get punched in the mouth. At the opening centre bounce Damien Hardwick walked past me and let me know a few things about what I was about to encounter. The fact that I remember that moment 25 years later makes me think it hit the mark. The ball was smacked into the ground by the umpire in front of 78,000 people and soon after a ball was kicked high to a pack of players. I had a decision to make: “Do I go into that pack or not?” To not go wasn’t the wrong decision in this instance, to go would have been the right decision. I didn’t go.



James Hird went. He marked the ball. I had that knot in my stomach you have as a footballer when there is an incident like that. We were smacked in every area of the game and lost by 70 points after beating the Bombers the week before in the final home-and-away round. Wayne Campbell (centre) leads the Tigers from the ground. Ray Kennedy For the Monday review we were back in the Graeme Richmond Room. I remember three things from the meeting: First, “Spud” yelled to a level where staff in other parts of the building went outside to see if there had been an earthquake. This is not made up. Second, he put up a list of players who had performed in big games and ones who hadn’t. He finished with the following: “I can tell you, this week is not just another f---ing game!”



Our mindset for the following week’s final against Carlton was completely different. Ruckmen Ray Hall and Mark Porter spent the afternoon going at each other like two raging bulls. Andrew Kellaway went into a pack in the first five minutes in a way that set the tone for his teammates. We beat the Blues by 11 points in front of 83,000. That’s a very long-winded way of saying that I expect we will see a very different Fremantle team on Friday night from the one that was beaten so badly by Hawthorn in Perth last week. Hawthorn captain James Sicily unloads at Patrick Voss at the end of the qualifying final. AFL Photos via Getty Images Only the Dockers will know whether they treated it just like another game, or were just nervous, or just met a team that, for some reason, was just more up for the fight. Strategy, game plan – call it what you will – is critically important in football and played a part in the Fremantle v Hawthorn game, as well as Sydney’s remarkable qualifying final victory over the Brisbane Lions.



But what was more obvious in both matches was the winning team’s intent to take the game to the opposition in every facet. I’ve always thought that if two players attack a 50-50 ball and one goes harder at it than the other, the chance of the ball falling to that player’s teammates is well above 50 per cent. Champion Data may prove me wrong, but until they do, I’m running with it. Sydney, for all their strategy and skill, attacked the ball and the opposition with a ferocity not often seen. The surprising aspect of the Swans’ performance wasn’t that they were ferocious – the way they sustained that ferocity was indeed incredible – but the score they put on the board. Going into the game, they were rank outsiders to win.I can’t imagine the odds of them putting 141 points on the board, in cyclonic winds for a quarter, and winning by 53 points.



The surprising facts about the Dockers were that they were beaten, and they only scored 40 points, and they were beaten by 32. The point of this is that for all the mechanics of the game, intent still accounts for so much. When you combine mechanics and intent, you get performances like Hawthorn’s and Sydney’s. Two days after that famous Richmond victory over Carlton in 2001, two planes crashed into the World Trade Centre buildings in New York, and the world changed. Three days after that, the AFL’s airline partner Ansett went belly-up, changing the way our team and its supporters travelled to Brisbane for the preliminary final.



We played to our full potential against a team that would go on to win the first of three consecutive premierships. We lost by 68 points. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: A witchy sequel lacking in magic, plus other new movies to watch this week
World.content:
(M) 130 minutes

When you’re a witch, time doesn’t work the way it does for the rest of us. At least, that’s one takeaway from Practical Magic 2, which sees Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman returning as the sisters Sally and Gillian Owens, members of a largely benign dynasty of witches who have dwelt in Massachusetts since Puritan days, the magic passing from one generation of women to the next.

Based on a novel by Alice Hoffman, the original Practical Magic didn’t altogether enchant either critics or the general public when it came out in 1998. But it’s since picked up enough of a cult to warrant this belated sequel, spearheaded by Bullock and Kidman as producers.

Dianne Wiest, Sandra Bullock, Stockard Channing and Nicole Kidman in a scene from Practical Magic 2. Warner Bros. Pictures via AP

The new film appears to be set in the present day – but here’s where the timeline gets wonky. In the first film Sally’s daughter Kylie, played by Evan Rachel Wood, was aged around 11. In Practical Magic 2, we’re introduced to a new version of Kylie played by Joey King, still only in her mid-20s almost three decades on.

World.title: English Premier League remains on Stan in $800m rights deal
World.content:
Nine’s streaming service Stan has extended its deal with the English Premier League to continue broadcasting the world’s most popular sports league until 2034.

The media group did not disclose commercial details of the deal when it announced the extension on Thursday morning, although it is believed to cost close to $800 million across the full six years.

Kai Havertz after finding the net for Arsenal in its match against Coventry City in August. AP

Now in its second season on Stan after Nine agreed to take over the current broadcast deal from telecommunications provider Optus, the Premier League has driven 50 per cent of growth for subscribers to the Sport tier, the company said. More games could be shown on free-to-air television, Nine said in a statement, with plans to promote the game across its other media assets, including recently acquired outdoor media and billboards business QMS.

Optus closed its Sport service when it relinquished a suite of sports rights, including the Premier League last year. It is currently subsidising the annual fees paid to the Premier League. Nine will pay the entirety of the new six-year deal, which will cost almost as much annually as it agreed to pay the NRL in a recent broadcast deal signed in June.

World.title: Miners, banks sharply lower as ASX slumps; Trump sends oil price warning
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets Miners, banks sharply lower as ASX slumps; Trump sends oil price warning Staff writers Updated September 10, 2026 — 10:44am ,first published September 10, 2026 — 5:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has fallen across the board in early trade after stocks fell on Wall Street as the price of crude oil rose back above $US100 a barrel amid further escalation in the US war with Iran, and as US President Donald Trump said prices will remain elevated until after the midterm elections in November. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 117.2 points, or 1.3 per cent, to 8794.2, with all 11 sectors in negative territory. Wall Street’s losses were broad. AP Mining stocks fell sharply with iron ore heavyweights weakening as the price of the key steel-making ingredient dropped below $US100 per tonne. BHP fell 2.1 per cent, Fortescue lost 2.3 per cent and Rio Tinto slumped 2.5 per cent in early trade. Losses for gold stocks were more muted, with the price of the precious metal steady at about $US4400 an ounce, as traders awaited US inflation data due later this week for clues to whether the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates. Northern Star lost 0.6 per cent and Evolution Mining was 1.6 per cent lower. Financial stocks fell with the big four banks sharply lower. Commonwealth Bank shed 1.5 per cent, National Australia Bank dropped 1.6 per cent, Westpac retreated 1.4 per cent and ANZ Bank declined 1.1 per cent.



Energy stocks are steady as oil prices continued to advance, with Brent, the international standard, fetching $US101.57 per barrel in early Asian trade. Speaking before today’s Republican convention in Texas, President Donald Trump downplayed concerns about oil prices and a war he said will end after the midterm elections, though hostilities show little sign of easing. A senior official from the Islamic Republic said Iran will escalate its counterstrikes if the US continues attacking its territory and infrastructure. Related Article Opinion

Oil As Trump’s Iran war drags on, we’re facing the next oil crunch Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist “The temperature just got turned up again,” said Kenny Polcari at SlateStone Wealth. “The risk premium is alive and well, and the risk to energy supplies coming out of the Gulf is real.” Woodside Energy dipped 0.1 per cent and Santos was 0.2 per cent higher while Ampol lifted 1.2 per cent. Technology stocks followed their Wall Street peers lower with WiseTech falling 1.1 per cent, Xero down 2.7 per cent and NEXTDC declining by 2.5 per cent.



The Australian dollar was trading at US72.16¢ at 10.36am AEST. Overnight, the S&P 500 index fell 0.5 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 405 points, or 0.8 per cent and the Nasdaq composite lost 0.6 per cent. Wall Street’s losses were broad, with retailers among the companies leading the market lower. Amazon fell 1.8 per cent and Starbucks fell 1.9 per cent. Nearly every sector within the benchmark S&P 500 lost ground, but oil companies pushed higher. Exxon Mobil rose 2.2 per cent and Chevron rose 1.9 per cent. Oil prices drove much of the action on Wall Street, with the price of crude climbing over $US100 for the first time since July. The conflict that began in February has essentially shut down traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, where a fifth of the world’s oil supply passed before the war began. Trump said that oil prices that have surged because of the Iran war likely won’t come down until after US midterm elections.



“Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump said. “I think the war’s going to end immediately after the election because they can’t hold out any longer.” Inflation was already stubbornly high when the US started its war against Iran because of the ongoing US trade war with much of the world. That trade war is also heating up, especially between the US and its close ally and trade partner Canada. Wall Street will get more updates this week on inflation, starting with a look at prices at the wholesale level on Thursday with the release of the Producer Price Index for August. It measures prices businesses pay for goods before they reach customers. That report will be followed up Friday with the release of the Consumer Price Index, or CPI, for August, which shows the more direct price impact for households. Related Article Updated

Phones Apple unveils its foldable iPhone Duo The latest reports are expected to show that the rate of inflation remains above 3 per cent. That has been an issue for the Federal Reserve, which is aiming to hold inflation at a target rate of 2 per cent. The central bank has been holding rates steady, but Wall Street is leaning toward a 62 per cent chance that it will raise its benchmark interest rate at its meeting next week, according to data from CME Group.



Rising Treasury yields in the bond market were also weighing down stocks on Wall Street Wednesday. The US Treasury Department on Wednesday said it would buy back up to $US6 billion ($8.3 billion) in long-term debt. That follows an announcement in August previewing plans for an unusually large buyback in an effort to contain rising yields, which make it more expensive for US companies to borrow money and also weigh down other investments, such as stocks. Bond yields had been holding steady prior to the announcement, but gained ground shortly after. “The simplest version here is that market interventions have a long history of not working very well,” said Guy LeBas, chief fixed income strategist at Janney Montgomery. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which tends to impact mortgage rates, rose to 4.85 per cent — its highest point since late October of 2023 — before easing to 4.83 per cent from 4.80 per cent late Tuesday. The yield on the 2-year Treasury, which tends to track expectations for Fed moves on interest rates, rose to 4.41 per cent from 4.39 per cent late Tuesday.



Bond yields have an inverse relationship to prices. Yields rise as bond prices fall. Rising yields signal that investors are demanding a higher return from Treasurys. Elsewhere on Wall Street, shares of Meta Platforms rose 6.6 per cent as the parent company of Instagram and Facebook launched a personal artificial intelligence agent, Muse, for people 18 and over who are looking for help with day-to-day tasks like schedules and shopping. Apple lost 0.3 per cent after unveiling its latest batch of products, including a foldable iPhone. Markets in Europe fell. With AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Less than half of Pacific Year 4 students meet minimum reading benchmarks, report finds
World.content:
A new report says less than half of year four students in the Pacific region reached the minimum expected proficiency level of reading in 2025.

The Pacific Community (SPC) has released its 2025 Pacific Islands Literacy and Numeracy Assessment.

Forty-four percent of Year 4 students reached the reading minimum proficiency standard.

For boys, this dropped to 38 percent, and for girls it went up to 50 percent.

Writing and numeracy was better, with 70 and 72 percent proficiency, respectively.

For Year 6 students, 70 percent reached minimum proficiency in numeracy, 54 percent in reading, and 53 percent in writing.

Boys' achievement was also behind girls' in this year bracket.

These figures were garnered from surveying approximately 41,000 students in each subject.

The numbers that participated in each of the three tests (numeracy, reading and writing) for each year group varied slightly because some students did not complete all three.

The assessment was administered in 15 countries and in 10 languages (English and nine languages identified by the participating countries).

The figures include most Pacific countries, but not Papua New Guinea, the French islands, the Marianas, Guam or American Samoa.

The assessment was implemented in Papua New Guinea in 2025, but the response rates from PNG's data collection did not meet the technical standards, so PNG 2025 data was not used in calculating regional averages.

Wellbeing a concern

The report said only around half of the students participating in the survey reported positive experiences at school.

A majority said they had been bullied at school.

"Around a third of students reported being tired, and around one in five reported being hungry or sad at school," the report said.

"Around one in ten students reported difficulties such as not having clean clothes or shoes for school and not being able to sleep or eat because they felt worried.

"An association was found between student performance and bullying levels, with students more likely to achieve the minimum expected proficiency levels for each subject domain if they experienced low levels of bullying. This does not establish a causal link, however."

More than three-quarters of students had teachers who reported feeling stressed at work and overwhelmed by their job.

However, almost all students had teachers who reported being proud of their work and who found their work fulfilling and inspiring.

Recommendations

Issues highlighted in the report included textbook availability and a shortage of teaching materials.

"The most commonly reported hindrances to curriculum implementation in 2025 were student absenteeism, inadequate instructional materials and teacher shortages, with around half of the students in the region attending schools with these obstacles."

The report makes several recommendations for governments and regional entities, including promoting reading as a national priority, and doing deeper studies at the local level for clearer insights into specific issues.
