World.title: Mount Albert Grammar School confirms student fatally struck by train
World.content:
Latest from scene of fatal train incident in Auckland Morning Report Download MP3 2m

Mount Albert Grammar School has confirmed one of its students died following an incident at Baldwin Avenue Train Station on Wednesday.

In a statement, headmaster Patrick Drumm said their thoughts were with the family of the boy and they were actively being supported.

"This morning the school has been focused on supporting staff and students who are also deeply affected by this loss. Our guidance team and pastoral staff are working closely with students and will continue to do so in the time ahead.

"We are grateful for the huge amount of support we are receiving from the wider educational community and beyond."

A westbound train passes the Rossgrove Terrace level crossing before stopping at Baldwin Ave station on Thursday morning. RNZ / Erin Johnson

RNZ understands students at the school had earlier been told to gather for an assembly.

Police said they had spoken to high school students who were at the Baldwin Avenue Station when the boy was hit by a train at 3.28pm on Wednesday.

Drumm said the school was operating as normal - continuing with the senior exam timetable.

"We respect the family's privacy at this time and keep them in our prayers and thoughts."

Auckland Transport said Western Line train services were operating as normal, although there may be occasional cancellations.

Inspector Kerry Watson said police had notified next of kin "and the community will appreciate that this will be devastating news for them".

Family members were seen crying at the station on Wednesday night.

World.title: ACT sets out plan to wind up Waitangi Tribunal
World.content:
The ACT Party wants to wind up the Waitangi Tribunal, saying its contemporary inquiries have become increasingly ideological and expansive.

The party is campaigning on four reforms that it says will end the tribunal's contemporary jurisdiction, and move the country on.

ACT leader David Seymour, who has previously branded the tribunal as "increasingly activist", said while the tribunal had made an important contribution, particularly in helping address historical grievances, the tribunal that existed today was different to the institution established in 1975.

"The original need for the Waitangi Tribunal has evaporated as our country has matured into a place with strong property rights, the rule of law, and restraints on the use of military power," Seymour said.

"The historical claims were clearly wrong to anybody, the government of the day illegally used military power to take away people's property. It won't surprise you I'm opposed to that, but it's not dealing with issues like that anymore.

"To have a Waitangi Tribunal that openly says 'well, actually, we don't think that the government is acting legitimately, despite putting in place perfectly legitimate elective policies', that goes beyond simply being an adviser."

ACT's policy document said every historical claim lodged before 1 September 2008 should be heard and resolved, but any lodged after would not be including contemporary or kaupapa claims.

"That was the time that Treaty settlements had to be lodged so that they could be settled," he said.

"There are some iwi - most notably my own Ngāpuhi in the Far North of the country - who have not yet come to a mandate amongst themselves to settle with the Crown, but we hope that as time goes on and as new generations come to the fore within Ngāpuhi, that it will be possible.

This would end the tribunal's power to inquire into contemporary government policy, conduct, and decisions, a power which has been used more under this government than any other in history.

Seymour denied shutting that down would be an attempt to avoid further scrutiny.

"Not at all. The government has put in place its elected mandate in a democratic society ... anyone is free to make recommendations, but we don't need a statutory taxpayer-funded organisation to do it.

"The allegations of breaches are things like 'there's not enough Māori involvement in geothermal energy ... I don't believe that's a breach. We have in our country a system of courts and democratic governance that upholds people's rights, and it has evolved."

He said the tribunal had been "incredibly inventive in saying that Treaty breaches are still occurring", and pushed back on the idea a group with independent expertise was needed to identify what government actions may constitute a treaty breach.

"They're clearly not expert or independent. They appear to be on a mission that includes creating equity, well, I'm sorry, but no government in history has created equal outcomes for all people despite some pretty spectacularly disastrous attempts by socialist governments around the world."

Te Pāti Māori has a "bottom line" policy to amend the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975 to make Waitangi Tribunal recommendations binding on the Crown, giving the tribunal more power to investigate and enforce breaches.

Seymour said that approach would make the Tribunal an unelected alternative governance system.

"That is an affront to every single New Zealander which - it shouldn't need to be said, but - includes every Māori New Zealander, who wants to be able to vote for the government that they want, and more importantly, vote out governments and policies that they dislike."

National's leader Christopher Luxon said he had not seen ACT's policy but the coalition took the Tribunal's advice onboard.

"As a government we listen to it and we have strong Treaty obligations ... the best way we can deliver those obligations is improving outcomes for Māori."

Luxon said good progress had been made for Māori in education, housing, and law and order over the past two and a half years.

The government has already launched a major review of the Tribunal's functions, but it is yet to be released publicly.

The review, which was part of National and New Zealand First's coalition agreement, promised to "refocus the scope, purpose, and nature" of the tribunal's inquiries back to their "original intent".

Christopher Luxon. RNZ/Nick Monro

Newsroom has reported the unreleased review does not recommend a curtailing of the Tribunal's ability to launch kaupapa inquiries.

Luxon said the review was now with Māori Crown Relations Minister Tama Potaka, who would "have more to say on that in due course".

He did not want to predetermine the outcome of the review but said many commentators wanted the tribunal looked at as Treaty settlements came to an end.

Carwyn Jones. RNZ / Mark Papalii

"On either side of that debate there is a question as we get through Treaty settlements as to what the future role of the Waitangi Tribunal is."

Te Wānanga o Raukawa lecturer for Māori laws and philosophy Carwyn Jones previously told RNZ that by examining contemporary issues, the tribunal was focused on what the legislation intended, and it was unclear what was meant by "original intent".

World.title: Decapitated dolphin washes up in Coromandel
World.content:
A decapitated dolphin has washed up on Pauanui beach in the Coromandel and the Conservation department wants to hear from anyone who knows what happened.

Conservation department investigation officer Hayden Loper said although the dolphin's body was decomposed, it appeared some kind of tool or implement had been used to remove its head.

Loper said marine scientists believed it was a bottle nosed dolphin, a species fully protected since 1978.

"We are asking anyone who saw what happened to this dolphin to come forward," Loper said.

"Pauanui is a small but busy settlement with a popular beach, so we're hopeful someone can provide us with information which may lead us to whoever is responsible."

World.title: Officer justified for punching man who strangled police dog, IPCA finds
World.content:
An investigation has found police were justified in punching a man who was trying to strangle a police dog during an arrest in Northland last year.

The Independent Police Conduct Authority report, released on Thursday, said a driver refused to stop for police in Kaikohe around 3am on 17 May 2025, then rammed two patrol cars before driving away at speed.

The officers decided not to chase the ute, but found it a short time later at a nearby sports field, where it had smashed through a gate and crashed into a tree.

A police dog tracked the driver who was hiding in nearby scrub.

The officers said he tried to run away so the dog was released and the man was bitten.

The man then started choking the police dog.

One of the officers punched the man in the face and torso to make him let go of the dog's neck, the report stated.

The man suffered a serious bite injury and, after being given first aid by the two officers, was flown to Middlemore Hospital in Auckland for surgery.

The man later complained to the IPCA that officers had used excessive and unjustified force during his arrest.

After interviewing the man and the two officers involved - as well as reviewing police records - the IPCA investigation found the dog bite and the use of force were justified.

The authority also found police staff discharged their duty to provide medical care to the injured man, which included applying a bandage and two tourniquets to stem heavy bleeding from the bite wound.

The man, who admitted to being under the influence of methamphetamine at the time, and the officers gave starkly different accounts of what happened during the arrest.

The IPCA ultimately sided with the officers, saying they did not believe the man was being deliberately untruthful, but that his recollection of events and the timeframes involved were likely affected by drug use and potentially by his injuries.

The two officers, who were interviewed separately, gave accounts that were consistent with their earlier reports and with each other.

Northland's top police officer, District Commander Superintendent Matt Srhoj, said staff had been dealing with a dynamic event in which two vehicles had been rammed, and an offender who showed complete disregard for people's safety.

"Our police dogs are valued members of the police whānau, and our staff have worked to prevent any injury to the police dog while trying to take the man into custody," he said.

The 40-year-old man was charged with a raft of serious driving and violence offences.

He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to home detention.

The report stated the man required several surgeries to repair an artery in his leg as well as muscle and nerve damage.

World.title: Victoria's largest amateur football league denies 'gender bias' accusations
World.content:
Multiple Victorian Amateur Football Association (VAFA) clubs have expressed disappointment with how women's competitions are being handled this season, as players across the league say the women's competition is being treated as secondary.

The VAFA is the state's largest amateur Australian Rules football league with about 300 teams and 12,000 participants.

Last week, Fitzroy Football Club and St Mary's Salesian released public statements expressing disappointment over two separate incidents that affected their finals campaigns.

Fitzroy celebrated its final home-and-away season win, believing the victory put it into the top four and its first finals series of the premier women's division.

However, the league had declared an earlier season game between two other clubs, St Kevin's and Kew, "abandoned" due to an ineligible player, and recalculated the match ratio for the teams, putting Fitzroy outside the four.

The club said it was "bitterly disappointed" not just with how the league managed the competition, but with its communication with clubs.

"To say we are frustrated with the decision is an understatement," Fitzroy said in its statement.

"We're incredibly proud of their season and all they have achieved. The same cannot be said for the VAFA's handling of this matter, and it goes to a concern that this premier women's competition is not being as well run as it should be.

"The fact the top tier of the VAFA has only nine teams creates a situation such as this to occur. As one of the top levels of women's football in Australia, it beggars belief that an odd number of teams are in the division. Would this happen in the men's premier competition?"

Loading Instagram content

Fitzroy president David Leydon said the club took great pride in playing in the premier women's division, "a very prestigious competition" that has taken them a long time to get into.

He said making finals was a big moment for the club

"And to have that ripped away from us courtesy of an arrangement that we were unaware of until after our last game, I was heartbroken," Leydon said.

He said the abandoned game should have been communicated to all other clubs in the competition.

Earlier in division two, St Mary's Salesian won an important preliminary final but were later disqualified after a player was ruled ineligible for finals.

The St Mary's player had only played two home-and-away games instead of the required three, following a rule change that year.

VAFA changed the requirement to three games at the start of the season and updated its website. But St Mary's claim PlayHQ, the platform the VAFA runs every fixture, team list and season through, still stated the old eligibility requirement for division two women's finals as two in-season games, upon which the club relied.

St Mary's said it would never have selected an ineligible player in a final had they known.

Loading Instagram content

The player missed most of the season due to maternity leave.

The club says it was not notified of the rule change, and that the men's eligibility rule was updated on PlayHQ this year, but the women's was not.

VAFA's response

VAFA strongly refuted any "any gender bias" in applying the competition rules.

It said the club statements, and subsequent social media comments on the posts, brought the integrity of the competition into question and framed the issues as being gender-based.

"Whilst we understand the emotions that such commentary provokes, the inaccuracy of these club statements is misleading and being considered by the board for potential breaches of the VAFA's policies," the VAFA told the ABC.

It said the ineligible St Kevin's player was never a matter that would affect Fitzroy's ladder position or qualification for finals, so Fitzroy was not involved in the initial enquiries into the game result.

VAFA CEO Jason Reddick said he was in touch with Fitzroy on the Sunday of round 18, the final home-and-away round, both over the phone and in writing.

Fitzroy asked for an investigation into the matter on the Monday. The VAFA looked into it and released its findings on the Friday, the day before the finals series commenced.

In response to Fitzroy asking if something similar would happen in the men's, the league said it was not a fair question.

"This is not a gender-based issue," it said.

"The matter is about the VAFA Rules pertaining to the playing of an ineligible player. We have the example of stripping reigning Premiers Uni Blues of all their points and fining them $22k for playing ineligible players in their Premier Men's team in 2022, so there is clearly no gender bias when it comes to applying the Rules of the VAFA competition."

Regarding St Mary's statement, the league said member clubs presented and voted on any rule changes each year, so all clubs knew the finals eligibility rules at the start of the season.

It also said it sent out a reminder ahead of the finals through its portal to all clubs.

'Just looks like flat-out discriminatory'

Multiple women's players across various VAFA clubs, who wished to remain anonymous due to fear of repercussions from the league, said they were not aware of the finals eligibility rule changes this year.

One player from a premier women's side said the women's competitions were treated "1,000 per cent" like an afterthought, particularly in fixturing, scheduling and grounds.

More women are playing footy than ever before. Why are so many leaving? The women's team from Kyneton's 15-month public and bitter saga suggests it is the canary in the coal mine of a widespread issue for women's players across the country.

She gave the examples of the women's division one, two and three having their grand finals at 9:40am, 9:20am and 9:20am respectively last weekend, which she said was "just awful".

The men's competitions received their fixtures months in advance, whereas the women received theirs just weeks before their season starts, she said.

"I think if it was like at least some of the men's teams got s*** locations and times, it would be slightly more understandable, because I know that obviously the council plays a big part in that [and)]in getting access to grounds at certain times. But it just looks like flat-out discriminatory," she said.

She said the issues around player eligibility also came down to broad structural issues within women's football, where clubs were often low on volunteers and didn't receive "a whole lot of help or guidance from VAFA about how to deal with situations".

Fitzroy says it is frustrated with the league. (Supplied: Fitzroy Football Club)

"That's another issue with, and this is not VAFA's fault, but by default, women have less community support and less money, less financial support, which means that the burden often feels heavier on women's teams to make sure that they're on top of all of this admin," she said.

"It's normally someone random who has no idea how football works, who's doing the team management stuff, which is checking who the players are and if they've got their correct numbers and all of that admin that goes towards eligibility and selection and reporting and all of the flow and stuff.

"So I do think that there's also a bit of like a burden on VAFA also to make more of an active effort to communicate changes, knowing that like this is all volunteer-run clubs."

Earlier this year, the ABC reported that VAFA women's players found issues with inequitable resourcing and fixturing by the league.

'Very under-resourced'

A source who has worked in senior administrative roles across different VAFA clubs, and who wished to remain anonymous for fear of repercussions at their club, said there were many issues with how the women's competitions were run.

"Firstly … it's tough for them. I think they're very under-resourced," they said.

"They're essentially set up as a men's competition traditionally and historically, and they've added women, you know, 10 years ago. And so that's always going to come with a need for serious transition and a need for serious recalibration."

Fitzroy says the club was heartbroken to learn it didn't qualify for the finals. (Supplied: Fitzroy Football Club)

They said there wasn't a clear strategy for the women's competition, pointed to "anomalies" across the competition, highlighted "fixture mistakes", and said, "we're having administrators at the VAFA giving wrong information to clubs".

"So that's just a reflection of, well, they're not resourcing it enough, and they're not actually prioritising women's footy in their strategic goals and operations, and it's reflected in the under-resourcing, which means you have these mistakes," they said.

Leydon said after Fitzroy released its public statement, the support was overwhelming, including from other clubs in the league.

"Hopefully it turns into something positive, and we can try and fix the way the women's program is conducted and get everyone to take it a lot more seriously," he said.

World.title: Aging Australia's parallels with fallen Test giant too close for comfort
World.content:
For the best part of the last three decades, the West Indies have been cricket's cautionary tale.

If you are a team that is at the peak of its powers, they are the symbol of exactly what not to do.

The story of the West Indies' decline can be told through three separate series against Australia between 1991 and 2000.

The 1991 series sees an aging Windies side filled with many of its greatest ever players hold off Australia to claim a 2–1 series win.

Mark Taylor's Australian side received a tickertape parade on their return to Australia after defeating the West Indies in 1995. (Getty Images: Patrick Riviere)

Four years later, with the Windies side looking markedly different, Australia manages to turn the tables and wins 2–1 in the Caribbean.

Five years after that, almost all of the class of 1991 is gone and the Windies are unceremoniously thumped 5–0 in Australia.

Since the 2000 series, the ledger of Test results between the two sides reads 22–2 Australia's way with a couple of draws thrown in there.

The current predicament Australia's Test team finds itself in is eerily similar to that of the West Indies three decades earlier.

It is a comparison that would be a little too close for comfort for the Australians.

As Australia unveiled its Test squad this week ahead of a pivotal tour of South Africa, all of the focus centred around the inclusion of one man: Marnus Labuschagne.

Labuschagne retained for South Africa Test series despite pressure Despite mounting pressure over his poor form, Marnus Labuschagne keeps his spot in Australia's Test squad for the upcoming three-Test tour of South Africa.

Even when he was scoring Test centuries at will in his first couple of years in the team, there was perhaps no more polarising player in Australia than Labuschagne.

Now that the runs have well and truly dried up, he has become the easy whipping boy.

The numbers when it comes to Australia's No.3 are now no secret.

There have been no Test centuries since July 2023.

In 23 Tests since that ton in Manchester against England, Labuschagne has averaged just 24.69, yet somehow remains a fixture in the side.

Labuschagne, 32, has no shortage of support despite statistically being one of the poorest performers in the Australian side.

Australia's chairman of selectors, George Bailey, pointed the finger at the batting cohort that has underperformed as a whole and even explained how Australia has increasingly used the metric of percentage of team runs rather than batting averages in a bid to raise the confidence of a team that has become increasingly bereft of it.

The truth of the matter is that Labuschagne is a symptom of Australia's problem, rather than the root of it.

Steve Smith (pictured) still remains the trump card in Australia's batting line-up at 37. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

That problem is, the depth of Australian cricket is nowhere near what it used to be.

Australia was able to completely take the mantle from the West Indies as the best team in the world three decades ago courtesy of boasting not only a tremendous first XI, but also a level of depth that made it plausible to suggest Australia A was once the second-best team in the world.

A look at the top 15 run-scorers in the Sheffield Shield from the 1995–96 season shows names like Darren Lehmann, Justin Langer, Michael Hussey, Adam Gilchrist and Damien Martyn among them, names that would eventually become mainstays within the Test side.

The top scorers in the most recent Shield season are far less heralded. Of the top 15, only Sam Konstas (fifth) and Campbell Kellaway (15th) are widely considered to be serious Test mainstays over the next decade.

Konstas's brief Test career has so far provided mixed returns, while the 23-year-old Kellaway is yet to represent Australia at the senior level.

Sam Konstas's first venture into Test cricket provided middling returns despite a promising start. (Getty Images: Santanu Banik)

Other players such as Ollie Peake, Lance Morris, Fergus O'Neill and Nathan McSweeney have been touted as future Test cricketers.

As things currently stand, there is no proof that any of them will have sustained success at the highest level, as much as Australia hopes they will.

As was the case for the West Indies at the start of the 90s, Australia's problem is that its oldest players still remain its best and most indispensable.

The next generation simply isn't banging the door down.

Five players from the West Indies XI that played in the fourth Test of the 1991 series against Australia — Viv Richards, Gordon Greenidge, Gus Logie, Jeff Dujon and Malcolm Marshall — did not play another Test after that calendar year, leaving a massive hole in the side.

The departures left the likes of Richie Richardson, Brian Lara, Curtly Ambrose and Courtney Walsh with a burden too great to bear despite their individual greatness.

Greenidge (left) and Richards (right) both played their final Tests in 1991, leaving a huge hole in the West Indies team. (Allsport/Getty Images/Hulton Archive)

Once Ambrose, Walsh and Richardson went, it was essentially Lara against the world, a hill too steep to climb even if you are one of the most talented batters the game has ever seen.

Richardson, a legendary No.3, shuffled his way around the line-up as the Windies looked to plug hole after hole left behind by the departing greats.

After playing 67 of his 86 Tests at first drop, Richardson batted in four different positions, none of them at No.3, in his final year of Test cricket, even opening as Steve Smith briefly did a few years back.

It is a situation eerily similar to what Australia finds itself in at the moment, with no young opener seemingly ready to fill the void left by David Warner and Usman Khawaja, leaving Travis Head, Labuschagne and Smith to all have their turn at the very top of the order.

Australia is struggling to find proper openers after the retirements of Khawaja (left) and Warner (right). (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

Whenever the collective age of Australia's Test side is brought up, the common retort from those within the camp is to list the team's accolades: Ashes series wins and Test Championship rankings.

The West Indies, too, were still formidable at the start of the 90s.

That provided little insight into what was to come at the back end of that decade.

Like the West Indies of the mid-90s, Australia's batting cracks have been papered over by an excellent bowling attack whose members remain elite well into their 30s.

Mitchell Starc, Pat Cummins and Josh Hazlewood still remain as good a pace trio as any, but the fact that they're relied upon to be so consistently excellent is an indictment on what lies beyond them.

The retirements of Ambrose (left) and Walsh (right) in 2000 signalled the end of the West Indies being a feared Test side. (Getty Images: PA Images/Rebecca Naden)

It is a similar situation to Ambrose and Walsh, who both played until their late 30s and ultimately proved to be irreplaceable.

The problem for Australia is that their most reliable replacements for their first-choice quicks — Scott Boland and Michael Neser — are also in the 36-plus age bracket.

So how exactly does Australia avoid the same fate as the West Indies?

Australia's superior cricketing infrastructure at the domestic level should ensure it doesn't completely crumble as a force.

Mitchell Starc (pictured) is still Australia's best Test paceman despite being 36 years old. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Even in their pomp, the West Indies dealt with politics between the different Caribbean islands and severe financial issues, problems that have only intensified as the team has gotten progressively worse.

Australia does not have these issues.

Australia would ideally like to stagger its retirements as well, to avoid a situation like what happened to the West Indies in 1991.

However, selectors must tread the fine line between playing youth for youth's sake and hanging onto its older core for a little too long.

Transitioning away from a golden generation is hard, and it is a struggle that is not exclusive to these two Test teams.

South Africa struggled after the retirements of some of its greats before winning the World Test Championship last year. (AP: Kirsty Wigglesworth)

South Africa has only begun to lift its head above water over the last two years after its own swathe of retirements, while Sri Lanka still finds itself in cricket's murky backwaters despite some of its best players retiring over a decade ago.

The good news for Australia is that it has experience of transitioning away from retiring greats successfully.

Almost 20 years ago, when the likes of Glenn McGrath, Shane Warne, Langer, Matthew Hayden and Gilchrist all departed within 18 months, the next generation was waiting in the wings.

This time around, as Australia gets set to bid farewell to another set of greats, the transition is almost certain to be nowhere near as smooth.

World.title: The NFL's MCG takeover just the latest step towards global domination
World.content:
As Melbourne hosts an NFL regular-season match for the first time, the real scale of the league's global ambitions has been laid bare.

The NFL will host nine international matches in 2026 across four continents in markets as far apart as Brazil, Germany, France, the UK and, of course, Australia.

There are few things more synonymous with the United States than American football.

From the community-focused appeal of local Friday night high school games to the ritual and history of big-time college football on Saturdays, football is middle America.

Then there's the NFL, monopolising US living rooms on Sundays at first, and increasingly Mondays and Thursdays as well.

The humble origins of professional football belie the monstrosity it has become, a process accelerated by TV in the 1960s after the merger of the National and American Football Leagues and subsequent expansion.

The decades since have seen the NFL develop into a cultural and economic behemoth.

The cultural dominance of the NFL

The numbers around the NFL are simply huge.

There are fewer more ostentatious displays of American pride than at a NFL game. (Getty Images: Justin Edmonds)

The league reported a staggeringly large total revenue of more than $US23 billion ($31.95 billion) for the last year.

For the record, that is almost 26 times what the AFL reported in the same period.

A relatively short, 18-week, 17-game season ensures that each and every match is either much-watch TV or the hottest ticket in town: Each match day is an Event with a capital E.

Sport has long dominated the TV market in the USA, but the scale of the dominance of sport, and one sport in particular, has to be seen to be believed.

Of the 100 most-watched shows in America in 2025, 95 were sporting events and 83 were NFL games, according to Nielsen ratings.

Incredibly, seven others were college football games. Only five other sports events made the top 100: Game 6 and Game 7 of baseball's World Series in 97th and 25th place respectively, the boxing match between Canelo Álvarez and Terence Crawford, the NCAA basketball championship between Florida and Houston, and the 2025 Kentucky Derby.

Note, not a single NBA (basketball) or NHL (ice hockey) game made the cut.

The 2025 Super Bowl had a staggering 127.7 million viewers, more than double the next most-viewed event, the AFC Championship Game a fortnight earlier, which drew 57.4 million.

The Super Bowl is invariably the most-watched event of the year in the United States. Nielsen reports that 19 of the top 20 most-watched broadcasts in American TV history are Super Bowl matches. Only the finale of M*A*S*H in 1983 bucked that trend, sitting 13th all time.

The Super Bowl is the greatest behemoth in American culture. (Getty Images: Ishika Samant)

Football is very clearly big business.

Perhaps an even more staggering point is revealed when the schedule is set for the seven-game World Series, the pinnacle of the Major League Baseball season. Broadcasters will purposefully ensure that matches are not scheduled on Sundays, so there is no clash with Sunday's NFL offering.

Last year's nine-day World Series between the Toronto Blue Jays and the LA Dodgers had games scheduled for Friday-Saturday, Monday-Wednesday and Friday-Saturday.

Game seven on that second Saturday night had 27.3 million viewers, the 25th-most-watched broadcast of the year, with 23 NFL games ahead of it.

Baseball may historically claim itself to be America's favourite pastime.

But the NFL has its sights set much wider. It wants the world.

Global expansion

Wembley Stadium hosted London's first NFL regular season game in 2007, and has been a regular stop on the circuit ever since. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

Heading into the 2026 season, there have been 62 regular-season NFL games played away from the USA.

London has hosted the most matches, with 42 regular-season games taking place either at Wembley (27), Twickenham (3) or Tottenham Hotspur (12) stadiums.

Mexico City hosted the first-ever regular-season match to take place in a foreign country in 2005, when the Arizona Cardinals smashed the San Francisco 49ers 31-14 in front of a record 103,467 fans at the Estadio Azteca.

It has gone on to host five matches prior to this season and will see the 49ers take on the Minnesota Vikings there in November, with matches scheduled until 2028.

Fans get into the spirit whenever the NFL comes to town. (Getty Images: Buda Mendes)

Canada has long been a destination for American football teams, with matches held there as early as the 1950s, but it has hosted relatively few regular-season games, with Toronto hosting six games all at the Rogers Centre.

This season, Australia will host a regular-season game for the first time. Sydney's Olympic stadium hosted the Denver Broncos and the San Diego Chargers in 1999, but that was an exhibition match.

NFL executive vice president of football operations Troy Vincent Sr said "the NFL is committed to expanding NFL action to international fans in their home countries" and is doing so more than ever this season.

Rio de Janeiro will host a match for the first time at the historic Maracanã, when the Dallas Cowboys and Baltimore Ravens clash in week three. It is the second city in Brazil to host a match, after São Paulo's Arena Corinthians hosted the Green Bay Packers and Philadelphia Eagles in 2024.

Brazil has already hosted one NFL game, at São Paulo's Arena Corinthians in 2024. (Getty Images: Pedro Vilela)

The Stade de France in Paris will host its first game as well — the New Orleans Saints and Pittsburgh will meet there — while other matches take place in Munich, Madrid and Mexico City.

Long-time base London will host three matches: two at Tottenham Hotspur and the other at Wembley.

Originally, there were only supposed to be eight matches, but the Jacksonville Jaguars made a special agreement with Wembley Stadium to play a second game there while their EverBank Stadium in Jacksonville was undergoing renovations.

The Jaguars' connection with London has been fruitful for the team's owner, Shahid Khan, who also owns English Premier League side Fulham.

Jacksonville Jaguars and Trevor Lawrence have made London their home away from home. (Getty Images: PA Images/Zac Goodwin)

It led some people to believe that the Jaguars could end up moving to London and becoming the first overseas franchise, but that has not materialised yet, with the team signing agreements that will keep them in Florida for the foreseeable future.

Not that an overseas franchise is a prospect that is off the table.

"At some point, there will be NFL teams outside the USA. I have no doubt that this will happen one day," NFL commissioner Roger Goodell told former NFL player Markus Kuhn for German broadcaster RTL/ntv last week.

NFL executive Peter O'Reilly told media earlier this year that the exception made for nine games this season "shows the momentum and, I think, the support for the model we have".

Some resistance building

The NFL confirmed it will play 10 games overseas in 2027, which, as things stand, is the most the league can host under the current collective bargaining agreement.

Berlin's Olympiastadion has hosted an NFL game in the recent past. (Getty Images: picture alliance/Sebastian Gollnow)

However, Goodell said that his goal was to play as many as 16 games overseas.

That would likely see every team play at least one overseas game, an important point for some semblance of competitive balance.

The Melbourne-bound 49ers will endure two international trips this year, to Melbourne and Mexico, and as a result will travel 61,324 kilometres — a distance equivalent to more than one-and-a-half times around the world.

The Carolina Panthers, by comparison, will travel about a quarter of that distance, just 14,065km.

That fact certainly irked the 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan when the schedule dropped earlier this year.

"That was our goal, to go 19 hours away to play a game," he said, sarcasm dripping from every word.

"We'll deal with it.

"I think there's eight international games [there's actually nine]. We've got two of them, so we're fired up about that."

Kyle Shanahan wasn't, perhaps, being entirely genuine when he said he was looking forward to a 25,000km round trip to Melbourne to start the season. (Getty Images: Luke Hales)

He went on to say that although it was "cool" for the league to be playing internationally, there was "not much benefit" to the teams playing the match, especially when it was in week one of the season.

"I don't see any pro," he said.

"It's cool for the league to play globally. I think that's awesome. But as far as the team doing it, no, there's not much benefit to it."

Managing director and head of NFL International, Gerrit Meier, noted that the prospect of further matches in Australia would depend a lot on how the players valued the experience.

"The teams coming back [to America after travelling to Australia for a game], they need to be healthy," Meier said in an interview with Reuters.

"They need to have a great experience. It needs to be a great game, because in the end, it counts. It's not an exhibition game.

"We're going to sit with the larger region and city and [ask] what all of you thought. Was it good? Was it not good? Would you want to have us back?

"We want to kind of see how the overall set-up has been working."

Tokyo will no doubt be a target market. The city has hosted 13 exhibition games dating back to the 1970s without ever having the real deal played out in front of an acknowledged crowd of Americanophiles.

How many matches could Australia host in the future?

The MCG will become the latest of the world's great stadiums to host an NFL game. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Craig Dooley)

Currently, each NFL team plays 17 games in the regular season over 18 weeks.

That means there are 272 matches per (regular) season, with each conference (the AFC and NFC) alternating who has eight or nine home games per season.

So, why would a team want to give up a home game to travel all the way across the world to play a match?

Partially, it is due to a long-term strategy by the league, anchored by its Global Markets Program.

Starting in January 2022, the Global Markets Program gives NFL clubs access to international territories to utilise for their own marketing and fan engagement purposes.

The teams that have nominated Australia as their primary market are the Las Vegas Raiders, Los Angeles Rams, Philadelphia Eagles and Seattle Seahawks.

Matthew Stafford and the Los Angeles Rams are one of three teams that have Australia as its primary focus commercially. (Getty Images: Sean M. Haffey)

So, with the Rams already having made the trip, does that mean the Eagles, Raiders and Seahawks will be lining up in the coming years?

In short, yes.

"I think that would be the plan, right?" Meier told Reuters last week.

"Overall, we're working off the hypothesis that we need to make a commitment to a market … We believe that at least one game per year should be something that we should be having in the markets that we commit to.

"And maybe over time, as we have, maybe, greater inventory, then maybe you play two games [per season] or so."

Hosting an NFL game is not cheap. According to The Age, the Victorian government is shelling out between $10 million and $15 million per game, with a view to making more back through tourism dollars.

The NFL set up a local office for Australia and New Zealand in Sydney in 2022, and has operated an International Academy on the Gold Coast since 2024, only the second such institution outside of the US, and interest in the NFL in Australia has developed over time.

"It's kind of moved from being an interesting market to actually being a strategic growth market," Meier said.

"We have a fast-growing fan base … The game itself is just a catalyst."

World.title: Women's tennis has a new world number one as US Open showdown looms
World.content:
Elena Rybakina ensured she will leave Flushing Meadows as the new world number one after a comprehensive win over Qinwen Zheng, despite top seed Aryna Sabalenka still being alive in her quest for a third straight US Open title.

Rybakina reached the semifinals for the first time and will face 2023 champion Coco Gauff, who beat fifth seed Mirra Andreeva 2-6, 7-6(9/7), 6-2.

The early program kicked off barely eight hours after Ben Shelton ‌beat Carlos Alcaraz in a five-set thriller that finished at 3:33 am, breaking the record for the latest ever finish at the US Open.

Zheng had cultivated a ‌reputation as one of the tournament's finest comeback artists but ran ⁠out of gas against Rybakina, losing 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 as ‌the Kazakh chipped away at her defences after ‌overcoming early mistakes.

"Becoming the WTA number one is something I've dreamed about since I was a young girl, it means so much to me," said Rybakina, who dethroned Sabalenka at the top of the rankings.

"I'm so proud of this moment. I want to thank my whole team for their support and being able to celebrate this achievement with me."

Meanwhile, Gauff got off to a dreadful start before ​recovering ‌to beat Russian 19-year-old Andreeva.

Gauff improved her level dramatically across the match, saving ‌match points in the ‌second-set tiebreak to move into the last four of her home slam for just the second time.

"Elena — she's the new world number one so it's going to be a tough match," Gauff said.

"I'm looking ‌forward to the battle. These are the moments you live for."

Sabalenka and American third seed Jessica Pegula are in the other semifinal.

Pegula is the only woman left without a grand slam title to her name, while Sabalenka is trying to win the US Open to avoid going major-less for the first time since 2022.

If Rybakina and Sabalenka progress, it will mark their second meeting in a major final this year, after Rybakina won the Australian Open title in January.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Overlooked by the whole AFL, Isaiah Dudley used the disappointment as fuel
World.content:
Isaiah Dudley's remarkable rise from state league footballer to the AFL finals has taken many onlookers by surprise, but those who worked closest with him always knew the Fremantle Docker could succeed at the highest level.

"For Isaiah it's never been about a lack of talent, he's got more talent in his football acumen than many, it was about just being physically ready for the challenge of AFL footy," said Paul Thomas, who coached Dudley at Central Districts in the SANFL.

"The value that we got out of him is exactly what you're seeing now in the Fremantle side."

Dudley has enjoyed a quick rise since making his AFL debut for the Dockers last season. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre/AFL Photos)

Dudley, listed as the shortest player in the league at 168 centimetres, was overlooked by all 18 clubs at the 2021 AFL draft.

That would have been enough for many footballers to give up their AFL dreams, especially when feedback from recruiters suggested his fitness and lifestyle were not up to scratch for professional football.

But for Dudley, it only served as motivation.

"They were the main two things, my lifestyle and my fitness, which kind of opened my eyes, realising that if I get them knuckled down, I can take my place anywhere," he said.

Dudley was a mature-age recruit for the Dockers. (Getty Images: Travis Hayto/AFL Photos)

Dudley gives a lot of the credit to his former coach.

"That's the thing with Thommo, he built good habits into me, and now the habits are living out and I've been playing every game, and I've been loving it," he said.

"I also became a better person, maturing, and then obviously with Thommo he drove me to become a better person and player.

"I'm a whole completely different person to what I was at SANFL level, not the one bloke who sits in the forward line just chilling.

"Now I'm up the ground working, bringing my talent and getting the most out of myself."

Hard yards pay off

But it was far from an overnight process, with Centrals putting added focus on improving Dudley's conditioning.

"The club put a little 10-week program into Isaiah, like a personal training type thing in the middle of a season, which then really took his game in leaps and bounds the following season," Thomas said.

Paul Thomas coached Dudley at South Australian club Central Districts. (ABC News: Che Corley)

It paid dividends, with Dudley's 2024 SANFL season catching Fremantle's eye.

He was invited to train with the Dockers before being picked up in the supplemental selection period on the eve of the club's first 2025 pre-season game against the Indigenous All-Stars.

By round three of his first year, he had already made his debut in the cauldron of a Western Derby against West Coast, kicking two first-quarter goals in Fremantle's victory.

Dudley's pressure has helped make Fremantle's forward line one of the most feared in the AFL. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

He played 16 games in his first year and has featured in all 24 of Fremantle's matches so far this season, kicking 28 goals.

As the Dockers look to bounce back against Geelong in a must-win semifinal at Perth Stadium tomorrow night, he admits he is living a dream that he sometimes has to remind himself is real.

Dockers wilt against masterful Hawthorn So good for so long this year, Fremantle chose an inopportune time to put in — by some distance — their worst shift of the season, going down by 32 points to a brilliant Hawthorn.

"I still pinch myself every day that I've gone from SANFL to now playing in an AFL finals series," Dudley said.

" It's a dream come true and I'm loving it. "

All while his former coaches and teammates watch on proudly from South Australia.

"I probably can't push enough just how much he makes us all smile still, when he does what he does on the footy field," Thomas said.

"He has the ability to light the crowd, he lights our locker room up as well.

"Seeing Perth Stadium come alight when he does something, and the commentators as well, isn't a surprise, but it certainly makes us all smile."

Dudley hopes his improbable story can inspire other footballers. (ABC News: Blake Kagi)

Dudley is hopeful his improbable story can encourage other footballers to overcome their setbacks and never give up on their dreams, and has a simple message for those who face disappointment in the draft.

"Always have a smile on your face, because if you don't get picked up from the draft, you've got many ways to get into the league.

"Lean into the coaches, the close network that you have, they're the people that are supporting you through the highs and lows."

World.title: Opals survive in last second after giving up 20-point lead at World Cup
World.content:
A short-handed Australian team is still alive and into the last eight at the FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup despite surrendering a 20-point three-quarter-time lead before ultimately beating Italy 82-80.

The Opals had a 69-49 lead heading into the final quarter of their qualification final against the Azzurre, but watched the Italians slowly chip away at it over the next eight minutes and 51 seconds before Costanza Verona's three tied the game at 77 with 1:09 left.

Zitina Aokuso made a lay-up off Izzy Borlase's drive to end a three-minute scoring drought for Australia and Ally Wilson's clutch free throws gave them a four-point advantage when Italy was forced to intentionally foul with eight seconds left.

The great escape appeared to be complete until a long-range bomb by Vittoria Blasigh off the inbounds pass left Italy trailing by just one point with five seconds remaining.

Borlase was then sent to the line but made only one of two free throws to give Italy a chance for one last play while down by two, and Francesca Pasa appeared to catch the defence napping by going for the tie rather than the win.

The speedy guard burst past Borlase and got her left-handed lay-up onto the backboard as the siren sounded, but the ball just rolled off the right of the rim and the Opals survived.

"We still have an opportunity to keep fighting and that's what we're going to do," coach Sandy Brondello said.

They moved into a quarterfinal against Spain, but will have to do it without some of their biggest stars.

Having already lost veteran Sami Whitcomb to a knee issue before the tournament and losing WNBA champion Alanna Smith to injury in their opening game against Puerto Rico, the Opals copped another huge blow against Italy.

Captain and star forward Ezi Magbegor played just four minutes of the clash before she went down during a drive to the basket.

Magbegor powered into a seam in the defence but was fouled from the side by Lorela Cubaj, causing her right knee to bend awkwardly inward.

Ezi Magbegor knew straight away she was in trouble. (Supplied: FIBA)

The Seattle Storm star immediately shouted in pain and hit the deck, appearing to be in tears on the floor before being helped off the court by training staff.

"It made my heart sink to see her go down," Brondello said.

"She's so impactful for us and we just pray that she's OK. We don't know. We'll see what the result is tomorrow. She's walking and that's a good sign."

Meanwhile, an ill Jade Melbourne played only three minutes.

The Opals are still alive and face Spain in the World Cup quarterfinals. (Getty Images: Mami Yasui/FIBA)

Borlase, a rookie guard with the WNBA's Atlanta Dream, picked up the slack and scored a game-high 30 points on 7/13 shooting from the field while knocking down 14 of 16 free throws.

The 21-year-old was named player of the match as she became just the fourth Opal to score 30 points at a World Cup.

"Something we speak about a lot is the Opals legacy," Borlase said.

"We really respect what the girls have done in previous tournaments. They've inspired us to want to play for Australia and I just hope I've inspired someone to tonight to want to play for Australia because there's no greater honour."

The tears were flowing for Italy after its second loss at the tournament by just one bucket, having missed a last-second three-pointer to lose 55-52 to reigning champions USA in the group stage.

World.title: Greyhound trainer handed lifetime ban for 'egregious' actions
World.content:
A greyhound trainer has been found "entirely unfit" to participate in the industry, with the governing body in South Australia issuing a lifetime ban and a $5,000 fine for dishonestly negotiating the transfer of an injured dog to another trainer.

Jack Clayton Trengove, who is from a prominent Broken Hill racing family, was already suspended for previous animal welfare-related matters.

In a sentencing decision handed down by Greyhound Racing SA (GRSA), an integrity hearings panel said Mr Trengove discussed the transfer of a greyhound named "Arctic Girl" to a trainer in NSW without disclosing an "unhealed hock fracture" on the dog's hind leg.

"We found that Mr Trengove knew of the fracture and that his failure to disclose it was dishonest," GRSA said in its decision.

"Arctic Girl was transferred to a trainer who was unaware of the true condition of her hock and commenced preparing her to race, thereby placing Arctic Girl at significant risk of catastrophic injury."

Mr Trengove pictured at the Broken Hill Racecourse last year. (Supplied: Broken Hill Racecourse)

The panel said that although the dog did not ultimately suffer such injury, "that outcome was due in significant part to the timely intervention and positive action of GRSA officers".

"This offending represents such an egregious example that stands in stark contrast to the standard and welfare expected within the industry," it said.

"Accordingly, the [panel] have concluded that this offending not only strikes to the core of the values upon which greyhound racing in South Australia operates, it has also concluded that his conduct makes him entirely unfit to continue participating in the industry."

The panel said it accepted the new owner's account that Mr Trengove had told her over Facebook Messenger that Arctic Girl had been off with a sore hock but was "good to go now".

It rejected Mr Trengove's account that he separately disclosed the fracture by telephone to the new owner.

The decision states the greyhound was returned to SA and rehomed.

SA greyhound trainer banned for dog's 'unnecessary suffering' One of SA greyhound racing's most prominent identities has been disqualified after a 12-month inquiry by the sport's controlling body.

Mr Trengove has been suspended since June 2025 when charges relating to animal welfare rule breaches were laid against him, after an investigation stemming from photos taken inside his kennel.

In the latest ruling, the panel also noted several racing-related infringements Mr Trengove had accrued in 2024 which included a failure to present a greyhound for veterinary examination, striking a greyhound and a failure to maintain a treatment record book.

In a statement, GRSA chief executive officer Brenton Scott said the organisation had adopted a zero-tolerance policy to animal welfare breaches.

"The vast majority of industry participants both love and care for their greyhounds and abide by the rules and welfare policies … but any variation to this is acted upon and considered seriously by our independent integrity process," he said.

In response to the outcome, Mr Trengove told the ABC he felt he was being targeted.

" I was not given a fair hearing … their process for the hearing panel is run very wrong. "

The statement from GRSA said Mr Trengrove did not attend the hearing and did not provide a defence, "despite being given a fair opportunity to do so".

The panel's decision document states Mr Trengove did not attend a hearing related to the latest counts on which he had been found guilty, but had attended other hearings related to separate counts.

In 2021, Mr Trengove was described by GRSA as having a "strong future ahead of him" in a since-deleted online blog.

GRSA said Arctic Girl had been "subsequently rehomed" as part of its own Greyhounds as Pets initiative.

World.title: 'Purpose I had is no longer': Hollands opens up on Blues axing
World.content:
Elijah Hollands is at peace with the end of his Carlton career, saying he realises there are more important things in life that he needs to focus on.

Hollands was one of seven players delisted by the Blues on Wednesday, with former GWS star Zac Williams, Jordan Boyd, Lachie Fogarty, Lewis Young, Flynn Young and Harry Charleson also among the casualties.

But it was Hollands' axing just months after suffering an on-field mental health episode that represented the biggest story.

Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636

Headspace on 1800 650 890

ReachOut at au.reachout.com

MensLine Australia on 1300 789 978

SANE on 1800 187 263

Carlton was fined $75,000 for its handling of Hollands during a round-six loss to Collingwood.

Hollands tallied just one disposal for the match, with his erratic behaviour catching the attention of fans even before the game started.

The 24-year-old was hospitalised days later before deciding to step away from football to concentrate on his mental health.

It meant Hollands wasn't able to add to his 47-game AFL career, 14 of which were played at Gold Coast.

His brother Oliver Hollands remains at Carlton.

Elijah took to Instagram to share his thoughts about the end of his time at the Blues, which could also spell an end to his AFL career.

Loading Instagram content

"Football means an extreme amount to me," Hollands wrote.

"My dad played professional footy, my great-grandfather played professional footy, my brother plays professional footy — it is everything I have lived and breathed for as long as I can remember.

"I have only ever wanted to do one thing my entire life: copy what was done before me and play AFL footy. It was something that I just knew I was going to do when I was a kid and it was all I ever cared about.

"And now, unfortunately, that purpose I had is no longer.

"I love this game, but I have come to realise that there are things in my life that are far more important than footy right now and they're the things I will now prioritise."

Hollands's father posts heartfelt message Elijah Hollands's father, former AFL player Ben Hollands, posts on social media pledging to help lift his son up and urging others to check on their friends if they are struggling.

Hollands thanked the greater AFL community for its support since his mental health challenges became public.

"As an extremely confident 18-year-old, I certainly envisioned my career going a whole lot differently, but I am OK with accepting that it just isn't in the plans set for me," Hollands said.

"I'll be moving into the next chapter of my life, leaving what will feel like a big hole to fill, but I am excited about what can come from having my health and mind in much greater shape."

Carlton's other big delisting was Williams, who joined the Blues from GWS at the end of 2020 on a six-year deal believed to be worth about $5 million.

The soon-to-be 32-year-old managed only nine games this year, with his time at Carlton plagued by injuries.

Tech.title: There aren’t AirPods with cameras yet and I hope it stays that way
Tech.content:
September Apple events are always a swirl of information and new, exciting products, and today’s was no different. Apple announced its first foldable, the iPhone Duo, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max; active noise cancellation (ANC) is now on the cheapest AirPods model, the AirPods 5; and a Siri Recap feature comes to the Watch Series 12 and Watch Ultra 4. But missing were the AirPods Pro with cameras that have been rumored throughout the year and, according to Mark Gurman at Bloomberg, are delayed until 2027. I’m happy about that and I hope we never get them.

I have too many concerns about a company — any company — putting cameras anywhere, especially in devices like earbuds that are now so ubiquitous in our daily lives. LED lights on glasses or earbuds do little to ease people’s minds when someone is recording them. And some Meta smart glasses users have shown people will hide their recording intentions. While recording in public in the US is generally legal, it can be very creepy. And with earbuds as common as they are, someone could wear them into sensitive situations unnoticed.

Rumors say that the cameras on the potential AirPods will be low-resolution and “aren’t designed” to take images or video, but instead use what they see to inform Siri AI and Visual Intelligence. That information could be used to help with turn-by-turn directions or identify writing and objects like books. Even with a low-resolution camera, it’s still potentially always gathering information about the world (and people!) around you. That invasion of privacy is something I cannot get past.

During today’s event, Apple introduced Audio Intelligence with the Apple Watch, which sounds like a precursor to the Visual Intelligence we’re expecting on the rumored AirPods Pro 4. In its support documentation, Apple points out that audio is not stored and there’s no way to access a recording, which could be the same for video data with Visual Intelligence, and that for its Siri Recap feature, any data used to create a summary is not even accessible by Apple. Any stored data — such as a Siri Recap or a bit of text the user can save with Live Rewind — is also end-to-end encrypted. People are not identified in the Siri Recap, either. Of course, none of this is live yet, so we’ll have to wait and see how well Audio Intelligence works once it’s released.

Functionally, a camera will only gather information if it can see things. What if you have thick, long hair? Or like to wear hoodie sweatshirts? Or fancy, elaborate jewelry? The AirPods would just turn into what they should be — earbuds. It’s possible the reason the AirPods with cameras have been pushed into 2027 is to find solutions to these problems. Or maybe part of the delay is Apple separating itself from the current public climate around cameras thanks to Meta and Flock.

The one immediate benefit of the AirPods with cameras could be accessibility. They could improve situational awareness for people with visual limitations or help hard-of-hearing users read lips. They could even figure out the person you’re speaking to and focus the AirPods’ mics on them for increased intelligibility.

When you take out privacy concerns or the fact that lots of people — and companies — look for opportunities to exploit people, there’s good that can be done. But it involves a lot of trust to be put in untrustworthy hands. I’m not sure I’m ready for that. Or if I ever will be. Whether any of us are ready or not, though, it seems the cameras are coming. The introduction of Apple’s Audio Intelligence on the new Apple Watch is evidence enough that the company is going all in on using sensors to analyze the world around us.

Tech.title: The black iPhone Pro returns
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple has seen reason: It has a black model in the iPhone Pro lineup again.

Last year, Apple went bold with its colors for the iPhone 17 Pro, offering a flashy orange, a shiny silver, and a dark blue. Don’t get me wrong, they looked nice. But there was no black (or dark gray) for the first time since the start of the iPhone Pro lineup, which Apple first introduced in September 2019 with the iPhone 11 Pro and Pro Max.

I care about this because I always buy the black phone. I learned my lesson with the iPhone 6: I got it in gold to mix things up and came to regret it. I don’t need something flashy — I need a phone that blends into the background and looks decent in whatever case I throw it into. After the iPhone 6, my next phone was the iPhone 7 in the excellent matte black (I wasn’t brave enough to endure the jet black model’s potential scratches), and I’ve only ever gotten the black or gray phones since.

My black titanium iPhone 16 Pro in a black Torras case (with a mostly black homescreen) still works very well, thank you very much, and I’m not in the market for a new phone. But when I make my annual mid-September visit to the local Apple Store to look at all the new iPhones, I won’t be rushing to see the iPhone 18 Pro in burgundy, blue, or silver. I’ll be beelining for the model in black.

Just look at this thing! It’s great!

Tech.title: The incomplete history of Duo devices
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Apple announced the company’s first device with a folding screen today, the iPhone Duo, but that’s where the firsts end. The Duo is not only far from the first foldable on the market thanks to the efforts of Samsung and Google, but it’s also not the first product to be called the Duo.

Former Apple CEO Steve Jobs popularized the saying “good artists copy, great artists steal,” but will the iPhone Duo’s folding screen, which features a custom nano-texture display material to help minimize the visibility of its crease, be enough to make us forget these other Duos that have come before it? Only time, or how aggressively Apple plans to market its Duo, will tell. Is there a Duo we missed? Let us know.

NEC TurboDuo

Merging the functionality of the TurboGrafx-16 console and the TurboGrafx-CD that added CD-ROM functionality, the NEC TurboDuo (later rebranded to just the Duo) launched in North America in 1993 after debuting in Japan a few years earlier as the PC Engine Duo. The console was developed as part of a joint venture between NEC and Hudson Soft but never reached the popularity of the original TurboGrafx-16; its short run ended on Christmas Day in 1995.

Google Duo

Photo by Dieter Bohn / The Verge

First released in 2016 and eventually merged into Google Meet in 2022, Google Duo was the company’s proprietary VoIP service meant to compete with products like Skype or Zoom and replace Hangouts. Its cross-platform availability included Android and iOS mobile devices as well as web browsers, and while it supported hi-def video calls, the service was also optimized for slow mobile networks.

Apple PowerBook Duo

The iPhone Duo isn’t even Apple’s first Duo. The PowerBook Duo predates everything Apple announced today by decades. It was an ultraportable laptop, and when Apple introduced it in 1992 it was the smallest and lightest PowerBook available, but still weighed over 4 pounds. Apple managed to shrink the Duo using an approach it still uses today: omitting built-in ports and expansion features. If you wanted to connect peripherals and accessories you had to rely on optional docks. If you’ve ever had to buy a USB hub to connect all your devices to your MacBook, you can thank the PowerBook Duo.

Apple MagSafe Duo

Photo by Dieter Bohn / The Verge

Twenty-three years after the PowerBook Duo was discontinued, the company announced the MagSafe Duo charger that could wirelessly charge an iPhone and an Apple Watch at the same time. However, it felt like a consolation prize for the Apple AirPower wireless charger, which was announced in 2017 but never materialized. The MagSafe Duo was discontinued just a few years later in late 2023, paving the way for the foldable iPhone to steal its identity.

Microsoft Surface Duo

Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

That’s right, the iPhone Duo isn’t even the first folding mobile device to be called the Duo. Microsoft’s Surface Duo launched in 2020 and managed to get around the issues with early foldables like the Samsung Galaxy Fold, which debuted a year prior, by skipping flexible screen technology altogether. Microsoft’s Duo instead had a very visible hinge between its pair of 5.6-inch OLED screens. But software issues, a disappointing camera, and outdated specs when it launched all resulted in the Surface Duo’s failure, even with an improved Duo 2 that launched a year later.

Asus ROG Zephyrus Duo

Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

Trade shows are the birthplace of weird laptops, but sometimes the prototypes that often debut just to draw visitors to booths make it into the mainstream. Such was the case with the Asus ROG Zephyrus Duo, a powerful gaming laptop with excellent specs, a wildly expensive price tag, and a pair of 16-inch OLED screens that can be vertically stacked or placed side by side.

Asus ZenBook Pro Duo

Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

The ROG Zephyrus Duo wasn’t Asus’ first attempt at creating a dual-screen laptop, or the first time it named a laptop a Duo. The ZenBook Pro Duo predates it by several years with a slightly different design. Beneath the ZenBook Pro Duo’s primary 15.6-inch OLED screen was a secondary 14-inch display located above the laptop’s keyboard. With an ultrawide 32:9 aspect ratio and less color fidelity, the smaller screen was designed to be a place to dock productivity tools like Slack or Gmail so they were still readily accessible but less of a distraction while working (or gaming) on the primary display.

Pebble 2 Duo

The Pebble Appstore is filled with stuff, but you don’t need much of it. Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

After convincing Google to open-source the Pebble’s operating system last year, Eric Migicovsky, the creator of what was arguably one of the first truly successful and capable smartwatches, resurrected the wearable under a new company called Core Devices. The Pebble 2 Duo, one of the first smartwatches from Migicovsky’s new company, isn’t as capable as the Apple Watch or devices running Android’s Wear OS, but its careful balance of simplicity, functionality, and a budget-friendly price make it a tempting alternative.

iRobot Roomba Duo

Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

It’s still just a prototype and may never find its way into consumers’ homes, but at IFA 2026 in Berlin last week, iRobot debuted the bizarre Roomba Duo. The prototype includes a beefy mobile dock with clean and dirty water tanks and the most powerful floor-cleaning suction the company has ever made. To ensure it can clean all areas in your home, atop the Roomba Duo is a deployable garage with a smaller Roomba Plus 757 inside that can easily fit into tight spaces and beneath furniture.

Retroid Pocket Duo

Image: Retroid

Mere hours before the iPhone Duo made its debut, Retroid revealed the full design of its latest dual-screen handheld it’s been teasing. The Retroid Pocket Duo is a modernized version of the Nintendo DS with dual 120Hz OLED screens featuring a 16:9 aspect ratio on top and a 4:3 aspect ratio between its controls. Full specs and pricing aren’t confirmed yet, but the Pocket Duo features a symmetrical dual thumbstick design, two pairs of shoulder buttons, and a headphone jack.

Tech.title: Automattic CEO Matt Mullenweg placed on leave
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Matt Mullenweg, the CEO of WordPress.com owner Automattic, has been placed on a paid leave of absence, as reported earlier by 404 Media. In an internal message by the outlet, Mullenweg claims Automattic chief financial officer Mark Davies “conspired” with board members to place him on leave.

“They voted to put me on a paid leave of absence. I voted against that,” Mullenweg wrote, referring to Davies, along with Automattic board members Ann Dunwoody, Toni Schneider, and Sue Decker, 404 Media reports.

Automattic spokesperson Megan Fox confirmed the company’s decision in an emailed statement to The Verge. “Matt Mullenweg is currently on leave from Automattic,” Fox writes. “Mark Davies, Automattic’s CFO, will lead the company as interim CEO. The Board has full confidence in Mark’s leadership and in the team’s ability to execute against the company’s priorities.” Mullenweg will remain on Automattic’s board, 404 Media reports.

Related Why Matt Mullenweg went to war over WordPress

“Automattic’s board has decided to ask Matt to step away from his CEO role and take a leave of absence,” Schneider said on the company’s internal message board, according to 404 Media. “We have asked Mark Davies to assume the interim CEO role while Matt is out. We’ve worked closely with Mark over the years and we’re confident he will steer the ship well while Matt is away.”

Update, September 9th: Added Automattic’s statement.

Tech.title: It’s the year of smartphone price hikes
Tech.content:
Paying more for a new phone seems almost unavoidable after Apple’s event today. The new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max start at $1,199 and $1,299, respectively — a $100 price hike over their predecessors. You can’t dodge the price hike by opting for an older iPhone, either, because Apple raised prices on those by $100, too. And it’s not just Apple. This year, the $100 price hike has been a trend across the industry.

Google and Samsung followed the same formula as Apple when they each launched new phones over the past few months. The Pixel 11 starts at $899, up from $799 for last year’s Pixel 10. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra launched at $2,099, $100 more than the Galaxy Z Fold 7 it replaced.

You could try looking for a phone from a brand outside the big three, but the price hikes persist there, too. Sony’s new Xperia 10 VIII costs £150 more, and this year’s Moto Razr phones also cost $100 more than their predecessors, each offering little to no significant upgrades to go with their higher prices. Smartphone sales data shows that the market for phones under $100 may be on its way to completely disappearing.

The price hikes stem from ongoing component shortages, driven by AI data center buildouts, that could last years and aren’t showing any signs of letting up. RAM price hikes have been among the most severe. Nothing CEO Carl Pei said earlier this year that memory costs for the Nothing Phone 4A had doubled by the time it launched. Nearly every component that goes into new phones, and other tech, is also getting pricier. Qualcomm, which makes the processors that power many new phones, raised prices on its chips earlier this month.

Apple was fashionably late to raise its phone prices, like it was late to launch a foldable, potentially signaling that both trends are here to stay.

Tech.title: Suno releases its first AI music model made with record industry help
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Suno’s new v6 AI music model is its first made with support from the record industry. Suno’s Jack Brody told The Verge that v6 was “trained from the ground up, with a new set of data that does not include the same data that our previous models were trained on.” The data includes content licensed from partners Warner Music Group, BMG, and Believe, as well as “user data.” It’s unclear whether that means v6 training data is completely free of dubiously obtained content.

One of the big changes in v6 is that there are actually three different models: v6, v6-wild, and v6-mini. Mini is the model available for free to all. It’s focused on fast, resource-light creation. The results it spits out are simpler and often have more artifacts that betray it as the product of an AI prompt. v6-wild is supposed to be more unpredictable. Brody said that v6-wild is designed for “happy accidents and natural imperfections.” Though, in my limited testing, I found it hard to notice a difference between wild and bog-standard v6.

All three models are dramatically better at understanding genre. I recycled a handful of prompts that I used with older models calling for “hyperpop” or “krautrock” songs that missed the mark by a mile. v6, on the other hand, nailed all the superficial hallmarks of any genre I threw at it.

What it remains incapable of doing, however, is actually delivering on the “natural imperfections.” As with v5, my attempts to get off-key, out-of-tune, or slightly dissonant results failed every time. No matter how hard you push Suno’s v6, it remains incapable of making anything other than harmonic and rhythmic perfection. Tell it you want “monotone vocals” and “no drums,” and it straight-up ignores you (see below). Repeated demands for “out-of-tune piano played haphazardly, with no regard for key or rhythm” that was “fully out of tune with the rest of the song,” delivered nothing of the sort.

It does retain the unnatural imperfections of AI music, with vocals especially seeming to produce more of the harsh-edged artifacts common with AI models than v5 did.

Suno’s v6 also has some under-the-hood updates that can fundamentally change how people interact with it. Now users can edit parts of a song using plain language within a chat, and changing individual elements like a guitar line or a single lyric doesn’t require regenerating the entire track. v6 can also mash together multiple elements from your Suno library, combining outputs into new creations.

Prompts are also no longer limited to text descriptions. Suno v6 can create tracks based on images, video, or other audio.

Suno v6 starts rolling out today, and the company says it will eventually retire its previous models.

Tech.title: OpenAI’s sly mathematical breakthrough sends a chill through academia
Tech.content:
OpenAI’s announcement Tuesday that it has solved one of mathematics’ legendary Millennium Prize problems should have been a moment of triumph. The result is both an undeniable achievement and a striking demonstration of just how rapidly AI is transforming mathematics. But before it was even formally announced, the breakthrough had been complicated by the unusual circumstances that prompted OpenAI to pursue the problem: After hearing other researchers were making progress, it seems to have thrown its considerable resources into a last-minute effort to beat them to the punch. The ensuing controversy has surfaced allegations of scooping, spying, and flagrant violations of long-standing academic norms that researchers fear could have a chilling effect on the field.

As Abhishek Saha, a mathematics professor at Queen Mary University of London, explains it, OpenAI has engaged in the “kind of things that mathematicians will generally not do.”

In a blog post published Tuesday, OpenAI said it took one of its unreleased models just 88 hours to find a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, a thorny quandary concerning the movement of fluids. On account of the $1 million bounty available for whoever solves it, the problem is among mathematics’ most heavily researched, but it has nevertheless stumped human researchers for close to 90 years. OpenAI said its model solved the problem by focusing a swarm of roughly 10,000 AI agents powered by its internal model on the task and hailed the achievement as a “milestone.”

“If you don’t want me to be nice, then I don’t have to be nice.”

But the timing of the announcement has raised eyebrows. Just one day earlier, New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster published findings on a related problem with Levent Alpöge, a researcher at OpenAI’s archrival Anthropic (although Alpöge was not, here, working on behalf of his employer). Buckmaster said he contacted OpenAI after learning the company had become aware of their progress, to ask when it began working on the problem and what data its model had been trained on. The conversation, he said, quickly turned sour, with an OpenAI researcher asking him, “Why would you ruin your career?” when he said he would go public with what happened. When he asked why going public would ruin his career, Buckmaster said he received the following reply: “If you don’t want me to be nice, then I don’t have to be nice.” OpenAI urged Buckmaster to instead publish the work and credit OpenAI’s internal model, dropping Alpöge as coauthor.

Buckmaster said he asked OpenAI whether it had accessed his sessions on Codex, which he had used while tackling the problem, but that OpenAI grew increasingly evasive, even hostile, in its responses. In statements since, including the blog post announcing the result, OpenAI has flatly denied using any specific user data. “We (the researchers and the agents) did not see any of their work through any means until they released it publicly — in particular, no specific user data was accessed in order to solve this problem,” the company said.
