For Apple, that means demonstrations of its updated iOS 27 and WatchOS 27, announced at WWDC in June, running on the new hardware. But we’ve been using the OSes for a while and don’t have to rely on passing demos during the hardware announcement: Here’s our experience with the beta and what to know about iOS 27 before you start using it, as well as our take on the new Siri in WatchOS.

On the upside, the memetic reaction to the Duo brought out the creative snarkers of social media.

Check out our complete coverage of Apple’s September 2026 iPhone launch and play-by-play commentary on the event in our archived live blog.

Preorders for the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max and Watches start soon, and they ship a week later. The Duo is up for preorder starting and ships at the end of October. And don’t forget the cases.

John Ternus’ event debut as CEO

After the initial cinematic opening promoting the new variable-aperture camera on the iPhone 18 Pro and Max, Tim Cook delivered a clever, well-done segue into Ternus’ first Apple launch as CEO.

Ternus came up through product design, and it showed during the event. If memory serves, we were provided with more specific hardware information about chips, device builds, cooling systems and so on than in a lot of earlier launches. That might not appeal to everyone, but it’s the type of thing that keeps me awake as we head into the second hour of these things.

There also seemed to be a lot more video shot across many locations around LA. This was likely to drive home the association between Apple and “pro” cameras, but it made a very nice change from a lot of static Apple Park and heartwarming family video.

Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Perks of the iPhone Duo

In addition to being its first foldable, the iPhone Duo brought a much longed-for feature back into the…fold.

Touch ID disappeared along with the iPhone’s Home button; the last holdout was the iPhone SE, which was discontinued in 2022. Even if you’re fine with Face ID, having a fallback method for logging in and approving purchases makes sense, and it’s certainly more convenient than having to enter a PIN code.

But it replaced Face ID rather than supplementing it.

We had some in-chat mockery about the ability to register multiple fingerprints for the Touch ID, but as someone who occasionally has dirty, greasy or otherwise electronics-objectionable hands, being able to use a clean finger sounds nice to me.

I like the simultaneous front and rear camera feeds, which lets us use the outer screen flipped toward the subject. It reminds me of methods introduced to get pets’ attention in the early days of phones and before phones had cameras; I remember using an app that mimicked different cat vocalizations, though I really spent a lot of time wiggling my fingers above my head.

Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

I’m also a huge fan of the nano-texture screen layer, which comes from Apple’s desktop displays and MacBook Pros. With its excellent anti-reflective properties, it makes the most sense on a phone. I’d like to see it on more than just the Duo.

My biggest concern about the Duo was the size. The iPhone 16 Pro Max I currently have occasionally feels a hair too big to use comfortably single-handed. But the folded Duo is a bit narrower.

Variable aperture camera on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max

Apple made a big deal about its mechanical aperture for the new 48MP main cameras on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, and it is a breakthrough for a phone.

Electronic apertures used by most small cameras and phones simply limit or increase the amount of light the sensor absorbs. A mechanical, bladed aperture physically changes the shape of the hole, which controls the exposure, and that determines what bokeh and bright highlights look like, as well as how naturally the depth of field is rendered.

So introducing a mechanical aperture should allow for more control over the quality of the look (as opposed to the quality of the image) of photos and videos. That’s notable.

But don’t expect a truly pro-lens look, though. It’s a six-bladed diaphragm, which isn’t even as good as some entry-level kit lenses, and eight blades is more or less the minimum for really nice-looking, soft bokeh. In its video showing off the camera, there was very little of it.

There are four aperture settings, f1.48-f4, which highlight the constraint of the small phone sensor and module. At f4 on a sensor that small, you’re essentially at infinite focus, whereas on a larger sensor, you might get up to f16 or f32. The bottom line is you don’t have a lot of depth-of-field variability to play with for that variable aperture.

I’m reserving judgment on the underscreen front camera for the moment, though.

The new iPhone Duo folding phone folds like a book or a passport. CNET

Burgundy Pro, Night Sky Duo

I’m a fan of deep, rich colors for phones, though I usually just cram them into a case and never see them again. At least based on the livestream, the burgundy looks like a nice change from the aggressive orange of the previous generation (though I do like it), and the navy-black Night Sky seems a lovely choice after my MacBook Pro-favorite Space Gray.

A20 Pro

In a switch-up from previous years, Apple launched its new laptop and desktop chip, the M6, ahead of the A20 Pro, which powers all three iPhones. Usually, the mobile processor comes first, and the computer chip inherits its major architectural changes from that. In this case, the A20 has the same 2nm process size as the M6, down from 3nm in previous generations.

A smaller process size allows for a denser die, which ultimately lets you fit more circuitry in the same size package.

In this case, it has the doubled Neural Engine of the M6, used for the on-device AI processing, from 16 to 32 cores. That’s likely an essential upgrade for decent performance with on-device Siri AI.

There are also more cores, both GPU and CPU, plus a shift from performance cores to super cores, which run at higher clock speeds.

It also has the packaging with the memory placement optimized for better heat dissipation because smaller process sizes and denser dies can generate a lot more heat than bigger ones. That, plus the switch to super cores, required it.

Apple also dealt with heat by adding a vapor chamber and a dissipation layer beneath the screen.

Efficiencies introduced by the chip theoretically improve battery life, according to the company.

iPhone Handoff

If you’ve got two iPhones, iPhone Handoff will let you share a single phone number, designating one eSIM as primary and the other as a companion. It sounds interesting, and would let you leave one phone at home or, with careful scheduling, let someone else pick up (for say an elderly relative or young child), but it’s one of those features that could suffer if it’s badly implemented. I’m not sure if it lets you save on the cost of a second line, since you still need to have an active SIM in the companion phone. I also wish it could work with a non-Apple phone.

It’s also kind of confusing, since Apple already has Handoff for sharing tasks across devices.

Watch Ultra 4 improved sensors

More sensitive, frequently polling sensors are an unambiguous win if you use them in a watch, as long as they don’t overwhelm the rest of the system (which I have no reason to think they do here). Better sensors in the Watch Ultra 4 mean more accurate readings and more easily recognized outliers.

Audio Intelligence sound recognition

The watches’ Audio Intelligence can, among other things, decode sounds into visual notifications for the hearing impaired. That’s a nice accessibility perk.

An AI-driven feature that I could really use, though, is real-time accent compensation in AirPods; the AirPods 5 received some tweaks inherited from the higher-end model, including improved active noise canceling. Translation is nice, but I have a lot of trouble understanding people with heavy accents of all kinds — a big drawback when you live in New York City.

It’s not all sunshine, though. There are a lot of things I just say “nope” about.

Always on AI

On one hand, I like the idea of a watch that can catch parts of conversations I routinely miss (Live Rewind), either because I’ve gone space cadet or because my hearing glitched, as it tends to do. But I’m also one of those Luddites who don’t like or use devices with always-on listening or recording.

I’m not a big fan of Apple’s “it only stays on our servers” Private Cloud Compute privacy narrative, which resurfaced Wednesday, especially since Apple Intelligence/Siri AI can also use hybrid (local plus cloud) and third-party-integration models. Even if it stays on your device, you still never know until after the fact what has obtained access to your data — and it may now include a lot of health data.

It may also be because I don’t find a lot of the commonly trotted-out use cases very compelling. Apple Intelligence and the upcoming dedicated Siri app can do the things everybody’s on-device AI can, which seems to be writing email, summarizing calendars, travel scheduling, creating shopping lists, generating wallpaper and so on.

To me, a lot of the AI used by the Watch Series 12/Ultra Health and related apps and on similar devices, such as Stuff, goes too far into the micromanaging-your-life zone. If it’s going to give a Readiness score of my ability to handle activities, I’m going back to bed and pulling the covers up over my head, because my body tells me it’s not ready for anything.

The iPhone Duo’s drawbacks

While the Duo has the same 48MP main camera as the iPhone 18 Pro and Max, it doesn’t have the same mechanical aperture or high-end features. This is actually a notable negative that I’d weight heavily when considering the phone.

The other thing I suspect will make things awkward is the screen aspect ratios. Folded, each side is just shy of 3:2 — it’s 1.45 instead of 1.5 — which has become nonstandard. 1.5 is the aspect ratio of full-frame camera sensors, which conceivably makes it nice for displaying them, but neither video or games use it. Opened, the large screen has a 1.4 aspect ratio, which is even more novel.

As a result, Apple has had to alter iOS 27’s screen layout settings, both to take advantage of the extra screen real estate (good), as well as to change where controls appear so you can use them comfortably (bad). Apple spins these as “optimizations.” But it means inconsistent user experiences and interface conventions between the Duo and the rest of the iPhone line.

Additionally, it means that the operating system will have to adapt a lot of existing non-Apple apps and content on the fly to run right on the device. That’s always a bumpy road.

While the Duo supports the Apple Pencil, it’s just plain odd. It works with the original, USB-C Pencil rather than the more recent Bluetooth version, which seems inconvenient for carrying around and using — it requires physical pairing with the device and plugged-in charging. Plus, it’s not really designed to be used with the phone, since there’s no way to dock it. It seems like the least-effort solution possible to a stylus.

Tech.title: Where’s the iPhone 18? Here’s Why Apple Didn’t Reveal a New Standard iPhone
Tech.content:
The Apple Sept. 9 event revealed a new lineup of devices, including new Apple Watches, the new iPhone 18 Pro and the first foldable iPhone Duo, with one glaring omission: The standard iPhone 18 was nowhere to be seen. Apple didn’t comment on the absent phone, but rumors say it will come early in 2027 — and there are several reasons why the company would delay its entry-level model to next year.

It’s a pivotal moment for Apple. The event was the first for new CEO John Ternus, who started his role on Sept. 1, and we’re learning in real time whether he plans to stay the course his predecessor, Tim Cook, set or take Apple in a different direction. The foldable iPhone Duo is a bold foray into a niche subset of phones that sell a fraction of the flat iPhones that make up the bulk of Apple’s earnings every quarter.

But Apple has masterfully navigated expanding its lineup with a product that fits between its existing devices. The iPad was introduced to fit the niche between phones and laptops, and the foldable iPhone seems aimed at the gap between smartphone and iPad. In the background is the RAM shortage, making memory and components pricier than ever — and indeed, the iPhone 18 Pro got a $100 price bump over its predecessors, and the current iPhone 17 got more expensive as well.

The iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable, automatically adjusts its display to its orientation. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Amid those conditions, there are potential reasons for Apple to push its more basic phones to next year. The easiest assumption is that it will make the company more money, with the iPhone 18 Pro undoubtedly priced higher than the iPhone 18 — anyone eager to upgrade right now only has the more expensive phones to choose from.

It’s possible that Apple wants to space out its different models to better meet demand, possibly accounting for the production complications that arise with parts getting pricier from the RAM shortage. Or maybe they just want to give the folding iPhone Ultra the limelight. Nabila Popal, senior research director at the International Data Corporation, feels this move is brilliant strategy and surprisingly not spurred by the memory crises or supply side constraints.

“It allows Apple to spread its shipments more evenly throughout the year and simultaneously allow the spotlight on the premium models this fall — especially the new iPhone foldable,” Popal said.

Releasing the iPhone 18 later may not dim the unit’s sales, either: In the first half of 2024 and 2025, the baseline iPhones released the fall before still made up 16% of Apple’s total shipments in those periods, Popal said.

One thing is for sure: Apple is making big shifts with its Sept. 9 event; its tagline, Surprise and Shine, is telling.

The iPhone Air (mostly) survived my unhinged screen time. Jesse Orrall/Zooey Liao/CNET

A lineup shakeup: Bumping the iPhone 18 to 2027 and no iPhone Air 2

Last year’s iPhone Air was a marvel of engineering, following what seemed to be a new trend of slim phones after the Samsung Galaxy S25 Edge released earlier in 2025. But what had been a trend has disappeared in 2026, with no high-profile phones released whose main claim to fame is an extremely slender width.

Presumably, that’s because Apple and Samsung lost confidence after the very low sales for either slim phone. The IDC reported that the iPhone Air sold just 7.7 million units over four quarters, and the Galaxy S25 Edge sold 2.3 million over five quarters. Neither phone exceeded 1.8% of total phone sales for either brand across those time periods, IDC said. It’s always possible that Apple does release another iPhone Air later on.

But all the work to slim down conventional phones seemingly hasn’t gone to waste — it’s likely contributed to trimming the width on foldable phones. The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold is 5 millimeters when unfolded flat, but Samsung has gone even further, with the wide-format Galaxy Z Fold 8 down to 4.5mm and the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra reaching 4.1mm when fully unfolded. Considering that the Galaxy S25 Edge was 5.8mm, the company’s best foldables reaching nearly 2mm thinner is an achievement.

So Apple is relegating its iPhone 18 to 2027, likely earlier in the year. That’s around when it launched the iPhone 17E (in March 2026), so the company could be bundling its baseline iPhone 18 and likely even cheaper iPhone 18E in the same event. This would set a new schedule for Apple: more affordable phones earlier in spring, and then the next generation of its top-tier premium iPhones in its typical September launch window. This gives each lineup its own well-deserved attention and spotlight, IDC’s Popal noted.

“Apple is spreading its portfolio to a wider consumer demographic and giving consumers more choice, which is always good for business,” Popal said.

The iPhone 18 could be accompanied by an iPhone 18E and even an iPhone Air 2, Popal predicts. Even if these will conceivably be cheaper than the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo models, they’ll still likely be pricier than their predecessors — because Apple’s already made its older iPhones more expensive.

Typically, when Apple announces a new standard iPhone, the previous version is discounted $100 and sold for another year or so. Instead, it’s raised iPhone 17‘s price at $900, ripping the band-aid off now before the next baseline iPhone launches at a higher price. This could better distinguish it from the traditionally cheaper E-series phones like the $600 iPhone 17E, which appeal to a different, more budget-conscious segment of the market, Popal believes. Apple knows consumers will feel the sticker shock of the price increases, which is why it’s retained the iPhone 16 in its current lineup — though it, too, has gotten a bump back up to its original $800 price, a change from the discounted $700 it had been up until this morning.

That twice-per-year release schedule matches what Samsung has done for years, with an event in January for its premium flat phones and then another in August for its foldables. We’ll have to see whether Apple turns its spring showcase into an announcement event — perhaps bundling it with the Macs and home accessories that have sometimes simply launched via press release. It’s a brand new day for Apple, and anything is possible under Ternus. We’ll just have to see what’s in store for iPhones, folding and flat.

Tech.title: Apple Is Actually Talking About AI Now — a Lot
Tech.content:
It wasn’t that long ago that I wrote about how Apple’s reserved AI strategy is probably its best yet. By not hemorrhaging money on AI features and tools and by focusing on hardware rather than going all-in on AI, Apple positioned itself to come out ahead while its competitors beat and batter themselves to out-innovate each other in AI.

Yeah, that’s out the window now.

During its September “Surprise and shine” event on Wednesday at Apple Park in Cupertino, California, the company opened with a discussion of AI. Not merely “intelligence” or even “Apple Intelligence,” but artificial intelligence specifically. Clearly, Apple is not timid about tying AI use to its hardware improvements. Here are the AI and Siri AI features Apple went all-in on during the event.

Welcome to the vanguard of consumer AI, Apple.

AI as core architecture

New Apple CEO John Ternus doubled down on the company’s seemingly new AI strategy. “As we look ahead, we see a future filled with enormous discovery and transformation,” he said. “AI makes entirely new kinds of experiences possible. And AI can become even more useful when it brings together your life with the apps, services and products you use every day. And this means the product at the center of your experiences becomes even more essential.”

That product at the center of your AI universe? Well, it’s an iPhone.

He called the iPhone an “intelligent personal hub,” framing it as an intersection of advanced AI capabilities and an understanding of your personal context. The system will use that context, including your calendars, contacts, routines, messages and app activity, to provide more relevant assistance to you as you go through your day.

Apple acknowledged that personalization and customization come with data privacy concerns.

During the event, Ternus emphasized that Apple Intelligence defaults to on-device processing, so your data stays with you rather than some far-off server. When extra power and capability are required, your requests extend to Private Cloud Compute, with privacy protections that ensure no one (including Apple) can access your personal data.

AI on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max

According to Lilian Rincon, Apple VP of AI product marketing, the new iPhone 18 Pro “is built to take full advantage of all the capabilities of Apple Intelligence.” With it, you’ll get access to the latest Apple Foundation Models and, perhaps most notably, the most advanced Siri AI capabilities to date.

The new version of Siri “goes further than ever before” by combining personal context awareness, on-screen and in-app action, and a dedicated Siri app that you can customize. On your device, Siri can cross-reference, take action and synthesize your information across 300,000 native and third-party apps, like Mail, Messages, WhatsApp, Outlook and beyond. For instance, Siri can combine details from your emails and texts to create a summary of what you need to do to prepare for an upcoming family visit.

Visual intelligence is also expanding, as Siri can “see what you see.”

Using the camera or display, you can have Siri see what’s in front of you to ask questions or execute actions. With this feature, you could upload a photo and ask Siri which produce is best for a recipe your mom sent you via email. Siri can reference the email, your photo and its real-world knowledge to give you an answer and then add the ingredients to your grocery list in a separate app. (I wouldn’t be surprised if this feature eventually comes to AirPods or smart glasses.)

The iPhone 18 Pro line also comes with a new dedicated Siri app right on the home screen, featuring customization options such as Expressive Voices. Powered by a new on-device model, you can customize Siri’s voice pacing and expressivity across the Siri app, Safari and Maps. Want more inflection in Siri’s audio? You can simply adjust it on a sliding scale.

Apple appears to be all-in on integrating Apple Intelligence into every part of the iPhone, from writing and notifications to surfacing important information from phone calls and taking or editing photos.

Powered by a new on-device model, you can customize Siri’s voice pacing and expressivity. Screenshot by CNET/Apple

Beyond the iPhone

Apple Intelligence is also coming baked into other hardware beyond the iPhone.

The new AirPods 5 let you access Siri hands-free, giving you access to all of Siri’s knowledge and capabilities without touching the device. AirPods 5 also come with built-in active noise cancellation and Live Translation to translate between different languages in real-time conversations.

The latest Apple Watch (Series 12 and Ultra 4) is rolling out with an Audio Intelligence feature that recaps conversations for you, along with a slew of AI health features to deliver a deeper understanding of your health metrics. Apple Intelligence brings summaries of your health trends, recommendations for recovery and a revamped health app – all of which you can read about in depth here.

Expanded language support

Apple Intelligence comes out in 16 supported languages with OS releases coming this month, including English, French, Spanish, German, Italian and Chinese (though Apple Intelligence will not be available in China).

Siri AI beta launches in English, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish coming in October.

Tech.title: We Scoured IFA 2026 to Find the Weirdest Tech. You Won’t Believe What We Saw
Tech.content:
If today’s Apple event and the new foldable iPhone Duo felt a bit too normal for you (we have seen lots of folding phones before), then I’ve got great news. CNET’s team just spent the last week playing with thousands of new tech innovations at the enormous IFA expo in Berlin.

We found beds that make soundwaves, laptops made to leave in the sun, advanced AI sex dolls and overall a lot of things that made us go, “….Huh.” Now I’m sharing them with you, from surprisingly clever gadgets to devices that made even seasoned tech reporters scratch their heads. Here’s what we found, and if we think it’s too weird to work in the real world.

Govee’s mood-reading skylight

Govee’s giant mood light was on display at IFA. David Watsky/CNET

Govee has long been at the forefront of strange home lighting creations, from literal curtains of light to spread across your garage to table lamps that look more like alien artifacts. Now Govee is showing off one of its oddest products yet: a dome-like ceiling light designed to mimic the sky and be “mood-responsive.”

In this case, mood-responsive means you can use Govee’s AI to talk about your mood or how you’re feeling, and the Govee app will suggest ceiling light color schemes to match. But the light can also create a specific blue wavelength designed to evoke blue skies and natural daylight.

Too weird to work? Not as weird as you may think. I’ve tested Govee’s AI before, and you really can generate lighting patterns based on your mood or random musings. But Govee already has so many lighting scenes in its app that I didn’t find it very practical — though definitely fun. I wonder how well it will work with a full ceiling light.

A gigantic tofu maker

The Nuvell plant protein maker is about the size of an espresso machine. David Watsky/CNET

If your two problems are not eating enough plant protein and having too much counter space, the Nuvell is here. This massive bean cooker and compressor is the size of an espresso machine and churns out blocks of tofu in as little as 30 minutes. It can make other vegan proteins depending on the legume you stick inside.

Plant protein made in the comfort of your kitchen. David Watsky/CNET

I asked the rep on duty whether the Nuvell could make cheese if you poured cow’s milk in. She claimed it could, but didn’t seem too confident.

Too weird to work? While it wasn’t operational at IFA, we assume the Nuvell does what it’s supposed to, since turning soybeans into tofu isn’t rocket science. The real question is whether it’s worth the space on your counter for this one-trick pony of a kitchen appliance.

A toothbrush with a built-in camera

A camera on your toothbrush is definitely a design choice. Dyson

Unless you’re a dentist, you probably don’t want a closer look at your teeth — but one intrepid brand came to IFA bearing a toothbrush that gets personal by using a built-in camera.

The Dyson Camerajet uses a camera with “Gap Optical Targeting.” Fortunately, you don’t have to personally review the 28 images per second the camera can take. Instead, an AI analyzes it for you and targets interdental gaps. From what we can tell, you can then aim the toothbrush’s jet of water at tooth gaps to make sure they get extra clean.

If you do want to play dentist like this, it’ll cost a sweet $500 for the advance.

Too weird to work? I’m calling this one too weird for sure. Price aside, you have to stand with your toothbrush in hand while holding your phone in the other to look at an enormous close-up of your teeth on the screen, then simultaneously brush and use the water flosser at the right angles to hit what look like gaps. The whole thing appears entirely unnecessary if you simply practice good brushing and flossing.

A tiny robot vacuum… for your bed

Yep — a whole robot vacuum, just for the bed. Creatulize

Creatulize came to IFA to show off the smallest robot vacuum in all of Berlin. The X1 Pro is the brand’s second-gen bed robot vacuum, designed to clean your bedding and mattress.

Using precision mode, the vac moves slowly and steadily across a mattress, sucking up dust, mites, hair and whatever else lurks. It can clean a king-size in about 20 minutes and has an easy-to-empty debris canister. Special sensors keep it from tumbling off the bed. When it hits an edge, it stops, turns and keeps on keepin’ on.

That’s one itty-bitty robot vac. David Watsky/CNET

Too weird to work? Mattress vacuums are becoming a thing, based on the idea that dirty mattresses exacerbate allergies. Nobody wants a dusty mattress, but whether or not you need a dedicated vacuum for it is up for debate. We’ll be testing the X1 Pro to find out.

An air conditioner trained to follow you

Midea’s new voice-controlled air conditioner follows you around the room with a stream of cool. David Watsky/CNET

One of the highlights we saw – and felt – was an air conditioner unit that sends custom cool air to you wherever you are. Midea’s new system uses spatial imaging and sensors to track your position in the room and deliver a stream of cool air your way. That means a cooler you and less energy wasted.

Midea’s smart AC works with the brand’s other air-quality appliances, including the humidifier. The two work in harmony through Midea’s smart sync to keep your home’s air at your desired temperature and humidity, no matter what Mother Nature has planned.

It’s also voice-activated, so you can turn it on or off, or activate the “mmWave sensor system” without getting up or even opening your phone.

Too weird to work? While the AC wasn’t officially up and running at IFA, Dyson launched a similar freestanding fan and air purifier that tracks humans in the room and spits fresh, cool air their way. We’re still testing that one in our lab, but would be surprised if the technology doesn’t live up to at least some of its promise.

SwitchBot’s AI shirt pin, the MindClip

SwitchBot’s AI clip sort of… spies on everyone around you. SwitchBot

If you thought AI was already in everything, just wait: SwitchBot is announcing the launch of its AI shirt device, the MindClip, at IFA. It’s made to clip onto your shirt pocket, collar, nearby strap or even belt. Once in place, it, well, essentially listens to everything that happens within a 3-meter radius for up to 20 hours and saves it for you.

The MindClip can recognize people by their voices and summarize conversations or events, ostensibly to help you with planning after a busy day. As far as AI goes, it’s no spying Meta glasses, but it is fairly invasive, especially for strangers you may be chatting with.

Too weird to work? This isn’t the first time we’ve seen an AI pin, although it is the smallest and least distracting version I’ve spotted. The problem is that none of them really took off, and some companies even pivoted to an entirely different product. So yes, it’s too weird to work for now, but maybe the rumored AI capabilities in Apple’s AirPods will be an exception.

The AI-powered companion doll from Lovense

Lovense’s updated AI companion doll also made an appearance at IFA. Lovense

Singaporean intimacy and sex toy company Lovense has brought the latest version of its AI “companion doll” to IFA, aiming to make it more lifelike than ever before. In addition to talking, remembering past facts and adjusting its personality, the silicone doll can blink, smile and look when called by its custom name. Users can also chat with the doll at a distance via a phone app and set up roleplay scenarios, if they prefer.

Too weird to work? Yes, the age of AI sex dolls is here. But it’s such an eclectic — and expensive (between $4,000 and $8,000) — proposition, this one is only for those with very specific tastes and a, ahh, particular relationship with AI. For others, Lovense also debuted several more conventional, AI-free toys.

A Eufy sensor that asks if you fell down

Eufy’s new sensor has a very, very specific purpose in the home. Eufy

When today’s home sensors can do nearly anything from recognizing when dogs bark to knowing when someone is tampering with a mailbox, it may sound strange to make a sensor specifically to say, “Oops, it looks like you fell down!” But that’s just what Anker’s Eufy brand has done.

There’s method behind this madness. The wall sensor uses a combo of algorithms and presence sensing with mmWave technology, no cameras necessary. It’s made to help those aging in place or living in rest homes without creating privacy concerns. The sensor even supports two-way audio, so family members or nurses can check in if they get an alert about a potential fall.

Quick note: As Anker consolidates its brand names, Eufy products are staying with us, but the Eufy name may not be around forever, so keep that in mind when shopping.

Too weird to work? In this case, not at all. I’ve already seen mmWave technology tap into Wi-Fi signals to help those aging in place, although Eufy’s sensor is the first I’ve seen that focuses on falls and enables two-way audio for a quick checkup. It’s a strong use of the technology.

A smartphone for your pet

The Petphone certainly makes a lot of claims about AI pet powers. Petpogo

Ucloudlink has brought the newest version of its award-winning PetPhone to IFA this year, showing a world where cats and dogs have their own smartphone, too. Sort of.

The Petpogo PetPhone is technically a smart pet collar, and we’ve reviewed many of those. But this version comes with two-way audio to talk to your pet with an app and AI features that interpret behavior and motion so pets can theoretically initiate a call themselves, as well as emotion analysis of barks, meows and other actions. It also supports more traditional capabilities like tracking and geofencing, and it alerts pet parents to out-of-routine behaviors.

Too weird to work? No AI features can accurately interpret specific barks or meows into moods and feelings. That’s (currently) nonsense. And trying to get your pet to “call” you with specific behaviors sounds dubious at best. So most of the innovations here are too weird, but the underlying collar functionality looks usable.

These headphones that turn into a Bluetooth speaker

TDM’s Bluetooth speaker headphone hybrid is confusing. TDM

TDM is showing off its unique Neo headphones, with a literal twist. In normal mode, they look like a typical pair of wireless headphones. But twist and collapse the earcups, and they form into a small Bluetooth speaker with up to 8 hours of music playback. The dual-device comes with an aux port, a USB-C charging port and a carrying case.

Too weird to work? When was the last time you saw someone with headphones and thought, “What a pleasant, private music experience that person is having, I wish there was a way for them to share it with all the people nearby?” Nope. No one likes it when you play music out loud in public spaces, especially when the same device could let you listen privately. I’m calling these headphones too weird to work.

A soundwave-creating smart bed

Amada’s acoustic mattress claims many different applications. Amada

Amada brought a fascinating mattress to IFA called the Soundwave Smart Mattress. Yes, it connects to a phone app. And yes, it really does produce sound waves or at least a “vibroacoustic experience” with vibration modes for presleep relaxation, meditation, focus and recharging. I’m not sure how vibration is supposed to help with those things, but CNET health expert Anna Gragert told me vibration therapy does have applications for recovery and disease treatment. The bed is made of polyurethane foam and polyester fabric, with a four-pin power connector.

Too weird to work? Well, Magic Fingers did have their day in hotel rooms across the US, but that day ended pretty fast. I don’t know if a bed with good vibrations is what the average home is looking for, but if you’ve tried it and it works for you, this could be a shakingly good upgrade.

This 8-pound laptop wants to photosynthesize

Oukitel covered the RG14-P’s lid in solar panels because, apparently, outlets are optional now. Oukitel

Normally, leaving a laptop baking in direct sunlight is a terrible idea. The Oukitel RG14-P treats it like a charging strategy instead. Nearly the entire back of its display is covered in solar panels, which Oukitel says can recharge its 95-watt-hour battery to 50% in about 6 hours under ideal sunlight.

The rugged Windows laptop also has a 14.1-inch touchscreen and a dual-battery system with a removable pack. It weighs roughly 8.1 pounds, however, so carrying it into the wilderness may require the sort of person who was already shopping for a solar-powered industrial laptop.

Too weird to work? Not really. Six hours of perfect sunlight for half a charge won’t replace a wall outlet, but it could keep the laptop alive during fieldwork or an off-grid emergency. It’s less “solar MacBook” and more computer for someone whose office occasionally lacks walls.
